Sunshine and workweek showers
Dry and cool weather for the weekend but showers will return this week
Sunshine and workweek showers
Dry and cool weather for the weekend but showers will return this week
Saturday will be a beautiful start to the weekend. Skies will stay clear and dry through this evening, and temperatures will reach the mid to upper 50s. The cool temperatures, clear skies, and calm winds will create favorable conditions for frost formation. A Frost Advisory has been issued for coastal Maine from Sunday 2 a.m. to Sunday 8 a.m., and a freeze warning sits over interior Cumberland and Androscoggin counties.
After the sun comes up, we have another comfortable fall day on Sunday with highs in the low to mid 60s. Cloud cover will increase ahead of the remnants of Hurricane Isaias, which will bring moisture and rain chances for coastal Maine Sunday night into Monday morning.
The next round of rain will arrive overnight on Monday and throughout the day on Tuesday. Temperatures will dip back down into the high 50s, setting a trend for more seasonable temperatures through the week.

title: 12-year-old girl dies after drinking Twix milkshake, reports say
text:
(Gray News) - A 12-year-old girl died after drinking a Twix milkshake, according to multiple reports.
On Thursday, Oct. 8, an investigation into the death of Mia Shay St Hilaire at Inner South London Coroner’s Court concluded that she suffered a severe allergic reaction after drinking a milkshake at the Pop Inn Cafe in London, the BBC reported.
She visited the cafe with her aunt and sister in London in August 2023.
CCTV evidence captured the moment cafe operator Baris Yucel made the drink in a blender that hadn’t been washed after its previous use.
She said Mia, who had a hazelnut allergy, had consumed some of a Twix milkshake “which had been cross-contaminated with hazelnut residue from a Kinder Bueno milkshake previously prepared in the same unwashed blender.
She developed rapidly progressing anaphylaxis and later collapsed at her aunt’s home.
She was taken to a hospital where she later died.
In a case brought by Southwark Council, the café’s food business operator, Baris Yucel, pleaded guilty to six charges.
Southwark Council said in a release that the charges included not making allergen advice available or visible to consumers, failing to manage allergen contamination during the food production process, and serving food that contained an allergenic ingredient that was not supposed to be present.

title: 17-year-old is living in hospitals with nowhere else to go, lawyer says
text:
WATERTOWN, New York (WWNY/Gray News) - A 17-year-old has been living in North Country hospitals since August because the system allegedly has nowhere else for her to go.
“This is a hard situation to be in for everybody,” Rebecca Simser, the teen’s lawyer, said.
Living without a plan
A stay-away order was issued in June because of the teen’s reported behavior problems that barred her from returning to her caregiver’s home.
Since then, Simser said the 17-year-old has moved through four homes and four North Country facilities.
“I have a family offense petition involving a minor alleged perpetrator, and so we are trying to protect the victim, which is our job, but we also need to be doing what’s in the best interest of the child,” Simser said.
According to Simser, her client has been living in hospitals since the end of August, with nowhere to go and no safety plans.
“She’s not in school at this point. I don’t know if she’s getting medication. She’s definitely not getting one-on-one mental health treatment because she’s discharged and just sitting in an ER bed,” Simser said.
No qualifying treatment options
Simser said her client doesn’t qualify for voluntary or involuntary inpatient treatment.
With no other options, Simser wants the court to declare her client “destitute” — legally homeless, with no income or support.
That status would mean the Department of Social Services would take custody of the teen.
Jefferson County’s Department of Social Services would have to file a petition, but Simser said she’s been told the agency won’t.
“I’m not saying that my client is blameless in all of this, but she’s not being afforded any protections that I can tell at this point,” Simser said.
A statewide issue
State numbers show this is a growing issue statewide.
Last year, over the course of three months, 52 children in New York experienced delayed discharge from the hospital or emergency room due to lack of available care or housing options, resulting in more than 5,100 days of medically unnecessary inpatient hospitalization.
“My hope is that if the system worked the way it was supposed to work, we could protect the victim, but we could also get services and help for my client and make sure that she wasn’t suffering and displaced, and lacking while she transitioned into a more independent form of living away from the victim,” Simser said.
Simser noted that she doesn’t fault any of the facilities.
The Department of Social Services was unable to comment on this specific case.

title: Philadelphia police officer killed, another injured after responding to reports of man with a gun
text:
(AP) - Authorities are charging Eric Lewis, 35, with homicide for the alleged killing of a police officer early Saturday morning, according to Philadelphia District Attorney Larry Krasner.
Shane Seiber, 40, was shot and killed in west Philadelphia after responding to a report of a man with a gun, police said. An officer who was with him was also shot.
Seiber, a 10-year veteran of the Philadelphia Police Department, and the other officer were transported to Penn Presbyterian Medical Center and underwent surgery, according to Police Commissioner Kevin Bethel. The surviving officer, who was shot 12 times, is in stable condition, Bethel said.
Along with charges for Seiber’s death, Lewis is facing a host of others, including attempted homicide, for allegedly shooting the officer and shooting at nine other officers who responded to the scene, Krasner said. None of those nine were injured.
Lewis is being held without bail and will be arraigned soon, Krasner said. Lewis was previously convicted of criminal offenses including assault, theft and carrying a firearm publicly, according to court records.
Gov. Josh Shapiro said he ordered flags to fly at half-staff for Seiber, who is survived by his wife and two children — a 7-year-old boy and a 3-year-old girl.
“This is a brutal, senseless, horrific killing,” Krasner said.

title: Maranacook golf holds off Winthrop for Class C title
text:
VASSALBORO — Maranacook senior Jack Fontaine has come through in plenty of big moments on the basketball court.
Saturday, he came through on the golf course.
Fontaine shot a 1-over 73 to take the Class C individual boys title and help the Black Bears win the team title on the Arrowhead course at Natanis Golf Course.
“It feels amazing. I did not expect this,” said Fontaine. “It’s just a hobby, really. I just play for fun.”
Maranacook finished with a score of 317 to beat Winthrop by one shot. It’ i’s the third state title for the Black Bears, who also won in 2022 and 2024. Calais (328), Dexter (332) and Houlton (336) rounded out the top five.
“This year was definitely different,” said Maranacook coach Ryan Meserve. “We didn’t play as well as we wanted to all throughout the (regular) season. We knew that if we could just get through one (good) day, we’ve got guys who have won state championships before … The team is super resilient, like each other as a team. We knew we needed just one good day.”
Winthrop’s Kaydence Allarie shot 83 to win the Class C girls title. Mattanawcook Academy’s Skylar Bard was second with a 90.
“It feels really good,” said Allarie, a junior. “I definitely knew that I could do it. I just needed to stay consistent and play my game.”
In addition to Fontaine’s round, Grady Hreben shot 79, Josh Herzing carded an 80 and Sam Dunton had an 85 for Maranacook.
Drew Mertzel, who won medalist honors last year, led Winthrop with a 76. Also for the Ramblers, Sam Corgan shot 79 and Lincoln MacArthur finished with an 80.
Fontaine has only played competitive golf for three years and wasn’t thinking about winning the title entering play Saturday. He had birdies on the fourth, 12th and 13th holes.
“Today is just (the mindset) of you versus you,” Fontaine said. “You’re competing against yourself.”
Ryan Farnsworth of Dexter was the boys runner-up with a 74. Mertzel, Beckett Peabody of Houlton and Chris Johnson of Kents Hill tied for third at 76.
Allaire said she struggled on the back nine, but her putting helped her out.
“The whole front nine, I felt pretty good about my game,” Allarie said. “I think that definitely helped, because I got my numbers a little lower.”

title: Democrats appear to be our only hope on healthcare
text:
I think I speak for many as I age, requiring more encounters with our healthcare system.
I used to speak of our need for a single-payer healthcare system in the U.S. I reminded people I knew about the fact that we are the only industrialized nation in the world that doesn’t provide healthcare for its citizens. I worked to encourage my political representatives to make the changes needed to bring about that end. Was it all for nothing? Now that I truly need healthcare, where am I?
Maine hospitals are cutting departments or closing down for various reasons — Medicaid cuts, nurse shortages, etc. Nursing homes, birthing centers and even local medical practices, especially in our more rural areas, are suffering as well. We read about this crisis almost every day in our newspapers. And we hear many explanations. OK, now what?
I have friends who have looked for solutions — from seeking alternative medicine locally to traveling to specialized treatment centers in other states and even to using eye surgeries, dental care and joint replacement in other countries. I’m not likely to do any of those things. I’m simply hoping for my government to provide the healthcare we all need.
One thing I do know — the government we have now won’t come to my aid. I believe the only hope for the changes we need will come under a government led by Democrats.
Betsy Braunhut
Deer Isle

title: 2 top Washington County finance officials resign, citing hostile work environment
text:
MACHIAS — Washington County’s provisional Treasurer Grace Falzarano and Finance Manager Sondra Small have resigned, citing a hostile work environment, poor communication within the finance department and loss of what had been a team environment.
Falzarano submitted her resignation to county commissioners Sept. 28, but they did not announce it until Thursday’s regular meeting. Her resignation took effect Friday.
Small, who had worked for the county since 2017 as finance manager and deputy treasurer, resigned as deputy treasurer in a Sept. 28 letter to commissioners but remained finance manager.
On Thursday, Small resigned as finance manager, effective Oct. 22, and said she would work through her two-week notice.
Falzarano became provisional treasurer in September 2025 after longtime elected Treasurer Jill Holmes resigned.
Holmes resigned amid a financial crisis last year that brought the county close to $8 million in debt. County officials said at the time that she transferred $400,000 in two transactions from a fund designated for services in the unorganized territory to the county’s regular budget, masking the debt.
Holmes had served as the county’s elected treasurer since 1999. She cited personal reasons for her departure.
Since Holmes resigned, the county has uncovered multiple instances of long-standing financial mismanagement, but found no evidence that anyone misused taxpayer money.
In her letter of resignation, Falzarano said she had completed the specific work she was brought in to do for Washington County: help move the county’s finances through the 2025 crisis and into 2026.
“In light of current hostile working conditions,” she wrote, “I feel it is the right time to step down.”
Falzarano had offered to leave office before Oct. 9 if commissioners requested, and said she had enjoyed working with several staff members in the county building and appreciated “the collaborative spirit demonstrated by several of the commissioners.”
In Small’s Sept. 28 resignation letter, she said giving up her deputy treasurer duties would narrow her daily focus, allowing her to “dedicate my attention to the many other daily tasks on my plate.”
In her Oct. 8 letter, Small resigned as finance manager, saying that “historically, this (finance) office operated as a true team where we all routinely took on any job that needed to be done without question, regardless of whether it fell within our official job descriptions.”
She wrote that “that team environment no longer exists.”
“Communication has failed within the office and has made it extremely difficult to stay informed and effectively complete my duties,” Small wrote, adding that “continuing in this position is no longer possible.”
After the resignations, the finance office’s remaining employees were Finance Director Jenny Windsor, who began working for the county in June, and Megan Huffman, who has worked for the county since at least 2023.
Washington County Commission Chairman David Burns said commissioners consulted the county attorney during an executive session before the regular meeting about how to meet the county’s banking and financial obligations without a treasurer or deputy treasurer.
The commission voted unanimously to authorize Windsor and Commissioner Courtney Hammond to sign checks for all county bank accounts and make online bank transfers.
“We are doing our best here to make sure that we meet all the statutory and Washington County needs in order to keep things moving forward in the face of a couple of vacations,” Burns said.
Commissioners also consulted the attorney about appointing a provisional treasurer effective Friday. They appointed Windsor to the position until at least Election Day, which is Nov. 3.
The county has discussed changing the treasurer’s position from elected to appointed. No one is running for treasurer this year, so Burns said Windsor’s provisional appointment may be moot after the election.
After commissioners approved Windsor’s appointment, Commissioner Billy Howard said he deeply regretted Small’s and Falzarano’s resignations. He said both had played important roles in helping the county through last year’s serious financial difficulties.
“People say we’re righting the ship now,” Howard said, “but we had one foot on the ship and one on the boat, one foot in a lifeboat. That’s how close we were to going under.”
Howard called the work to adopt better accounting practices and reorganize budgets “serious stuff.”
He said, “I can’t applaud them enough for their help to get us through this past year.”
Burns agreed that their departure was a loss.
“But we will move ahead and we’ll find new people,” he said, “so you know those that are on board right now are going to help us through this transition. We’re thankful for that.”
Hammond extended the nautical analogy, saying the finance department faced a major workload last year.
“It was all hands on deck,” he said. “That’s for sure.”
In other matters, the commission adopted two policies. One outlines communication procedures, including public information and intergovernmental coordination. The other establishes interim financial procedures and addresses audit findings and financial priorities outlined in the 2022 and 2023 audits.
Those priorities include recording all financial transactions in a general ledger by individual fund, reconciling bank accounts monthly, keeping supporting documents for bank transfers, tracking grant applications and spending and monitoring cash flow.
Commissioners approved an early $1.5 million payment toward the 2026 tax anticipation note, or TAN, to save on interest.
Windsor said the county has enough cash to make the payment, even though it has yet to receive $5.4 million in tax revenue from municipalities.
She also said employee benefits spending could exceed the budget by as much as $500,000 by year’s end, adding to overtime overruns that commissioners were already tracking.
If the benefits overrun materializes, the county may need to borrow more through the 2026 TAN. Windsor said she was comfortable making the $1.5 million payment now.
Commissioners also discussed whether to weigh in on proposed data center projects. None supported the current proposal for an underwater data center in Eastport, but they said they might support a land-based project.
Hammond said a data center in the unorganized territory was more realistic than one in an organized municipality and suggested the commission consider a resolve on the issue at its November meeting.
This story was originally published by The Maine Monitor, a nonprofit and nonpartisan news organization. To get regular coverage from The Monitor, sign up for a free Monitor newsletter here.

title: Matt Dunlap’s honesty and grit is just what we need
text:
Not interested in dull, boring candidates? Frankly, I’m exhausted by waking up every morning with another shocking presidential declaration that makes my skin crawl. Stop the emotional whiplash coming from Washington, D.C.
Give me old fashioned Maine honesty, a working-class advocate, a focus on economic fairness, mixed with understated Down East humor. Washington could use some slow-paced storytelling that reflects the gritty, independent spirit of Maine focused on making lives better.
Give me Matt Dunlap, a “fur trapper, publishing editor, radio talk-show host, cook, waiter and bartender.” With hard work, he became a trusted Maine legislator, secretary of state, and now an auditor who lives year-round in Maine — unlike his opponent.
I will joyfully vote for Matt Dunlap for U.S. Congress. 
Carole Beal
Blue Hill

title: Despite weakening, Isaias still poses threat to Southeast
text:
CRESTVIEW, Fla. (WEAR) — Isaias is now a post-tropical storm but remains a threat as it drenches the Southeast.
The National Hurricane Center said in its final advisory that the storm’s sustained winds fell to 35 miles per hour.
The storm made landfall on Florida’s Panhandle on Friday, Oct. 9, as a Category 2 hurricane.
At least four storm-related deaths have been reported, two in Florida and two in Alabama.
Hundreds of thousands of customers are without power across the Southeast.
Homes and businesses were damaged across the region, with the roof of at least one gas station getting shredded to pieces.
Much of the Southeast is still at risk of flash flooding as the storm continues to weaken.
The area will also experience strong wind gusts as well as the threat of spin-up tornadoes.

title: Bruins rout Flyers for 2nd straight win
text:
BOSTON — Fraser Minten had a goal and two assists, Pavel Zacha scored his first goal of the season and the Boston Bruins beat the struggling Philadelphia Flyers 5-1 on Saturday.
Mason Lohrei, Marat Khusnutdinov and Casey Mittelstadt also scored for Boston (4-2), which won its second straight game.
Starting for the fifth time in the Bruins’ first six games, Jeremy Swayman faced just three shots in the opening 30 minutes and finished with 14 saves. His bid for his second shutout of the season was spoiled when Porter Martone got a power-play goal 6:32 into the final period. Swayman earned his 136th win, tying Andy Moog for eighth on Boston’s all-time list.
Dan Vladar made 27 saves for the Flyers (0-4-2), who are the Eastern Conference’s only winless team.
Top Boston defenseman Charlie McAvoy served the final game of his six-game suspension to start the season from a slashing incident during last spring’s playoffs.
Coming off a lopsided win over Utah at home on Thursday, the Bruins jumped ahead on Zacha’s goal 12:21 into the opening period when he took a backhand pass from David Pastrnak in the slot and fired a wrister that broke into the net off Vladar’s right pad.
Following a tough loss at Ottawa on Thursday, the Flyers were outshot 19-3 in the opening 30 minutes and 22-8 through two periods.
Lohrei beat Vladar over his shoulder with a wrister with 2:48 left in the second, making it 2-0.
Khusnutdinov scored off a nice feed from Minton just under two minutes into the third.
Flyers winger Michael Bunting played his second game after signing as a free agent this week.
Up next
Flyers: Host the Carolina Hurricanes on Sunday night.
Bruins: Visit the San Jose Sharks on Tuesday night, the first of a four-game road trip.

title: The Latest: Isaias weakens after making landfall as Category 2 hurricane
text:
Isaias weakened quickly after making landfall on the U.S. Gulf Coast near Destin, Florida, as a Category 2 hurricane Friday evening. Its powerful winds left hundreds of thousands of people in Alabama and the Florida Panhandle without power early Saturday. It was the first hurricane of the Atlantic season.
Here’s the latest:
Storm surge warnings are discontinued, but high winds remain a threat
That is according to Robbie Berg, a warning coordination meteorologist with the National Hurricane Center in Miami.
“All tropical storm surge warnings have been discontinued as of this morning, but there are still high wind warnings for portions of the Southeast,” Berg said. “So even though it has become post-tropical, it still does remain a wind threat, as well as a heavy rainfall threat. We could see some areas of significant flash flooding over the next couple of days.”
Hurricane Simon strengthens as it approaches Mexico
Simon has strengthened into a powerful Category 4 hurricane as it barrels toward Mexico’s coast.
The National Hurricane Center in Miami said early Saturday Simon’s maximum sustained winds increased to 150 mph (240 kph). A storm of that strength or greater is considered a major hurricane. Simon could bring as much as 10 to 20 inches (25-50 cm) of rain over parts of southwestern Mexico, with some areas receiving up to 30 inches, the center said.
The bulletin also urged residents to take immediate action to prepare, saying the hurricane will make landfall early Sunday, but tropical storm-strength winds could arrive much sooner.
Simon is expected to bring heavy rainfall to parts of southwestern Mexico, possibly concentrated along Jalisco’s coast and in parts of Michoacan, Colima and Nayarit.
Isaias weakens overnight but is still considered a flood threat
Isaias weakened overnight and was no longer considered a hurricane, but flash flooding threats and the potential for tornadoes persisted Saturday as the storm moved inland across Alabama.
The storm, now considered a post-tropical cyclone, made landfall Friday as a Category 2 hurricane, then quickly moved north through Alabama as its wind speeds dropped sharply to 35 mph (55 kph). But the possibility of life-threatening storm surges still loomed for parts of the Florida Panhandle.
Hundreds of thousands of customers are without power
Parts of southern Alabama also were flooded, with officials in Mobile reporting downed trees and power lines. Roads in Houston County, which is in the southeastern corner of the state, were closed because of similar conditions.
More than 911,000 customers in Florida, Alabama and Georgia were without power early Saturday, according to poweroutage.com.
One Floridian describes intense winds, impassable roads
Tim Mowry rode out the storm from his home in Pensacola, Florida. He says the wind was so intense it sounded like a train whistle as it whipped through a crack on his patio door.
He said overall the storm wasn’t as bad as he expected. He had standing water in his backyard and parts of a fence were ripped down. He also lost power but was able to rely on a generator. Mowry said his son, who lives nearby, was unable to drive to Mowry’s house due to downed trees and power lines blocking the roads.
“As far as Pensacola-wise we really got fortunate,” Mowry said.
Pensacola mayor says airport sustained some damage
Pensacola Mayor D.C. Reeves said on his Facebook page that the airport “took some damage.” Some power was out downtown, he said, and there were trees and power lines down in some areas.
Meanwhile, strong winds blew the roof off a hotel in the city.
Gov. Ron DeSantis warns that flooding threat persists in the wake of Isaias
Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis says there were no confirmed reports of fatalities from Isaias and that all state-owned bridges and major thoroughfares in the state are now open.
DeSantis warned that flooding dangers persist, especially in areas far east of the storm where it will continue raining.
“The risk of flooding is still high,” DeSantis said. “Sometimes these things happen a day or two days after the storm goes through. So the flooding story is not over.”

title: Sen. Angus King calls agreement with Russia 'fraud'

Sen. Angus King, I-Maine, is calling President Trump's new agreement with Russia "fraud."
On Friday, President Trump announced a diesel deal with Russia in an effort to lower fuel prices ahead of the midterm elections. He said Russia agreed to immediately supply over 300,000 tons of diesel "to the American and Global Marketplace," with 500,000 tons to follow in November, and another 1 million tons "immediately thereafter."
In a statement, Sen. King says the deal helps Russia "far more" than it helps the U.S. He also says it will not impact American wallets, but rather help Russian President Vladimir Putin's war against Ukraine.
"Instead of pursuing solutions that are consistent with America’s values, President Trump has decided to ease energy sanctions on Russia. In doing so, he chose Putin over the American people, which will ultimately help fuel that autocracy’s bloody, unprovoked war of aggression on Ukraine," King said.
Sen. King also says the deal is a "slap in the face" to Congress members who voted for the Lindsay Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, and that those Congress members should demand an immediate reversal of the decision.
"This deal comforts our enemies and will do little for Americans. It’s a fraud," King said.

title: Simon strengthens into a Category 4 hurricane as it approaches Mexico’s coast
text:
MIAMI (AP) — Simon has strengthened into a powerful Category 4 hurricane as it barrels toward Mexico’s coast.
The National Hurricane Center in Miami said early Saturday Simon’s maximum sustained winds increased to 150 mph (240 kph). A storm of that strength or greater is considered a major hurricane. Simon could bring as much as 10 to 20 inches (25-50 cm) of rain over parts of southwestern Mexico, with some areas receiving up to 30 inches, the center said.
The bulletin also urged residents to take immediate action to prepare, saying the hurricane will make landfall early Sunday, but tropical storm-strength winds could arrive much sooner.
Simon is expected to bring heavy rainfall to parts of southwestern Mexico, possibly concentrated along Jalisco’s coast and in parts of Michoacan, Colima and Nayarit.
“This rainfall will produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides, especially in areas of steep terrain,” the NHC said.
Jalisco suspended classes on Friday and Monday in 22 coastal municipalities and began evacuating dozens of people from at-risk areas. It also asked the tourism sector in Puerto Vallarta, a popular destination for U.S. tourists, to ensure that both workers and visitors are fully accommodated in shelters or safe zones by Friday afternoon.

title: Lapierre Scores Five as County Soccer Offenses Erupt Friday
text:

title: Traveling van holding tens of thousands of Epstein files makes stop in Lewiston
text:
Traveling van holding tens of thousands of Epstein files makes stop in Lewiston
The Donald J. Trump and Jeffrey Epstein Memorial Bookmobile takes trips across the country, opening its doors to those in the community to explore the released Epstein Files while also relaying the history between Epstein and President Trump.
In the traveling van are over 400 volumes of files at around 800 pages each, totaling 2,500 pounds of paper.
Dani Bensky, who was abused by Epstein, travels with the van, sharing her story.
"I keep saying that it feels kind of strange to take this around the country and just basically campaign for basic human decency, because it's never been political for us," said Bensky. "So I hope people walk away with the sense of humanity at the end of it all."
Bensky said she hopes the magnitude of the number of documents inside of the bookmobile for onlookers to see is what sticks out.
"We used to really live in isolation and think that we were buried in our own shame and really be locked into our own stories," answered Bensky. "But once we found each other and we started talking about how many of us there were, we're talking about numbers of over 1000. We think the number is closer to 1400 at this point, of survivors and victims just within the Epstein and Maxwell case. So, just remembering how big this is. And it's oddly validating to see this much paperwork."
Joining Bensky on Saturday was Matt Dunlap, Democratic candidate for Congressional District 2, who said, if elected, he would make further investigation, removing the statute of limitations and accountability a priority.
"It's just an extraordinary story of how simple authority that we derive from the electorate as public officials can be abused and to power over people, change their lives, traumatize them and keep them anonymous, keep them quiet," stated Dunlap. "And it shouldn't be quiet."
The bookmobile will be back in Lewiston on Sunday before leaving the state, continuing its journey across the nation.

title: UMaine study explores whether music can help older adults maintain brain health
text:
ORONO — University of Maine researchers are studying whether listening to music or learning to play an instrument could help older adults maintain cognitive function as they age.
The three-year study, led by Rebecca MacAulay, an associate professor of psychology at UMaine, is funded by the National Institute on Aging and will compare two 12-week music programs for adults with normal cognition and mild cognitive impairment.
If the approach proves successful, MacAulay said the program could eventually be offered through senior centers, libraries, retirement communities and other community organizations.
“I think it could be immense,” MacAulay said of the potential impact. “It’s something that could help people maintain cognitive abilities longer.”
The study will enroll 48 older adults, half with normal cognition and half with mild cognitive impairment. Mild cognitive impairment involves changes in memory or thinking that are greater than expected with normal aging but are not severe enough to significantly interfere with daily life.
Participants will be randomly assigned to one of two groups. One will learn to play the soprano recorder, while the other will participate in music listening and appreciation activities.
MacAulay said researchers expect both activities could provide benefits, though potentially in different ways.
“We really expect that people could get benefits in both groups,” MacAulay said. “We think the benefits are going to be different.”
How music may support brain health in older adults
Researchers will examine memory, attention, thinking skills, social connection and emotional well-being. They will also study cognitive control, including abilities such as multitasking, dividing attention and avoiding distractions.
Those abilities can decline with normal aging and may decline more sharply among people at risk of dementia, MacAulay said.
“The goal is helping people to maintain healthier brain function and social function as they get older,” she said.
Participants will complete testing before and after the 12-week programs. They will meet once a week in a group setting and complete activities at home between sessions.
Those in the music training group will receive a recorder and music stand. Participants in the music listening and appreciation group will receive digital music players and headphones for at-home activities.
No previous musical experience is required. People who already read music or play an instrument will not be eligible because researchers want participants without formal music training.
The recorder was chosen in part because it is inexpensive, portable and relatively easy for older adults to use.
“It’s portable and affordable,” MacAulay said.
The program uses a recorder with a fingering system that can be easier for people with limited finger dexterity, including those with arthritis. MacAulay said a recorder can cost about $10, making the program easier to expand if future research supports its use.
Social connection is another focus of the music study
The group setting is also an important part of the research.
In an earlier pilot study, participants frequently described social connection as an unexpected benefit. Some who were initially uncomfortable in social settings said the program helped them feel connected to people with similar interests.
MacAulay recalled receiving messages around Christmas from former participants who sent photos of themselves playing the recorder with their grandchildren.
“There’s something about jamming in a group,” MacAulay said. “You get that camaraderie.”
Social connection emerged as one of the top benefits reported in the pilot study, along with perceived improvements in attention and thinking, she said.
The new research builds on that pilot study, which suggested potential improvements in cognitive function but did not include a comparison group. The current randomized study will allow researchers to more carefully examine how different types of musical activity may affect participants.
MacAulay said music may engage the brain in several ways. Listening can stimulate areas involved in hearing, while learning to play an instrument also requires attention, movement and coordination.
“Music really is keeping the brain active in so many different ways,” she said.
Study could inform future Alzheimer’s and dementia research
Because the project is a feasibility study, its main goal is not to prove that either activity prevents dementia.
Instead, researchers will examine whether participants attend sessions, complete their activities, stay enrolled and learn the material. They will also determine whether their testing methods are sensitive enough to detect changes.
The findings could help researchers decide whether to move forward with a larger clinical trial.
The study is also notable for including older adults with mild cognitive impairment, a group sometimes excluded from similar research. Of the 48 participants, 24 will have normal cognition and 24 will have mild cognitive impairment.
That split will allow researchers to examine whether the programs affect the two groups differently.
MacAulay’s interest in the project began after she met Philip Edelman, director of UMaine’s School of Performing Arts at a faculty event. MacAulay studies cognitive aging, while Edelman brought expertise in music education.
Their conversations eventually led to a larger question: What happens when older adults with no musical background are taught to play an instrument?
Their early work also uncovered a practical challenge. Most beginner music materials are designed for children.
MacAulay and Edelman developed materials specifically for older adults, using larger visuals, more repetition and other adjustments intended to make learning more accessible.
UMaine researchers hope program could expand into communities
Those materials have since been organized into manuals that researchers hope could eventually allow community organizations to run the programs themselves.
“The idea is that we would disseminate this,” MacAulay said. “Really, if it is so, we could just turn this over. It’d be turnkey.”
Edelman is a co-investigator on the project. Shannon McCoy, a UMaine associate professor of psychology, is also a co-investigator and will serve as the study’s statistician.
Nathan Sprangers, a former UMaine student who studied in the School of Performing Arts and now teaches in the community, will lead the music instruction.
Researchers plan to hold the programs at community locations rather than requiring participants to travel to the UMaine campus, making it easier for more older adults to participate.
The first groups are expected to begin in the spring, with 12 participants in each study condition. A second round is planned for the fall, bringing total enrollment to 48.
The three-year project began in September and runs through August 2029. Researchers expect to begin analyzing outcomes toward the end of the study’s second year and use the findings to prepare for a larger trial.
Ultimately, MacAulay said the research is aimed not only at people at risk of Alzheimer’s disease but at supporting healthier aging more broadly.
“We really see this as being something that is for all older adults,” she said.

title: Katahdin is greening faster than any other New England summit
text:
High above the tree line on Katahdin, where biting winds and sub-zero winters hold the rocky landscape in a frozen grip for much of the year, the mountaintop is turning noticeably greener.
Four decades worth of satellite observations reveal that alpine tundra across the Northeast are undergoing widespread vegetation expansion, not just at the advancing tree line but well above it, too. The new growth is transforming rare, high-elevation ecosystems once thought buffered from rapid change.
And Katahdin, Maine’s highest peak at 5,268 feet, is greening faster than any other New England summit. Vegetation has increased there by 7.9% from 1984 to 2024, according to a recent study in the journal Ecosphere by scientists at Dartmouth College and the Appalachian Mountain Club.
“Greening isn’t necessarily good or bad, but it’s happening,” said Dartmouth College geographer Jonathan Chipman. “The reason may be a concern. It might mean rare plants are being crowded out by aggressive interlopers that can now live in areas when they couldn’t survive in the past.”
The study used thousands of NASA images to track greening on 35 alpine summits from New York to Quebec. Co-author Jordon Tourville provided field perspective as an alpine ecologist with the Appalachian Mountain Club to explore the potential reasons for the greening.
As a geographer, Chipman said he is often asked to work with other researchers to analyze or map data in their fields of study. As an avid climber, he has long wanted to use his skills to research what is happening at the tops of New England’s summits.
“I grew up in New England,” Chipman said. “I climbed Katahdin when I was a kid. I climbed Mount Washington too many times to count. A lot of people, including me, are very concerned about the future of these precious little sky islands.”
For Mainers who hike Baxter State Park or look up at the Longfellow Mountains, the findings suggest that environmental pressures are actively reshaping the summits of New England that are so isolated that naturalists call them “sky islands.”
These summits support fragile plant communities, such as cushion plants and arctic sedges, that survived the last ice age and thrive in conditions too harsh for trees. Some animals are found only in these areas, such as the Katahdin Arctic butterfly, or breed only here, like the American Pipit.
There are only about 50 square miles of alpine ecosystem in the Northeast, Tourville said.
“That makes it the rarest ecosystem type in the region,” Tourville said. “We suspect that because they’re so small, and because the plants there are already existing really at the edge of what plants can withstand, that any amount of change will destroy this system.”
Across Maine’s six studied alpine summits — Katahdin and North Brother in Baxter State Park and Sugarloaf, Bigelow, Saddleback and Mount Abraham in the Longfellow Range — greenness expanded over the four-decade study period, but not at the same pace.
While Katahdin clocked a 7.9% greening trend, the average greening rate of all the peaks studied was 5.2%. Records show a 5.8% increase at North Brother at Baxter, a 5% increase at Sugarloaf, a 4.8% increase at Saddleback and a 4.7% increase at mounts Bigelow and Abraham.
Ground mapping on Katahdin shows that greening is hitting alpine sedge meadows particularly hard. The windswept lawns of Carex bigelowii appear to be undergoing invasion by the woody dwarf heath shrubs that thrive in warmer temperatures and higher nutrient levels.
Baxter State Park officials acknowledged that the shift is a serious concern. They have been collaborating with other researchers to map Katahdin’s alpine plant boundaries, monitor trail corridors and track shrub encroachment into sedge meadows, according to park manager Kevin Adam and natural resources director Nava Tabak.
Strict “stay-on-trail” policies, supported by visitor quotas, summit stewards, signage and string fencing are the park’s most vital tools to help the fragile root systems withstand atmospheric stresses, Adam and Tabak said.
But researchers suspect warming temperatures are hardly the only environmental force at play.
The greening trend accelerated through the 1980s and 1990s before flattening around 2005 to 2009, a trajectory that aligns with ecological recovery following federal Clean Air Act regulations that curbed acid rain and sulfur pollution across New England peaks.
“A lot of people focus on temperature, but I think we missed the nitrogen signal,” Tourville said. “The soils in the alpine zone are extremely nitrogen poor. For decades, we essentially dumped nitrogen fertilizer up there. That probably had a pretty profound impact.”
Topography and severe weather also shape the landscape. Sheltered east- and north-facing slopes across the region’s peaks showed rapid greening, but exposed ridges seem to have resisted plant expansion.
For park stewards, the 40-year satellite record provides a crucial baseline to guide future conservation. But it also highlights a fundamental disagreement over how to manage wilderness in an era of global climate change.
Tourville argued that traditional, hands-off wilderness management may no longer be enough.
“My message to them was, it might be time in the near future to rethink that stance in terms of hands-off, no management up in the park, especially in the alpine zone, because climate change does not respect park boundaries,” Tourville said. “And climate change is not hands-off.”
Baxter State Park leadership firmly defended the park’s “Forever Wild” mandate, arguing direct human intervention is not the answer.
“Our response to stressors from climate extremes, as illustrated by this research, is to continue to minimize human impacts so that the natural communities and species have the best chance to adapt,” Adam and Tabak said in an emailed statement. “Though our approach to stewardship of the Park’s alpine areas is unique, these areas may over time serve as an experimental control that can be compared with other northeastern alpine areas that are more directly managed.”
This story was originally published by the Maine Trust for Local News. Penelope Overton can be reached at poverton@pressherald.com.

title: Maine cannot afford to lose Susan Collins’ bipartisan voice in Washington
text:
KC Johnson is a professor of history at Brooklyn College and lives in Scarborough.
By now, most of us have seen the ad dozens of times. Four (identified) female narrators castigate Sen. Susan Collins for never standing up to President Trump.
The narrators focus on three issues: the Iran war, Medicaid cuts and the Supreme Court’s reversal of Roe v. Wade. They cite four votes by Collins: against a measure to invoke the War Powers Resolution on the Iran war, in favor of a measure to allow Senate debate on Trump’s major funding bill last year and to confirm Brett Kavanaugh and Neil Gorsuch, two of the five justices who voted to overturn Roe.
The ad doesn’t mention that Collins (along with 2nd District Democrat Jared Golden,
whose votes followed a similar path) subsequently voted in favor of invoking the
War Powers Resolution on Iran. Or that she voted against passing the Trump 2025
spending bill.
Most misleadingly, the ad does not note that Collins has voted to confirm all three pro-choice justices on the Court (Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan and Ketanji Brown Jackson). Nor does it reveal that she broke from Trump to oppose the 2020 confirmation of Amy Coney Barrett, who provided the fifth vote necessary to reverse Roe. In fact, if the Court consisted solely of justices who earned Collins’ support, it seems likely that Roe would still be the law of the land.
The thrust of the ad, funded by a group called WinSenate, seems to be that independence or open-mindedness is a bad thing in a senator. Two of the narrators place independence in air quotes as they describe Collins. And the three issues chosen — Iran, the 2025 spending bill and Trump’s Supreme Court nominees — are ones where Collins has taken independent positions from the president.
Perhaps such a claim is unfair to WinSenate. Their ads identify a website — winsenate.org — where Maine voters can go to learn more about the group’s positions, which is funded by a super PAC affiliated with Senate Democrats.
I visited the website to try to get more information on why the organization seems so hostile to an independent approach in the Senate, and in particular what justification the group could have to attribute the reversal of Roe to Collins, given her opposition to Barrett’s confirmation.
The website consists solely of a photograph of the American flag. It provides no statement of principles about the group’s mission, no rationalization for its hostility to a senator who doesn’t always vote a party line and no explanations to bolster its claims.
The two WinSenate ads about Collins analyzed by the fact-checking website PolitiFact
are rated “false” and “mostly false.”
As someone who voted for Joe Brennan in the 1996 Senate race, Chellie Pingree in
2002, Tom Allen in 2008 and even Shenna Bellows (who lost by a greater than 2-1 margin to Collins) in 2014, I understand the impulse to vote against Collins. But 2026 is not 1996, nor even 2014.
With Collins chairing the Appropriations Committee, her demonstrated clout on behalf of the state highlights her importance to the state.
Perhaps more importantly, at a time when American politics is more polarized than it’s been in decades, it’s critical to maintain one of the Senate’s few bipartisan voices — especially since the Democrats’ replacement nominee, Troy Jackson, seems likely to be little more than an automatic vote for whatever position Bernie Sanders or Elizabeth Warren take, rather than an independent vote for Maine.
A 2026 vote for Collins provides a way to resist the two parties’ race to ideological extremes — and, perhaps, also a way to reject misleading ads that, as here, quite literally wrap themselves in the American flag and hope that voters don’t look too closely into their underlying claims.

title: Lincoln Academy gets its turn, wins first Class B golf championship
text:
VASSALBORO — For years, with players like Bailey Plourde and Kellen Adickes coming through the program, the Lincoln Academy golf team had seen individual success at the Class B state championships.
Team success, however, kept eluding the Eagles. It was always another team’s time, another team’s turn at the top.
Until Saturday, that is. With medalist Colin Mitchell leading the way with a 2-over 74, Lincoln won its first state championship, shooting 317 to hold off Freeport (326), Yarmouth (334), Cape Elizabeth and Fryeburg Academy (both 341) in the Class B tournament at Natanis Golf Course.
“It was a huge goal of ours. We won KVACs, which was nice, but we knew that this was a bigger goal on our minds,” Mitchell said. “We knew it was definitely doable. … We knew if we played well, we would have a fighting chance.”
Freeport’s Ryan Savona finished second to Mitchell with a 76. He was followed by Henry Stone of Gray-New Gloucester and Caden Chretien of Nokomis at 77, and Declan Hickey of Yarmouth at 78.
Carla Ferraris of Fryeburg Academy and Kathryn Peterson of Lake Region tied for girls medalist honors at 90.
Lincoln Academy finished ninth the last two seasons and had only one top-five finish the previous four years while failing to qualify twice. But after winning the KVAC B qualifier by 15 strokes, the Eagles had the answers this year.
“It’s been on my mind for a couple of years,” coach Todd Brackett said. “This team has a lot of potential. They’re young, and we’ve seen it coming up.
“They’ve had some great (individual) performances, but just never put it all together. Obviously, it came together today.”
In addition to Mitchell, the Eagles got a 79 from Brody Day, an 80 from Drew Nichols and an 84 from Max Blake — all juniors. The medalist honors were particularly sweet for Mitchell, who shot a 91 in the tournament last year and began making frequent trips to Natanis in the spring to ensure he’d be ready in October.
“This is one of the first courses to open in the spring. It’s kind of far from my house, but it’s worth the trip,” he said. “(Then) I’d play every day in the summer, like four to five hours a day, if not more.”
The work paid off Saturday. Mitchell got his round going with birdies on the fourth and sixth holes, and after bogeys on the eighth, ninth and 11th, he played his final seven holes at even par to maintain his lead.
“I felt like I was still swinging it good, so I just had to trust that,” he said. “It’s easy to drift out of focus a little bit. … I definitely checked back in mentally.”
Savona’s 76, combined with Liam Nihill’s 81, Will Obrin’s 84 and Charlie MacDonald’s 85, kept Freeport close. Savona opened with a birdie, then got two more on the 11th and 17th while playing the back nine at 1 under.
“It got kind of scrappy for a little bit, but I felt like I held it together well,” he said. “I made a couple of double (bogeys) out there, and my mentality was (that) it wasn’t even a bad double, I hit a couple of bad shots. I still feel solid about my game.”
Yarmouth also got an 82 from Lucas D’Alessandro, an 86 from Rory Truesdell and an 88 from Charles Hughes. Cape Elizabeth was led by an 82 from Charlie Lampman. Fryeburg’s Sergio Trejo shot an 81.
Lake Region’s Shane Plummer also finished in the top 10 with an 80 that tied him with Lincoln Academy’s Nichols for seventh.

title: Deputy body camera video offers glimpse inside home weeks before children found dead
text:
LADSON, S.C. (WCSC/Gray News) — South Carolina authorities released body camera footage this week showing a mother and her daughters weeks before the two girls were found dead inside the home.
The footage offers the clearest look yet at daily life inside the Ladson-area home, where Emory Deacon, 2, and Harlow Deacon, 15 months old, died.
The Charleston County Sheriff’s Office said the two young children were found starved to death at the home during a welfare check by deputies on Sept. 29.
Authorities said the girls died three to five days before they were found, with their mother, Justine May, facing charges that include two counts of homicide by child abuse.
According to the Charleston County Sheriff’s Office, deputies had responded to numerous calls at the Pinewood Drive residence before ultimately finding the children dead.
The body camera footage released shows Charleston County deputies visiting the home on Aug. 30 and a mobile crisis unit visit on Sept. 12.
The Aug. 30 footage is about 22 minutes and begins with May answering the door while holding Harlow, who can be seen wearing only a diaper.
Deputies entered the home as a dog could be heard in the background. The home appears well-maintained, with music playing from a speaker in the kitchen.
During May’s conversation with authorities, Harlow was placed on the floor and soon began crawling while Emory was sitting on the couch.
Most of the discussion between deputies and May centered on her former fiancé, Zachary Deacon.
Deacon, who is also the girls’ father, said he had requested multiple welfare checks at the home, telling authorities about what he described as May’s unusual behavior.
Deacon and May ended their eight-year relationship in early August. They had been engaged for five years.
A caseworker could be seen taking notes throughout the conversation with May during the home visit, while the children could be seen interacting with others in the home.
In the Sept. 12 footage, May is seen for most of the video, which took place at the home’s front door. Dogs could once again be heard barking, along with occasional sounds of children playing.
May answered the door, asking authorities, “How may I help you?” before telling them that no one could enter the home.
May asked whether her ex-fiancé requested the welfare check. Authorities said it was May’s parents who made the call.
May shared that she was frustrated but not suicidal when she was asked about her mental state, including whether she was hearing or seeing things.
“My family has been taunting the **** out of me,” May can be heard saying.
May told authorities Deacon was spreading “crazy lies,” including that she was having a mental breakdown. She also said she had cut off contact with her family because they were “harassing” her.
May also mentioned an email from her mother, describing it as “horrible.”
“I’m clearly not crazy,” May said at one point. “And no, I’ve never had any mental health issues.”
At the very end of the visit, both of the children could be seen on video with May holding Harlow and Emory standing in the doorway.
May was said to have shared screenshots online of text messages and emails that she described as coming from concerned family members following the authorities’ checks at the home.
One email expressed concerns about May’s parenting.
The Charleston County Sheriff’s Office said authorities found the children dead after they were called back to the home following a 911 call asking deputies to conduct a welfare check.
According to the sheriff’s office, the caller said that the two girls had not been seen in a while, and that their mother was acting differently and was seen walking around the neighborhood by herself.
When deputies arrived at the home on Sept. 29, they said May exited the house and was crying and speaking incoherently. Upon entering, that’s when they saw the two children dead that afternoon.

title: Maine State Police investigating fatal crash on I-95 in Gray
text:
Maine State Police are investigating a car crash that killed one passenger and injured two drivers and an additional passenger Friday night on I-95 in Gray.
Police say 31-year old Megan Stuart, of Auburn, was northbound in a 2010 Honda Fit near mile marker 60 at around 11:47 p.m. on Friday when she swerved to avoid a deer, striking a guardrail and spinning into oncoming traffic. The vehicle crashed head-on into a northbound 2016 Chevy Malibu.
Stuart’s passenger, 38-year-old Soda Mao, of Auburn, was killed in the collision. Stuart was transported to Maine Medical Center with non-life-threatening injuries, and the driver and passenger of the Chevy Malibu suffered minor injuries.
The Falmouth Fire Department and Cumberland County Sheriff’s Office assisted at the scene. Authorities shut part of the Maine Turnpike down for approximately 20 minutes to clear the scene and closed lane 1 for two hours.
The crash remains under investigation, according to Maine State Police.

title: Susan Collins is Trump’s senator
text:
Sen. Susan Collins is no longer Maine’s senator. Despite claiming moderate or fiscally conservative credentials, Collins backed President Trump in 96% of votes.
A ProPublica investigation shed light on her involvement in a pay-to-play scheme. Trump’s Corleone-style team (Bondi, Blanche, Patel) used favors to ensure her loyalty. The investigation into her was never completed. Collins, now millions of dollars richer than when first elected, serves Trump’s whims, not Maine citizens, and so must be replaced.

Portland

title: Maranacook golf holds off Winthrop for Class C title
text:
VASSALBORO — Maranacook senior Jack Fontaine has come through in plenty of big moments on the basketball court.
Saturday, he came through on the golf course.
Fontaine shot a 1-over 73 to take the Class C individual boys title and help the Black Bears win the team title on the Arrowhead course at Natanis Golf Course.
“It feels amazing. I did not expect this,” said Fontaine. “It’s just a hobby, really. I just play for fun.”
Maranacook finished with a score of 317 to beat Winthrop by one shot. It’ i’s the third state title for the Black Bears, who also won in 2022 and 2024. Calais (328), Dexter (332) and Houlton (336) rounded out the top five.
“This year was definitely different,” said Maranacook coach Ryan Meserve. “We didn’t play as well as we wanted to all throughout the (regular) season. We knew that if we could just get through one (good) day, we’ve got guys who have won state championships before … The team is super resilient, like each other as a team. We knew we needed just one good day.”
Winthrop’s Kaydence Allarie shot 83 to win the Class C girls title. Mattanawcook Academy’s Skylar Bard was second with a 90.
“It feels really good,” said Allarie, a junior. “I definitely knew that I could do it. I just needed to stay consistent and play my game.”
In addition to Fontaine’s round, Grady Hreben shot 79, Josh Herzing carded an 80 and Sam Dunton had an 85 for Maranacook.
Drew Mertzel, who won medalist honors last year, led Winthrop with a 76. Also for the Ramblers, Sam Corgan shot 79 and Lincoln MacArthur finished with an 80.
Fontaine has only played competitive golf for three years and wasn’t thinking about winning the title entering play Saturday. He had birdies on the fourth, 12th and 13th holes.
“Today is just (the mindset) of you versus you,” Fontaine said. “You’re competing against yourself.”
Ryan Farnsworth of Dexter was the boys runner-up with a 74. Mertzel, Beckett Peabody of Houlton and Chris Johnson of Kents Hill tied for third at 76.
Allaire said she struggled on the back nine, but her putting helped her out.
“The whole front nine, I felt pretty good about my game,” Allarie said. “I think that definitely helped, because I got my numbers a little lower.”

title: Spaghetti models, rapid intensification, storm surge. Confused? Here’s what hurricane terms mean
text:
It’s a confusing time when a hurricane threatens, and some terms used by officials aren’t known by everyone, so here’s a storm glossary.
Tropical cyclones
Let’s start with the broad category of these storms, called tropical cyclones. In the northern hemisphere, a tropical cyclone is a rapidly counterclockwise-rotating storm that forms in Earth’s warmer areas and is organized with a center that winds flow out of. Tropical cyclones rotate clockwise in the southern hemisphere.
Hurricanes and typhoons
The strongest tropical cyclones in the Atlantic and eastern and central Pacific oceans are called hurricanes. In the northwest Pacific they are called typhoons and in the south Pacific and Indian oceans they are called cyclones or tropical cyclones.
Tropical depressions, tropical storms
In the Atlantic, the weakest of these systems are called tropical depressions. They have winds of less than 39 mph (63 kph).
When a tropical depression reaches 39 mph (63 kph) but is weaker than 74 mph (119 kph), they are called a tropical storm and receive a name from a pre-established list.
Category 1 and 2 hurricanes
When a tropical storm hits 74 mph (120 kph), it achieves hurricane status. There are five categories of hurricanes based on maximum sustained wind speed in a rating system called the Saffir-Simpson Scale.
The weakest is a Category 1, with winds of 74-95 mph (120-150 kph), and it will have dangerous winds that produce some damage. Tree branches will snap and some will be uprooted. Extensive power damage is likely.
A Category 2 has winds of 96-110 mph (155-175 kph) and can be disastrous, with near-total power loss expected near the center.
Major hurricanes: Category 3, 4 and 5
When hurricanes sustain winds exceeding 111 mph (180 kph), they get major hurricane status, with devastating consequences. Even well-built homes may be severely damaged by a Category 3 hurricane with winds of 111-129 mph (180-210 kph).
A Category 4 hurricane is considered catastrophic, with winds of 130-156 mph (210-250 kph) that leave entire areas uninhabitable for weeks or months.
The scale tops out at Category 5, when a hurricane’s winds exceed 157 mph (250 kph). A high percentage of the homes in the disaster region will be destroyed. Power outages could last for months.
Storm surge and tide
Storm surge is the deadly rise of water generated by a storm that’s above and beyond the normal tide. It starts in the ocean but could include rivers and canals. Storm surges once caused nearly half of a hurricane’s deaths, but surge-related fatalities have come down with warnings and education to about 11% of all direct deaths. Surges can reach as much as 20 feet or more and that does not include waves, which are on top of storm surge.
Storm tide is storm surge plus tides.
Eye and eyewall of hurricane
A hurricane’s center is called the eye. It is calm inside the eye, but it is crucial to the storm’s formation and continuation. It is circular and is usually 20 to 40 miles (30 to 60 km) in diameter, but can be bigger. The smaller the eye is, the stronger the storm. After a while, a storm can form a new second eyewall around the first in a process called eyewall replacement that temporarily weakens the storm’s intensity but enables it to grow larger overall.
The outside of the eye is the eyewall and it is the storm’s most dangerous area with the strongest winds. When an area on the ground is hit by the eyewall, it will be buffeted by intense winds, then get a break before being slammed by the other side of the eye in a second round of the storm’s strongest winds.
Landfall
When the eye of a hurricane or tropical storm goes over land, that point is called landfall. But high winds, rain and storm surge can cause all sorts of damage many hours before landfall, and last many hours thereafter. Landfall is not necessarily where the strongest winds are, and the wider swirl of a storm can spread destruction across large areas.
Dirty side of a hurricane
The right front quadrant of a hurricane or northeast part of the eyewall tends to cause the most damage as the strongest winds blow counterclockwise around the center, so this at times is called a storm’s dirty side. In the southern hemisphere, it’s the left front quadrant that is the dirty side.
Forecast and spaghetti models
There are dozens of computer-generated models that forecast changes in each storm’s track and intensity. They vary because each one uses different assumptions about how storms operate and some prove better during certain storms and worse during others. Forecasters advise to avoid concentrating on one individual model. When many or all of the models are put on one map, they generally show an overall sense of what will happen. Sometimes they show a lot of lines going in different directions, which can look like cooked spaghetti.
Hurricane cone
The National Hurricane Center’s official forecast is not one specific line, but rather a cone of uncertainty that expands with time, up to five days out. That cone shows the most probable area where the eye of the storm could move over time, but it doesn’t mean the storm will be in the center of that cone. It is designed so that 67% of the most likely tracks fall within the cone.
Watches and warnings
A hurricane or tropical storm watch means conditions are possible within an area during the time specified by the National Weather Service. A hurricane or tropical storm warning means those conditions are no longer just possible, but expected. One way to think about it: A watch is having the ingredients to bake a cake, while a warning comes when the cake is pretty much done.
Wind shear
Wind shear is a change in wind speed or direction, or both, and it can weaken a storm. Crosswinds at high levels, such as 40,000 feet (12,200 meters) above sea level, can often decapitate a storm. Wind shear also can describe when winds up at the top of the storm blow in different directions than at bottom or middle.
Rapid intensification
When a storm, usually fed by unusually warm water, suddenly gathers a lot of strength, sustaining winds that increase in speed by at least 35 mph (56 kph) in 24 hours, it is called rapid intensification. This is a dangerous situation if it happens close to land.

title: Several Usher, Chris Brown concert dates abruptly removed from tour schedule
text:
COLUMBIA, S.C. (WIS/Gray News) - Several concerts featuring Grammy winners Usher and Chris Brown have been abruptly canceled.
The two were set to bring their R&B tour to Columbia on Oct. 29 at Williams-Brice Stadium, but the date was one of the events suddenly removed Friday from the tour’s website.
Other tour dates around the same time were also removed, including stops in Baltimore, Cincinnati and Indianapolis.
“Event canceled. Unfortunately, the event organizer has had to cancel your event,” a Ticketmaster message online said when inquiring about those events.
No official reason for the cancellations was immediately provided.
However, the BBC reported that Brown was expected in London for sentencing on Oct. 26 after pleading guilty to charges in a 2023 nightclub attack.
Ticketmaster noted that those who had purchased tickets to the events would receive a refund within the next three weeks.
