title: Veteran brothers reconnect after 40 years through video chat
text:
Veteran brothers reconnect after 40 years through video chat
Two brothers who served their country and had not seen each other for 40 years were reunited today through a video chat organized by Placer County.
The brothers, one living in Grass Valley and the other in eastern Connecticut, have been separated by nearly 3,000 miles. While they have kept in touch over the phone, they had not seen each other in four decades.
Placer County facilitated the reunion, allowing the brothers to connect face-to-face virtually.
"I think it's a great opportunity for us to help both of these veterans maybe become a little more healthy in their mental health," said Steve Johnson, a Placer County Veterans Service officer. "I can't imagine that it's a great feeling not to be able to see your family for such a long time."
The Placer County Veterans Office is now working with a nonprofit to provide the brothers with internet access and tablets so they can continue connecting face-to-face.

title: High school golf rankings gave players a new perspective this season
text:
VASSALBORO — Colin Mitchell saw the rankings. The Lincoln Academy junior didn’t agonize over them, but yeah, he checked them out.
Sixth in Class B, 16th in the state, according to the Maine high school golf rankings that made their debut this fall.
“I kind of saw it as an opportunity to prove myself,” Mitchell said after winning the Class B individual state title Saturday afternoon at Natanis Golf Club. “I’m sixth. I’ve got nothing to lose, really.”
The idea for a statewide ranking had percolated in Brian Bickford’s brain for a while. How could Maine Golf, the state’s governing body for the sport, make it happen?
“I always was intrigued by Heal points,” Bickford said, referring to the system by which the MPA ranks teams to seed the tournament in most high school sports. “For me, it kind of brings the state together.”
How does a player from Fort Kent compare with a player from York when they’ve played entirely different courses all season, in different conditions? This ranking system helps quantify what had been unquantifiable.
Bickford, the executive director for Maine Golf, who also coaches the University of Southern Maine golf team, enlisted Alex Grant in the endeavor. A 2024 Nokomis High grad and a member of the USM golf team, Grant worked on creating the ranking system.
An information technology major, the project was right in Grant’s wheelhouse. The rankings include the player’s score, course slope and course rating. To put it in basic terms, the better a player shoots on a tougher course, the higher he or she will rank.
It goes beyond the eye test and score comparisons. Taking a course’s rating into account gives a more accurate measure of a player. A plus-2 on a more challenging course has to be considered more impressive than an even-par round on an easier one, right?
“I wish it was something I had when I was in high school, whether I was ranked 1,000 or first,” Grant said.
Winthrop junior Kaydence Allarie knew entering her round Saturday that she was the top-ranked girl in Class C. She was a little nervous, especially with 18 holes to play rather than the typical nine played in the regular season.
Allarie probably had the healthiest attitude toward the rankings.
“Anything can happen,” she said. “You pretty much just play and do your best. I just wanted to stay consistent and not worry about everyone else. Just be me.”
The more rounds played, the more accurate the rankings should be. Anyone can have a bad day, the kind that makes you want to give your putter a Viking funeral. Anyone can have a great day, too, when every tee shot finds the middle of the fairway and you read every green perfectly.
The rankings work as a complete picture, Grant said. As the season moved from late August to early October, the minimum number of matches required to be ranked increased.
“The more the merrier. It gave you a better ranking,” Grant said.
The rankings, available for viewing at mainegolf.org, rank individual players in each class, as well as teams. Going into Class B state championship, Mitchell and his Lincoln Academy teammates figured through the ranking that Freeport and Fryeburg Academy would be their top competition for the team title.
In Class C, the top-ranked team was Winthrop, ahead of Dexter and Calais.
To the MPA’s credit, they love it.
“I feel a little guilty. People keep thanking me and congratulating me, and I had little to nothing to do with it,” said Todd Sampson, the MPA assistant executive director.
To the MPA, submitting results for the rankings was strictly voluntary this fall. The MPA doesn’t have any plans to use the rankings in determining which golfers play with whom at the state championships. Maybe that’ll change in a few years, when there’s more data to analyze and any kinks or bugs have been ironed out.
Sampson said a few athletic directors have expressed interest in using the rankings as a barometer for choosing all-conference players, since it covers a player’s complete season of work if data is entered dilligently after each match.
For this debut season, the rankings gave high school golfers something to talk about. And for some, maybe a little motivation.

title: ‘Ray Gunn’ Review: Brad Bird’s Latest is a Blast From Futures Past
text:
‘Ray Gunn’ Review: Brad Bird’s New Film Is an Animated Blast From Futures Past
Brad Bird has directed seven movies. To varying degrees, all of them except Ratatouille (which he was brought in to finish after its original director left Pixar) concern themselves with retro futures. Tomorrowland may be Bird’s weakest film, but it’s his best title, because it describes the place where pretty much all of Bird’s films are set: The past’s vision of an imaginary tomorrow that never came to pass.
Now he’s made perhaps the purest expression of that ethos to date. Ray Gunn, directed by Bird at Skydance Animation and released by Netflix, takes place in a sprawling sci-fi city called Metropia that looks like Coruscant from Star Wars: Episode II — Attack of the Clones; an endless grid of towering skyscrapers so tall they’re navigated by rocket-powered elevators, surrounded by bumper-to-bumper mid-air traffic from thousands of hovercars. But the story Bird follows, one he’s supposedly wanted to tell for more than 30 years, is pure Raymond Chandler or Dashiell Hammett, with a grizzled private eye on the trail of a mystery that threatens to unravel a secret about the very nature of this society.
READ MORE: The Biggest Disney Box-Office Bombs Ever
The film’s title is also its protagonist, who — if someone could have plausibly created a futuristic world built of flying cars and matter-manipulating lasers in 1942 — might have been played by Humphrey Bogart. In Ray Gunn, he’s voiced by Sam Rockwell, who brings appropriate levels of world-weary decency to the role of this gumshoe desperately clinging to his principles in a world defined by its lack of them. But with creditors regularly visiting his office to repossess his furniture, he reluctantly takes a well-playing but sleazy job keeping tabs on Metropia’s biggest pop star, the fiery Venus Nova (Scarlett Johansson).
The universe of Ray Gunn with its laser blasters, jet packs, and all sorts of other fanciful gadgets, feels familiar from a century of genre fiction. But Ray’s adventure with Venus is full of surprises, as Bird and co-writer Matthew Robbins, take the viewers through a crime story more fitting for film noir than a children’s cartoon. (Ray Gunn is rated PG, but it’s darker and more mature than typical animated fare.) It also boasts some inspired casting choices, most prominently the great, gruff Tom Waits as Eyera (pronounced “Ira”) as Ray’s spindly alien sidekick, whose loyalty special powers (like a literally photographic memory) are nearly as valuable to Ray as his boundless loyalty.
Like so many of Bird’s movies, Ray Gunn is an affectionate love letter to all of his obsessions. There are aliens who are clearly designed as homages to 1940s character actors like Peter Lorre and Sydney Greenstreet. Venus’s swooping hairdo suggests she would have been played by Veronica Lake in the live-action version of this film. There are weapon and vehicle designs that could have been pulled straight out of Buck Rogers or Forbidden Planet.
But despite all of that vintage flavor, Ray Gunn somehow doesn’t feel stodgy or old fashioned. It’s got a frenetic pace, a solid sense of fun, and an ample supply of stellar chase scenes from Bird, who may be the most underrated working director of action in animation and live-action in Hollywood today. (Remember: This is the guy who directed Mission: Impossible - Ghost Protocol, and those incredible scenes atop the Burj Khalifa.) He really takes his time establishing and fleshing out the world of Metropia, introducing various bits of tech that he can then pay off later in all sorts of inventive and satisfying ways. (Just wait until you see what he does with those rocket-powered elevators.)
It’s been eight years since Bird’s previous directorial effort, Incredibles 2, and more than a decade since his last original film, Tomorrowland. In that time, the present has only gotten bleaker, and optimistic sci-fi films have grown rarer and rarer. Ray Gunn isn’t precisely a hopeful movie, either; its retro future is rife with crime, corruption, and racism. (Aliens like Ray’s pal Eyera face discrimination and bigotry from most of the native human population.) Still, there’s something appealing about its nostalgic futurism now. We can’t go back to a time when a brighter tomorrow seemed inevitable. But at least Brad Bird’s still around to give us a glimpse of one every so often.
RATING: 8/10

title: Needle exchanges save lives
text:
My dad died in 2003, just before his 58th birthday. Since before I was born he had been an alcoholic and a heroin user. He died of liver cancer brought on by hepatitis C. He likely contracted that hepatitis from a shared needle.
I don’t know if there were needle exchange services where he was then. Probably not; it was the 1970s, when even having “drug paraphernalia” was criminalized in the United States. Criminalization did not stop people from using. Those who ran clean needle services were usually activists, risking imprisonment in their attempts to halt the spread of diseases.
Dad was a Navy veteran. He’d complained of abdominal pain and loss of appetite for years. By the time he was diagnosed by a Veterans Affairs doctor in 2002, his cancer was terminal. He said his earlier attempts to have his pain addressed were probably dismissed as “drug-seeking behavior.”
It can be uncomfortable to be around people who use street drugs. Just because someone uses does not mean that they deserve to catch a deadly illness. I don’t pretend to know why Dad started using. But I’m reasonably confident that people use drugs for reasons that are very real to them; they stop for their own reasons too.
Addiction is complicated. I know people who were given powerful pain medicines during hospitalization and quickly became addicted to them.
Helping people avoid reusing needles is good. One needle not getting shared can mean one person not getting hepatitis or HIV that day. That’s why it’s called “harm reduction.” That person might be someone’s dad, mom, brother, sister, daughter, spouse or friend. Everyone is someone’s something.
Siiri Cressey
Lewiston

title: Philadelphia police officer killed, another injured
text:
Philadelphia police officer killed, another injured after responding to reports of man with a gun
Philadelphia District Attorney Larry Krasner said Saturday afternoon that 35-year-old Eric Lewis is being charged with homicide for the alleged killing of a police officer early Saturday morning.
Shane Seiber, 40, was shot and killed in west Philadelphia after responding to a report of a man with a gun, police said. An officer who was with him was also shot.
Seiber, a 10-year veteran of the Philadelphia Police Department, and the other officer were transported to Penn Presbyterian Medical Center and underwent surgery, according to Police Commissioner Kevin Bethel. The surviving officer is in stable condition, Bethel said.
Along with charges for Seiber’s death, Lewis is facing a host of others, including attempted homicide, for allegedly shooting the officer and shooting at nine other officers who responded to the scene, Krasner said.
Gov. Josh Shapiro said he ordered flags to fly at half-mast for Seiber, who is survived by his wife and two children — a 7-year-old boy and a 3-year-old girl.
GaNun is a corps member for The Associated Press/Report for America Statehouse News Initiative. Report for America is a nonprofit national service program that places journalists in local newsrooms to report on undercovered issues.

title: 84-year-old woman dead after vehicle falls from parking garage
text:
HONOLULU (HawaiiNewsNow/Gray News) - An 84-year-old woman was pronounced dead after her vehicle fell from a high-rise parking garage in downtown Honolulu Friday afternoon.
According to the Honolulu Police Department, just before 2:30 p.m., the woman was driving north on the fifth floor of the parking garage at 1088 Bishop Street. Her vehicle struck and broke through a retaining wall, then fell about five stories before landing on its roof on the sidewalk along Hotel Street.
Emergency response
Emergency crews responded to the scene on Hotel Street just before 3 p.m.
Crews were seen around the SUV, which was crushed upside down outside a convenience store.
There was visible damage to the fourth-floor railing of a parking structure directly above the vehicle.
EMS pronounced the woman dead at the scene.
Police said she was wearing a seatbelt at the time of the crash.
Investigation underway
Hotel Street was temporarily closed between Bishop and Bethel streets as police investigated.
Authorities have not yet determined if speed, drugs or alcohol were factors in the crash.
This is the fourth non-traffic fatality on Oahu this year, compared with zero at this time in 2025.

title: Coyotes are often misunderstood, and confused for other animals
text:
One of our regular readers, Joan from Portland, wrote to us with a handful of questions about coyotes, which always strike me as one of Maine’s most misunderstood mammals. That title might actually go to the fisher (often, and inappropriately, called the fisher cat) because everyone wants to ascribe nocturnal noises to them, when 99% of the time it is actually a fox. That said, the coyote and its many noises deserve some attention.
Coyotes have an interesting history in Maine, because they weren’t always here. I grew up in Hollis, a wonderfully small rural town where coyotes were often heard (and seldom seen). But they aren’t just in rural areas; coyotes can be found across the entire state, often thriving in suburban and surprisingly urban areas too.
If we go back to the 1920s, these wild dogs (canids) had never been seen in the state. The first recorded sightings are from the ’30s. They expanded their range northeast, coming into the state to fill a void left by the extirpation of wolves. That niche was opened after humans killed off the eastern wolves that once lived in Maine, eradicating them in the 19th century.
As the coyotes moved into these newly accessible areas, they encountered some wolves en route and began hybridizing, which gave us the variety of coyote hybrids, often called “coywolves,” that are seen in Maine today. To be a bit more specific, they are officially called eastern coyotes, one of the nineteen subspecies of coyotes across Northern and Central America.
It is worth reflecting on these mixed genes a bit further. The eastern coyote is a majority coyote with other canines mixed in. A study published in 2014, led by Javier Monzón of Stony Brook University, looked at eastern coyote genomes and found that genetic parentage broke down as: 65% western coyote, 17% western wolf and 18% eastern wolf. Furthermore, there were some eastern coyotes with four canid parentage, thanks to dogs contributing. Those broke down to: 61% western coyote, 14% western wolf, 14% eastern wolf and 11% domestic dog.
I emphasize this point because we see a lot of reports of wolves in Maine. While it is possible that eastern wolves could wander into Maine, there are no established populations of them here, but plenty of wolfish-looking coyotes.
Despite their wide distribution, coyotes are rarely encountered in Maine. You are more likely to find signs left behind, like footprints or scat. Their droppings are most likely to be confused for that of a large dog, but a dog’s diet is consistent, and so is their poop. A coyote will typically have scat showing their omnivorous diet, with many indigestible contents like hair (from the small mammal prey) and seeds (from fruit).
The next best way to detect their presence is through their loud vocalizations. Howling is perhaps the most iconic of their noises, typically given in long-distance and territorial communications. I also hear my local coyotes doing a lot of dog-like yipping, sometimes mixed with howls. This mixing can be done by just a couple of individuals, vocalized in a way to sound like a large group, which is known as a “Beau Geste” effect. They are so vocal, which is how they got their specific epithet: latrans, which is Latin for “barking”, so Canus latrans is the “barking dog.”
The last thing we need to address, given all the coyotes around us, is that they are generally harmless, unless you are a small rodent. In general, coyotes are much more afraid of humans than humans need to be of them. That said, keeping them wild is important, so do not leave food out for them. And while a cat is larger than most coyote prey, you should keep your cats safe and indoors all the time anyway as cats are also the No. 1 anthropogenic cause of mortality in birds.
Have you got a nature or wildlife question of your own? It doesn’t have to be about birds! Email questions to [email protected] and visit www.maineaudubon.org to learn more about birding, native plants, and programs and events focusing on Maine wildlife and habitat. Maine Audubon Staff Naturalist Doug Hitchcox and other naturalists lead free bird walks on Thursday mornings starting at 7 am, at Maine Audubon’s Gilsland Farm Audubon Sanctuary in Falmouth.

title: Off-duty ICE agent shot after allegedly assaulting 72-year-old man and his daughter while drunk
text:
FRESNO, Calif. (KMPH) — An off-duty Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent is facing charges after police say he assaulted an older man and his daughter early Friday morning in Fresno.
Investigators said a woman found the agent, 32-year-old David Gonzalez, sleeping on her front lawn.
The woman told her 72-year-old father, who went outside and told Gonzalez to leave.
According to police, Gonzalez woke up and appeared drunk, then allegedly assaulted him.
Authorities said that as the woman tried to intervene, Gonzalez allegedly attacked her. The woman’s father then pulled out a gun and shot Gonzalez.
The woman called her boyfriend, a police officer, who arrived to arrest Gonzalez.
The off-duty agent was taken to a hospital for treatment and was listed as being in serious condition. He is facing felony assault charges.

title: Despite Hurricane Isaias, couple celebrates wedding weekend on Florida’s coast
text:
PENSACOLA BEACH, Fla. (AP) - Even the approaching hurricane couldn’t dampen the celebratory atmosphere at a wedding in Pensacola Beach, Florida.
On Thursday evening, David and McKenzie Pipes welcomed guests to their wedding weekend at a beachfront condo. Caterers, bartenders and guests arrived ahead of the storm to celebrate the couple based in Perdido Key, Florida.
Couple celebrates a year after wedding
Though the two wed a year ago, this weekend was their celebration with friends and family.
As a bright orange sunset took over the sky, the Pipeses headed down to the beach to take pictures as their dog Hank ran around in the sand.
Ceremony rescheduled around storm
The couple did have to make some changes: They moved their wedding ceremony and reception to Sunday after Hurricane Isaias is expected to pass, and some out-of-town guests canceled.
Still, family arrived from Maryland and Arizona to celebrate the happy couple, and nothing in the excitement hinted at the storm ahead.

title: How Texas landowners are fighting back against Trump's border wall
text:
How Texas landowners are fighting back against Trump's border wall
The message from the Trump administration has been clear: It is moving ahead with a $46 billion border wall project stretching from the Pacific Ocean to the Gulf of Mexico.
But in Texas' Big Bend region, the administration has run up against intense opposition from landowners, many of whom are unwilling to cede parts of their property for what they see as a waste of taxpayer dollars.
That resistance is complicating President Donald Trump's signature infrastructure project in a fight that has become a test of just how far the administration will go to fulfill its vision of a fortified southern border.
The administration has committed billions of dollars and waived environmental and other protections to plow ahead with the project despite the region's historically low illegal crossings, its formidable natural barriers and a surge of bipartisan opposition that has scrambled traditional border politics.
The federal government has sweeping authority to force the project through. But a judge has now paused construction across the region, giving a major boost to landowners who have sought to impede the wall by refusing to cooperate with government surveyors, protesting at county meetings and gearing up for court battles.
"Landowner resistance has slowed this project to a crawl," said David Keller, a landowner suing to stop the Big Bend border plans. The administration, he added, was "woefully unprepared for the hornet's nest they stirred up."
Trump has long pledged to build the border wall
Building a wall along the U.S.-Mexico border has long been a key campaign promise for Trump. And the administration pushed ahead with it after Republicans last year approved $46 billion for the border wall as part of a sweeping immigration enforcement package.
Although illegal crossings have plummeted under Trump, the administration says walls, vehicle barriers, surveillance technology and patrol roads are needed to keep them low.
Customs and Border Protection says it's building an average of about 12 miles or 20 kilometers of barrier a week. On Friday the agency said they've built over 260 miles of border barriers under the second Trump administration: "CBP is on track and constructing border barrier faster than ever," the agency said in a statement.
In Big Bend, where construction began in September, the administration plans to spend $7.5 billion to fortify the border along a region stretching more than 500 miles (800 km).
In August, the Border Patrol arrested 8,870 people along the southern border. In Big Bend, which makes up roughly one quarter of the entire U.S.-Mexico border, it arrested 161.
"The American people have already seen the consequences of an unprotected border," said CBP Commissioner Rodney Scott after a lawsuit filed by landowners against the Big Bend project. "We cannot allow any region — including Big Bend — to be exploited again."
Landowners gird for court battles
Unlike in other border areas, much of the land in Texas is privately or state owned.
The government must acquire authorization from owners to survey and build and if they refuse, can take them to court. The process by which the government takes someone's property for public use in exchange for compensation is known as eminent domain and courts generally defer to the government in these cases.
That hasn't stopped Dianna and Dan Burbach.
The Burbachs began receiving paperwork in July seeking permission to survey their property, along with a map showing where the project would run behind their house. An August letter said the government had an "immediate need" to enter and warned that it could go to court within 90 days.
Dianna, 63, and her husband, 79, arrived 25 years ago and raised four children in their orange adobe house on property stretching to the Rio Grande. Now retired, they worry construction could worsen flooding and leave 15 acres (6 hectares) of their land behind the wall.
"We're going to let them take us to court, do eminent domain," Dianna said. "We'll fight it that way."
A Justice Department official said CBP has reached agreements with dozens of Big Bend landowners but that the administration has hired eminent domain attorneys in Texas in anticipation of the disputes. Across the southern border, about 70 such cases have been referred to the department during Trump's second term, and 50 have already been resolved — none required going to trial, said the official, speaking on condition of anonymity under ground rules set by the government.
The No Big Bend Wall Coalition, which says its network includes more than 200 landowners, recently sued to block construction. The plaintiffs argue that Homeland Security is misusing its authority in a region with little illegal cross-border activity.
Lawsuits aiming to stop or slow the border wall projects have largely been unsuccessful. But in a major win for opponents, a federal judge temporarily barred wall construction in the Big Bend area. Plaintiffs argued the administration had overstepped its congressional authority by issuing sweeping waivers to bypass environmental and other regulations.
Keller said the judge's ruling was "unqualified good news" but uncertainty over its future meant the landowners would continue their fight.
It's not immediately clear how long the judge's order will slow the government, which late Thursday asked the judge to put aside her order while they appeal.
The administration also argued in the court filing that leaving segments along the border without adequate border security infrastructure could lead to a funnel effect where illegal immigration or smuggling would flow to the area that was least fortified — specifically the Big Bend region.
Protesting contractors and lobbying local officials
Other opponents are pressing local governments not to assist contractors. Charlie Angell, a tourism operator, said that the government wanted access to his land for the border project, and his partner, Bibiana Gutierrez, attended county meetings throughout the region.
They and other land and business owners have staged protests, patrolled areas where contractors are working to look for possible violations, and hung signs telling contractors they're not welcome at local hotels or restaurants.
In Terrell County, residents unsuccessfully urged officials not to lease airport land to a barrier contractor. In Jeff Davis County, a proposed agreement allowing another contractor to use a county road has not yet been approved.
The financial incentives for some of these cash-starved counties are clear and some local officials have argued they have little leverage on a federal plan.
"We're not in control of the border wall. We're not," Terrell County Judge Dale Lynn Carruthers told a room crowded with people who had come to speak out against the airport lease. She said if they didn't lease the land, the contractor would just buy it elsewhere. "We're just a little old Terrell County."
But Angell and Gutierrez argue that the local opposition has more strength than some might realize.
"If we had rolled over, the wall would be up," Gutierrez said.
CBP said it continues to seek voluntary access agreements while completing the project's design, but will refer disputes to the Justice Department when necessary. Landowners will be compensated regardless of how access is obtained, the agency said.
The opposition has bipartisan support
After a yearslong surge in crossings at the southern frontier, border security and immigration were key reasons Republicans voted for Trump and his approval ratings on those issues are among his strongest.
But with illegal crossings plummeting, even some Republicans who voted for Trump on the issue of border security have questioned the need for the multi-billion dollar infrastructure through Big Bend.
Local sheriffs opposed the project early, and bulldozing in Big Bend National Park prompted Republican Sen. John Cornyn to press Homeland Security about Texans' concerns.
Laura Allen, a Republican rancher who voted for Trump twice, is now receiving notices that a vehicle barrier will cross the property where her family raises sheep and goats. She credits Trump with shutting down the border but says spending billions on barriers in Big Bend is unnecessary.
"I didn't vote for a wall," she said. "I wanted our border secured. He accomplished that."
Terrell County's Republican sheriff, Thad Cleveland, who spent 26 years in the Border Patrol, is among those speaking out against the project in Big Bend. He said that in the rugged county he polices, drones and surveillance towers make more sense than a wall to find and stop illegal border crossers.
"We have the advantage of time and distance out here," he said.
The land itself is a natural deterrent, critics say
In some areas, the river is flanked on both sides by steep limestone cliffs, and up and down the region, people have to trek through inhospitable desert terrain to get to the nearest paved road or pass through Border Patrol checkpoints.
Reaching Gary Grabowske's land requires grinding along rocky mountain trails and through gullies carved by flash floods. From the top of a 450-foot (137 meters) cliff, the Rio Grande is visible far below. There is no electricity, running water or internet and, Grabowske argues, no plausible route for a vehicle entering from Mexico.
"You can't take a dirt bike to the bottom," said Grabowske, gesturing to the canyon below. "You can't take a mule to the bottom. You're scrambling down there, hand over fist." He added: "There's no vehicle in the world that could cross any of this."
Opponents say the fight reaches beyond whether a wall makes sense in Big Bend. They see it as a test of how far the federal government can go when landowners stand in the way of one of its priorities.
"We're a pretty tough bunch," said Allen. "But if we're going to be run over and have our land taken by our own government, what makes anybody else in this United States think that they're exempt?"
Ranchers try to resist
The Zuberbueler ranch in Val Verde County was founded in 1898. Brothers Bill and Patrick own and lease thousands of acres of the craggy land stretching to the river. Their Angora goats and Rambouillet sheep roam over the land, stopping at a network of water troughs.
Bill remembers when, back in February, he first got the letter giving him five days to respond to a request to access his property for construction and raising the possibility of the government using eminent domain. He worries about how the construction will affect his livestock, especially their water supply. And while his animals could pass through the vehicle barriers, the cowboys herding them could not.
"There's not a lot of grass out here, but every square foot is important to my bottom line," said Bill.
They have so far refused to allow anyone onto their land to survey or build. They feel the weight of their family's legacy and the sacrifices previous generations made to build the ranch up.
"Regardless of what happens, we have to say we tried," said Patrick.
___
Associated Press writer Alanna Durkin Richer contributed from Washington.

title: SpaceX warns of collision risk as satellites begin to crowd Earth's orbit
text:
SpaceX warns of collision risk as satellites begin to crowd Earth's orbit
Thousands of satellites now orbit Earth, providing services like streaming entertainment, weather tracking, and internet connectivity, but Florida Tech’s Dr. Don Platt says it's a lot like a busy highway.
Related video above: SpaceX’s Falcon 9 rocket taking off from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida last week
"The more traffic, the higher the risk of a crash," Platt told WESH 2 News. "If there is a situation where there's more debris and it's harder for a spacecraft to get into orbit and stay there without getting destroyed, that definitely will have an impact on your life here on the Earth."
SpaceX stated that it works to avoid collisions but noted that other operators could improve their practices. During the International Astronautical Congress conference this week, the company put forth the need for stricter tracking measures.
"These are like obstacles on a road – if you can measure them, you can predict where they're gonna be and you can avoid them. What you can't avoid is other operators who maneuver without telling you where they're gonna go," said Michael Nicolls, senior vice president of Starlink.
The company reported having more than 11,000 satellites in low-Earth orbit and revealed that it experienced approximately 164,000 close calls in the last six months, most of which were caused by unannounced maneuvers by other operators.
SpaceX is advocating for better communication and automated systems to address these challenges and is urging other operators to use its Starlink Space Safety website to share flight data.
The company recently announced it would no longer launch Starlink satellites from Florida with Falcon 9 rockets, ending what in recent years had become a common practice on the Space Coast.

title: ‘Deeply disturbing’: 9 dead in Pennsylvania shooting, police chief says
text:
ERIE, Pa. (WICU/WSEE) — Nine people are dead after a shooting Friday night, authorities said.
Police said the suspected shooter died of a self-inflicted gunshot wound.
Witnesses said the suspect was seen firing a weapon before entering a house.
Police respond to scene
Police arrived at the scene near 7th and Perry streets, and tried to get the man to surrender. Additional gunshots were then heard from inside the home.
“At this time we can confirm that the suspect is deceased. Based on the information currently available to us, there is no ongoing threat to the public,” Erie Police Chief Rick Lorah said.
There is no word yet on a possible motive. The identities of the victims have not been released.
“I want to be candid with our community. This is one of the most difficult and heartbreaking scenes our officers and investigators have ever encountered. The loss of life is devastating, and the circumstances we are working through are deeply disturbing,” Lorah said.
An investigation into the matter is ongoing.

title: Off-duty ICE agent shot after allegedly assaulting 72-year-old man and his daughter while drunk
text:
FRESNO, Calif. (KMPH) — An off-duty Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent is facing charges after police say he assaulted an older man and his daughter early Friday morning in Fresno.
Investigators said a woman found the agent, 32-year-old David Gonzalez, sleeping on her front lawn.
The woman told her 72-year-old father, who went outside and told Gonzalez to leave.
According to police, Gonzalez woke up and appeared drunk, then allegedly assaulted him.
Authorities said that as the woman tried to intervene, Gonzalez allegedly attacked her. The woman’s father then pulled out a gun and shot Gonzalez.
The woman called her boyfriend, a police officer, who arrived to arrest Gonzalez.
The off-duty agent was taken to a hospital for treatment and was listed as being in serious condition. He is facing felony assault charges.

title: Don’t waste one vote this November
text:
The Aug. 23 letter declaring the writer’s intent to cast a write-in vote for Graham Platner in November was alarming. The writer is apparently unaware that a write-in candidate must file a declaration of write-in candidacy in Maine 70 days prior to the election, or the vote won’t count.
This election is paramount. We must unseat Sen. Susan Collins as a step toward healing the damage done by this presidential administration and, to do so, we must unite behind Troy Jackson. A vote for an undeclared write-in candidate — or any other candidate besides Jackson — is a wasted vote.
I was also a Platner fan, but we cannot afford to risk the continuing soaring cost of foreign war, gasoline, groceries and healthcare, or continue suffering the unending assaults on our lands, air and freedoms by casting philosophical votes. The preservation of democracy is a task we must not fail to achieve this November.
Robin Johnson
Waterville

title: Let’s deny Maine’s 12% gift to Donald Trump
text:
Dan Rabata of Cape Elizabeth is a retired U.S. Air Force lieutenant colonel.
A September New York Times/Siena poll found that “in Maine, 12% of voters who said they preferred Democrats to control the Senate also said they planned to support
Ms. Collins.”
With both the Maine Senate race and control of the Senate rated as toss-ups by the Cook Political Report, that split may be decisive in handing Senate control to Donald Trump — again.
Sen. Susan Collins understandably wants us not to pretend that Trump is on the ballot. That ship has sailed. He is the issue, the elephant in the room. Given Trump’s plummeting popularity and negative polling on every major issue, Collins has no choice but to tear up the Trump signs on her lawn.
Trump desperately needs to retain Senate control. Losing it opens up all kinds of difficulties for him. No more confirmations of unqualified hacks. Release of all the Epstein files. Investigations of corruption. Subpoena power. Control of legislation. Votes to end his war. Accountability. Trump knows he is in serious hurt if Collins loses her seat and with it the Senate majority.
What cards can she play to distance herself from Trump? That’s tricky.
She could cite roll-call data showing that she has cast the deciding vote 56 times against her own party. Not particularly impressive against the 144 times when she cast the deciding vote in line with her Republican majority. And not impressive at all against how those same 200 votes would have gone with a Democratic senator in her seat.
How about her high-profile stances against Trump’s nominees? Hasn’t her “moderation” served to rein in some of the worst excesses of Trump/MAGA? Even though she voted for Brett Kavanaugh, Neil Gorsuch and Robert F. Kennedy Jr., didn’t she stand up against Pete Hegseth, Amy Coney Barrett and Todd Blanche? She did. Did it matter? No, all were confirmed by a Republican-controlled Senate.
Are her occasional positions against unpopular GOP priorities genuine or “independent only when it doesn’t make a difference”? Does it matter? Not much, since the outcome is almost always the same: her opposition does not carry the day. When it does, it is usually damage control to mitigate the chaos created by her own party.
Example: First come the Trump-initiated and deeply unpopular Canadian tariffs. Then follow a couple of exceptions to avoid complete disaster, leaving behind a Maine more negatively affected than nearly all other states. Even if her moderate, bipartisan impact is minimal, isn’t it better than nothing? Shouldn’t we applaud it as an example encouraging other Republicans to move in that direction?
Unfortunately, the contrary evidence is clear. Even GOP incumbent Sens. Cassidy and Cornyn, who rarely departed from the party line, have suffered primary losses to significantly more “MAGA” challengers. In this hyperpartisan climate of bend-the-knee fidelity to the Trump agenda — one that is decidedly unfriendly to Maine interests — Susan Collins’ ability to influence what happens in today’s Senate is greatly diminished.
Given the enormous stakes, the strategic imperative is to flip the Senate. Anything less is a lost opportunity. I urge the 12% to reconsider. They may achieve a costly Pyrrhic victory — one that wins a lesser objective but overlooks and loses the greater objective.
We can’t have it both ways. A vote for Susan Collins (regardless of what she does in her individual capacity) endorses continued Republican control of a Trump-compliant Senate. One may even admire her for her past efforts but a vote for her — however well-intentioned — is a vote for the very Trump-controlled agenda of chaos, cruelty and corruption that the 12% despise.

title: Trump's Medicaid cuts strip refugees and other legal immigrants of their health coverage
text:
New restrictions have stripped Medicaid coverage from certain legal immigrants, including refugees and victims of human trafficking, as part of broader federal changes to the health insurance program that are expected to force millions off their coverage.
The change effective Oct. 1 cut from Medicaid what is estimated to be hundreds of thousands of people who legally immigrated to the United States, many of whom work and pay taxes, in the latest Trump administration policy to target foreigners.
The move is part of sweeping changes to Medicaid under President Donald Trump’s 2025 tax cut and policy law, with many set to take effect early next year. The Medicaid changes are projected to result in 7.5 million fewer people with health insurance, according to the Congressional Budget Office’s 2025 estimate.
Advocates say that without Medicaid, people will not be able to afford private insurance and will either delay care or end up in emergency rooms, adding pressure to strained health system. For immigrants, the cuts could be felt more acutely, compounding the effects of other administration efforts to restrict their access to public assistance as part of a broader immigration crackdown.
“This is about telling every immigrant in the United States that they are not welcome here and that they should leave,” said Ben D’Avanzo, a senior strategist at the National Immigration Law Center, which has pursued litigation against the Republican administration over its immigration agenda.
Refugees, asylum seekers, victims of human trafficking and domestic violence are among those who have lost coverage. Green-card holders were not impacted.
Lauren Bis, a White House spokesperson, said in a statement that “immigrants must be able to support themselves without taking from overburdened benefits programs paid for by hard-working American taxpayers.”
D’Avanzo said many people who have lost coverage will likely only realize when they need medical care. But for some, the change has been felt immediately.
Dwindling supplies of lifesaving medication
In Tucson, Arizona, María Chacon has been caring for her son Jesus for almost five years since a car accident at 17 left him unable to breathe on his own. He requires a ventilator, a feeding tube and daily medication, and must be turned once every two hours to stop sores from forming. Chacon said he sometimes opens his eyes.
The family is originally from Mexico and entered the U.S. on a T visa, offered to victims of human trafficking, in 2018.
Chacon said Medicaid has helped cover almost $25,000 per month of care for her son, which includes a small stipend for her and her husband as compensation for being long-term caregivers. She said doctors have explained that even if they both worked 24 hours a day, they would not be able to cover the cost of his care.
“Since that day I haven’t been able to sleep. We haven’t been able to eat or anything. We’re wondering what we’re going to do?” Chacon said.
Jesus takes medication that Chacon estimates costs $7,000 a month. The supply runs out in mid-October. Without coverage, she does not know how her son is going to survive.
Chacon found out just days before the cuts that she was losing care. She called the state’s Medicaid offices to appeal. Although she is in the process of obtaining a green card, Medicaid coverage would only kick in five years after she is approved.
Steven Camarota, research director for the Center for Immigration Studies, a right-leaning think tank that seeks less immigration, said the administration “is trying to nibble around the edges” with the Oct. 1 cuts, finding piecemeal ways to curb immigration into the U.S.
Camarota believes the government should screen legal immigrants for income potential and education, reducing the number who might rely on public benefits once they cross the border.
“You need immigrants who are unlikely to need welfare,” he said, or those with high educational attainment.
The administration recently revived a federal rule that could deny green cards to immigrants who use public benefits that could include food stamps, Medicaid, housing vouchers and others.
Chacon believes the cuts to Medicaid coverage are part of the administration’s clampdown on immigrants. She said her son is in no condition to travel.
“I know that’s what he’s doing, but, as my son is, I couldn’t go to Mexico,” Chacon said.
Millions more will be dropped from Medicaid
Medicaid, jointly funded by states and the federal government, has become a political focal point during Trump’s second term. The president has pushed to root out what he describes as fraud in the program. In July, the administration deferred over $1 billion in Medicaid payments to California and Minnesota, claiming there was suspected fraud; critics argued the move targeted Democratic-led states.
As more people are cut from Medicaid, the federal government is predicted to reduce program spending by $911 billion, according to healthcare research nonprofit KFF.
In Arizona, officials said 29,000 legal immigrants were cut from Medicaid rolls on Oct. 1. In Florida, estimates are closer to 177,000. Overall, more than 281,000 immigrants from nine states and the District of Columbia are estimated to lose Medicaid coverage, according to KFF.
As more states implement various restrictions to coverage, 7.5 million people are expected to lose coverage by 2034, according to analysis by the Congressional Budget Office.
Without coverage, people will turn to emergency rooms for care. When people delay seeing a doctor, conditions can worsen and become even more expensive to treat.
“At the end of the day, it does raise the cost for the states because once you get these people in for something that could have been prevented, they could not go to the doctor because they were uninsured; they most likely will end up at a hospital in an emergency room,” said Carmen Feliciano, the vice president of policy and advocacy at UnidosUS, a Latino civil rights organization.
UnidosUS partners with community organizations to help provide medical care, but Feliciano said they already are overwhelmed and would not be able to support the number of people who are going to lose medical coverage in the coming months.
“We are not going to have the capacity to serve all the people who need it,” Feliciano said.

title: Horrified by Maine Library Commission proposal
text:
I was horrified to read that the Maine Library Commission is trying to limit tiny volunteer libraries (“Maine’s volunteer libraries thrive with tight budgets. State rules could make that harder,” Oct. 5). Really? That makes me very sad and angry for the small towns with limited resources.
My grandmother and mother were both teachers and instilled the love of reading and researching in me. I grew up frequenting the library regularly — and I still do as an adult. Our library in Gray is a friendly place to meet fellow book lovers and attend various groups, talks and more.
The ability to borrow books via interlibrary loans is fabulous and the opportunity to use the computers available when I have a power outage at home is invaluable. Certainly even a library that is open only a few days a week is better than no library.
Jan Strout
Gray

title: At least 2 killed by fallen trees since Hurricane Isaias made landfall on Gulf Coast, authorities say
text:
BIRMINGHAM, Ala. (WBRC/Gray News) - Authorities are reporting several deaths since Hurricane Isaias made landfall Friday night in the Florida panhandle.
Two people were reportedly killed in Alabama, with a third in Florida due to fallen trees. Rescuers said those numbers could also increase as crews continued their damage assessments.
According to Birmingham Fire and Rescue, crews were called to a home on Monterey Drive after midnight Saturday regarding two people being trapped inside.
One person was pronounced dead at the scene once rescuers were able to check the home, before later updating their investigation, stating that the second person was also killed.
The Escambia County Sheriff’s Office in Florida additionally confirmed a fatality early Saturday morning since Isaias’ landfall as a Category 2 storm, stating that a downed tree had taken the life of a resident.
Hurricane Isaias battered several states on the Gulf Coast with heavy rain and wind as it tracked north before being downgraded to a post-tropical cyclone later Saturday afternoon into evening.

title: Christa Pike released from hospital, recovering in prison, attorneys say
text:
NASHVILLE (WVLT/Gray News) - Christa Pike has been discharged from a hospital and returned to the Tennessee prison where she has been housed for more than 30 years, her attorneys said.
Pike is receiving continued medical care at the Deborah K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center, according to a statement from her attorneys with Federal Defender Services of Eastern Tennessee and the Tennessee Office of the Post-Conviction Defender.
Deborah K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center is the primary state correctional facility and intake/classification center for female offenders in Tennessee.
Pike, 50, survived two doses of pentobarbital as the state sought to give her a lethal injection eight days ago for the 1995 beating and stabbing death of classmate Colleen Slemmer. The drug didn’t kill her, and her arms were left burned and blistered, according to her lawyers. For the first few days of her hospitalization, Pike was unconscious and on a ventilator.
Her first steps on Wednesday were “limited,” and she required some assistance as she walked on Thursday, her lawyers said in a statement. She is also regaining mobility in her arms, and she was able to eat for the first time.
Gov. Bill Lee has ordered an independent review of the Department of Correction’s actions and paused the remaining scheduled execution this year while the review is underway.
TDOC Commissioner Frank Strada has offered his resignation and is expected to step down this month. An interim commissioner has not yet been announced.

title: Why voting is a Christian duty
text:
The Rev. Ben Cooke is the pastor at Emmanuel Lutheran Episcopal Church in Augusta.
Election season is in full swing; in-person voting in the midterms is now only a few weeks away. So I’d like to take this opportunity to encourage everyone to get out and vote.
As an Episcopalian priest, I regard voting as a Christian duty. It’s our duty because, as Christians, we are called to love God and to love our neighbors as Jesus would love them. Jesus who was always with the poor and the oppressed, the downtrodden and the marginalized.
Voting is an opportunity for us to support policies and platforms that will benefit the least in our society, as Jesus did and commanded us to do. As activists Ken Butigan and Patricia Bruno say on Christian calling: “Our vocation as Christians is to respond to God’s call to join in the divine dance of compassionate and nonviolent love, collaborating with God’s healing power to fashion the conditions for true peace.”
That does not mean we will always agree on how to go about joining the dance of faith. We do not all vote the same, but it does mean we will faithfully seek to live out our Christian values in the way we vote. Elections are not perfect; frequently our candidates fail to live up to their campaign promises.
Despite the human feelings of elected leaders, democracy is still one of the greatest safeguards of the poor. As former British Prime Minister Winston Churchill said: “Democracy is the worst form of government, apart from all the others we have tried.”
Despite democracy’s failings, I believe the right to vote is a fundamental safeguard of our ability to love our neighbors as Jesus would love them. When you have the vote, you matter to those you elect; without it, we are all dependent on the whims of those in power.
Alongside the right to vote, the right to protest is another of democracy’s great protections for the poor. In the Book of Common Prayer, used in worship in my tradition, many of the prayers are called petitions; these are our prayers that ask God for something.
In America, we know petitions as letters of protest presented to legislatures. They are more than just this. Petitions are complaints to someone in power, asking for or even demanding justice for someone who does not have power.
The right to protest nonviolently is a cornerstone of our ability to petition those with power in our nation. Through protest, we demand that the powerful do justice for the poor. Without this right to petition through protest, we don’t even have a prayer for justice for the poor.
I encourage you to not only exercise your right to vote this November, but to nonviolently join “No Kings: Vote Early” protests on Oct. 17 around the state. Let us petition our elected leaders, the powerful in this land, through peaceful protest. Making it clear that the people of Maine wish to continue to choose their government in accord with their faith and conscience. That we do not support monarchy, the unitary executive theory, one-party rule, or any other obstacle to free and fair elections. So shall we all be empowered to make God’s will be done on earth as it is in heaven.

title: Adult acne is real, but there are ways to treat it
text:
Adult acne is real, but there are ways to treat it
Adult acne is real, but there are ways to treat it
As a teenager, Gillian Maegan Montalbo's pimples weren't too bad — just a few bumps on her forehead and nose.
Video above: Dermatologist says skin, nails and hair can reveal health clues
But as an adult in the workforce, the breakouts returned and intensified. The acne on her cheeks and chin made her hesitant to look her bosses in the eye.
"It really took a toll on my self-esteem and my self-confidence," said Montalbo, a marketer and content creator who lives in the Philippines.
Pimples and acne are an uncomfortable hallmark of teenage years, but adults can have breakouts too. Acne can also happen on other parts of the body like the chest and shoulders. And then there's bacne, the internet's term for back breakouts.
The best treatments vary from person to person depending on what's causing the acne and how it looks. And breakouts can leave behind dark marks and scars that take even longer to heal.
Pimples come and go, but if breakouts stick around and cause discoloration or changes in skin texture, it's a good idea to see a dermatologist.
"We know how to treat acne. We know the cause of it. So don't suffer alone," said Dr. Crystal Aguh, a dermatologist and director of the Ethnic Skin Program at Johns Hopkins School of Medicine.
Teenage acne tends to affect the forehead, nose and cheeks. Older adults and women in particular can experience hormonal acne that pops up along the jawline and chin, Aguh said. Taking steroids can also trigger acne for some people.
Pimples happen when tiny pores in the skin get clogged by oil, bacteria and dead skin cells. They can fade over the course of weeks to months, but if patches persist and spread, it could be a sign of acne, which dermatologists consider a medical condition.
"Essentially, you're not getting a break from a breakout," Aguh said.
Acne is caused by many factors including genetics, hormones, environment and even diet — like eating excessive amounts of dairy. The causes of facial and body acne are similar, although skin bacteria sometimes plays a larger role in body acne.
Breakouts can look like milder, painless white bumps or dark specks known as whiteheads and blackheads, or more painful red bumps and deeper cysts — a mark of cystic acne.
There are OTC and prescription treatments for acne
Don't pick or pop your pimples, no matter how strong the urge or how satisfying it might be.
"Everyone wants to pick and squeeze. That will almost always make things worse," said Dr. Lauren Fine, founder of Fine Dermatology in Chicago.
Picking can drive inflammation deeper into the skin and cause acne to spread. It also increases the risk of marks and scarring. For darker-skinned people, those marks take longer to go away because their skin produces extra pigment when stressed, Aguh said.
Treatments for acne range from over-the-counter creams and lotions to prescription-strength medications. Dermatologists say it's somewhat easier to treat acne on the face compared to the rest of the body because the face has more sweat glands and doesn't dry out as easily. It's also harder to apply some treatments like creams to hard-to-reach areas like the back, so doctors often prescribe oral medications.
For milder forms of face acne, dermatologists may recommend face washes or creams containing benzoyl peroxide, salicylic acid or retinoids like adapalene.
For more frequent breakouts, they might prescribe higher-strength regimens like antibiotics or medicines with tretinoin. Isotretinoin may be an option if those medicines don't work, or for cases of severe cystic acne.
Treatments for adult hormonal acne, particularly in women, can differ from what's done for teens. Some dermatologists recommend birth control, which can help stabilize hormones, or treatments like spironolactone.
Shots of cortisone can help treat active acne spots in a pinch, but they aren't a long-term fix, Fine said.
Pimple patches containing a gel called hydrocolloid can absorb fluids from oozing pimples and stop you from picking at them. Aguh said they are suited only for mild forms of acne; Fine said the patches have given some of her patients discoloration and she doesn't recommend them.
Experts say exfoliants and face washes containing glycolic acid can help discoloration fade. Over-the-counter products containing adapalene and retinol creams can also help.
For more serious scarring, dermatologists can recommend more aggressive treatments like lasers that probe deeper into the skin.
It can take time to develop the right treatment plan, and longer still to see results. When starting a new treatment, some people can also experience skin purging: breakouts that happen when a product quickly brings clogged pores to the surface of the skin.
Montalbo's acne cleared up within a year after seeing a dermatologist, but she was still dealing with acne scars. After that, she had to rebuild her self-confidence.
She said a strong support system was essential to getting through some of the hardest moments. Her dad, who also struggled with acne, was the one who encouraged her to see a doctor and find the right products. She also had a close friend who traveled with her overseas for a vacation during the worst of the breakouts, and mentioned in passing that she'd never even noticed Montalbo's acne.
"When you are with the right people, they won't mind how you look," Montalbo said. "Because to them, what's important is how you treat them."

title: Bernie Sanders rallies with Troy Jackson in Bangor as Senate race tightens
text:
BANGOR, Maine — U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders urged a crowd of more than 600 people to vote for Troy Jackson to help Democrats regain control of the U.S. Senate, signaling how serious progressive leaders are taking Maine’s pivotal senatorial election.
“We cannot allow the United States Senate to remain under Republican control,” the Vermont independent said. “If you want to hold Donald Trump and his disastrous policies accountable, the only way we do that is by electing a Democratic Senate.”
The Bangor rally was the first of three planned appearances with Democratic nominee Troy Jackson this weekend. Get-out-the-vote events are scheduled for Lewiston and Biddeford on Sunday. It came a day after a new poll showed a close race and two days after the candidates’ second debate. The contest could help decide control of the U.S. Senate.
Jackson, the former Maine Senate president, focused his remarks on the central message that the government should work for the people, not wealthy donors and corporations. He pointed to his time in the Maine Legislature as an example of his commitment to the people of Maine, and pledged to fight for progressive policies like Medicare for All.
“We’re not from the left, we’re not from the right. We’re from the bottom, and we’re rising,” Jackson said. “I’ve had the honor of having some power in me for 20 years, and I’ve tried to remember one thing: It was never mine. You gave it to me.”
Saturday’s rally was Sanders’ first public appearance in Maine since he rallied in Bar Harbor in June with Graham Platner, whom he had backed for the Senate, and Jackson, who was then running for governor. Platner withdrew in July after an ex-girlfriend accused him of rape, and Jackson replaced him on the ballot. Sanders told NBC’s “Meet the Press” in August that he would endorse Jackson if asked.
Jackson was political director of Sanders’ 2016 presidential campaign in Maine and backed him over Hillary Clinton as a superdelegate. Sanders was among the first prominent endorsers of Jackson’s gubernatorial campaign, which ended with a third-place finish in the June primary. The rally also followed former President Barack Obama’s endorsement of Jackson on Thursday.
A Washington Post-Schar School poll released Friday showed Jackson leading Collins, 50% to 46%, among likely voters, a lead within the margin of error . The survey of about 800 likely voters was conducted Sept. 30 to Oct. 5, before the candidates’ debates. In it, 58% said Collins has been too supportive of President Donald Trump’s agenda.
Collins has long relied on ticket-splitting Democrats to win, and polls have shown her trailing before. She was behind in every 2020 poll before defeating former House Speaker Sara Gideon by nearly 9 points. A Bangor Daily News analysis last month found she likely needs at least 1 in 10 voters who backed Kamala Harris in 2024.
The second debate, hosted by WMTW on Thursday, turned personal. Collins said high earners should pay more into Social Security but did not say whether she would raise or eliminate the cap on taxable income. Jackson accused Collins and her husband of profiting from the Iran war, prompting Collins to demand an apology. Reporting on the couple’s stock holdings did not show them profiting from the war.
Jackson and Collins are scheduled to debate again Tuesday, with WABI and WAGM hosting, and Thursday, with News Center Maine, the Portland Press Herald and Maine Public hosting. The final debate will be held before a live audience at the Gracie Theater in Bangor.

What to do if you encounter wild animals after a major storm
text:
PANAMA CITY, Fla. (WJHG/WECP/Gray News) - Wildlife may be more visible after a major storm, especially in flooded areas.
The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission advises people to keep their distance and give animals space.
The FWC says:
- Alligators and snakes: Keep away. You may see more after a storm. Report concerns about an alligator to the Nuisance Alligator Hotline at 866-392-4286.
- Manatees and sea turtles: Rough weather can strand manatees or wash sea turtle hatchlings ashore. Report a stranded, injured or dead manatee, or a hatchling found tangled in seaweed or somewhere it doesn’t belong, by calling the Wildlife Alert Hotline at (888) 404-3922.
- Bears: Secure food that could attract bears. If spoiled food is in storm debris, keep it separate from other debris. Report conflicts to FWC regional offices during business hours or call the Wildlife Alert Hotline at (888) 404-3922 after hours.
More information is available at Wildlife and Storms and in FWC’s Storm Safety with Wildlife video.

title: CMMC asks labor board to review nurses’ union case
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
LEWISTON, Maine - Central Maine Medical Center is asking the National Labor Relations Board to review its challenge to the hospital’s newly certified nurses’ union.
In September, nurses at the Lewiston hospital voted overwhelmingly to unionize in hopes of negotiating for improved working conditions and benefits.
Before the vote was certified, CMMC asked the National Labor Relations Board’s regional director to block the election results. That request was denied.
The hospital has now filed a request asking the full labor board to review the case, arguing it was not given an explanation for why its original motion was rejected.
A lawyer representing the nurses’ union responded this week, calling the hospital’s appeal “a bad-faith waste of the Board’s time and resources.”
The National Labor Relations Board has not yet ruled on the hospital’s latest request.

title: UNE to launch Nor’easter Global Network during second annual Industry Exploration Day
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The new professional network will connect students with alumni, employers and mentors to support lifelong career development
BIDDEFORD — The University of New England will launch a new University-wide professional network on Wednesday, Oct. 14, connecting students with alumni, employers, faculty, professional staff and other professionals to help them build the relationships, skills and industry knowledge needed to navigate an increasingly dynamic workforce.
The Nor’easter Global Network UNE’s second Industry Exploration Day, an immersive career and networking event that brings employers and industry professionals directly to UNE students to explore career pathways, emerging workforce trends, internships and employment opportunities.
Together, the initiatives represent an expanded approach to career readiness at UNE that extends beyond preparing students for their first jobs. The Nor’easter Global Network is designed to support students and alumni across career stages through meaningful professional connections, mentorship, shared expertise, and access to opportunities.
“Preparing students for successful careers means giving them more than a strong education: It means connecting them with the people, experiences, and opportunities that will help them put that education to work,” UNE President James Herbert said. “The workforce is changing rapidly, and universities have an important role to play in ensuring graduates are prepared to adapt and succeed. Through the Nor’easter Global Network, we are connecting students with people, resources, and professional experiences that will help them build successful careers while strengthening the workforce in Maine and beyond.”
At the center of the network is UNE CareerConnect, a new digital hub designed not only to help Nor’easters discover meaningful connections, but to create a space where knowledge, expertise, and opportunities can easily be shared across the community. More than 17,000 student, alumni, faculty and professional staff, and employer accounts have already been imported into CareerConnect ahead of its Oct. 14 launch, creating an immediate foundation for the network to grow.
The network is designed to grow alongside its members. Students who draw on professional advice, industry expertise, and mentorship while at UNE can remain engaged after graduation, sharing their own experiences with future students while continuing to benefit from connections throughout their careers — forming a continuous cycle in which students become professionals, professionals become mentors, and relationships across the UNE community generate new knowledge and opportunities.
Rather than functioning as a traditional career fair, the annual event emphasizes exploration and relationship-building, giving undergraduate students across disciplines opportunities to speak directly with employers, alumni and industry professionals about career pathways, workforce trends, internships and future employment.
UNE launched Industry Exploration Day in 2025 as part of its broader effort to embed career readiness throughout the student experience. Nearly 30 employers and dozens of industry professionals participated in the inaugural event, representing sectors including health care, finance, technology, construction, hospitality, media and business services. This year’s will expand that reach with over 45
The Nor’easter Global Network and Industry Exploration Day are led by UNE’s Office of Career Readiness and Workforce Development, which was established in 2025 to integrate career development across academic programs, strengthen connections with employers and professional networks, and prepare graduates to adapt to a rapidly changing economy.
“We pay it forward at UNE” Ashley Bigda, M.S.Ed., director of Career Readiness and Workforce Development at UNE, said. “By building a culture of professional trust and reciprocity, the network creates pathways for lifelong mobility. We’re creating a career culture that keeps bringing Nor’easters back to a community invested in one another’s success.”
The University of New England is Maine’s largest independent university, with two beautiful coastal campuses in Maine, a one-of-a-kind study-abroad campus in Tangier, Morocco, and an array of flexible online offerings. In an uncommonly welcoming and supportive community, we offer hands-on learning, empowering students to make a positive impact in a world full of challenges. We are the state’s top provider of health professionals and home to Maine’s only medical and dental colleges, physician assistant program, and pharmacy school, in addition to a variety of other interprofessionally aligned health care programs and nationally recognized programs in the marine sciences, the natural and social sciences, business, the humanities and the arts. Visit www.une.edu.

title: Demolition and sale of buildings shows mismanagement by University of Maine System
text:
Lincoln Tiner earned bachelor’s and master’s degrees in history from the University of Maine and is a prospective student of historic preservation.
The University of Maine System (UMS) cites sustainability as a factor in decisions such as demolishing Crossland Hall and the proposed sale of Handley Hall. Yet, one has to wonder, given their actions, if the system administration knows what that word truly means.
In case a reminder is needed: Merriam Webster’s definition of “sustainable” states it is “of, relating to, or being a method of harvesting or using a resource so that the resource is not depleted or permanently damaged.” If we apply this to the university system’s responsibility of maintaining campus infrastructure, then they would not be depleting and permanently damaging what I consider perfectly good buildings all to later insist on spending millions for new ones.
In Maine, we take care of our things with the understanding that doing so will make them last longer. If you want your vehicle to reach over 200,000 miles, you don’t neglect to change the oil. With that same logic, if UMS expects to run sustainable campuses, they must invest properly in maintenance.
Handley Hall was donated to the University of Maine at Augusta (UMA). In 16 years, the university has allowed this building to go from turnkey to supposedly being so dilapidated that selling it and moving an entire program — while putting it at grave risk of closure — is somehow more affordable. To me, this defies logic.
If UMS simply took responsibility and maintained their buildings appropriately, this would not be an issue. Maintaining a good building is far less expensive than neglecting it and spending money for a new one.
A crucial reminder: This is not their money. It is ours — our tax dollars as hardworking Mainers. And under this current leadership, I believe it is being wasted on failures such as Hotel Ursa and years of staggering salaries for administrators, culminating in the university’s $19 million budget shortfall.
Our tax dollars should be spent on funding — rather than cutting — the faculty, staff, and programs that are teaching the next generation. If we want bright young minds to stay in our state then we cannot continue to allow our university system to be so irresponsible with its finances.
I believe Crossland Hall and Handley Hall are symptoms of much deeper systemic issues with the University of Maine System caused by chronic mismanagement and a lack of accountability to the public. If we are to truly address this issue, then we must listen to those who spend their careers having to work with these administrators.
The University of Maine Faculty Senate recently expressed dissatisfaction with campus and system leadership and the UMA Faculty Senate unanimously passed votes of no confidence in campus president, Jenifer Cushman. Both bodies cited the lack of shared-governance practices with decisions, and at UMA the forced move of programs was cited as a contributing reason for the vote.
I urge our elected representatives to listen to these faculty senates and address this chronic mismanagement. I believe the University of Maine System is well overdue for new leadership.

"Nightmare on the Ridge" at Wallingford's Fruit House and Orchard is offering Mainers plenty of scary attractions all month long. Now in its 10th season, the attractions take months to build, wire and test, but it is all worth it come October.
