title: FBI arrests cybersecurity executive and ransomware expert in major hack on agents' data
text:
FBI arrests cybersecurity executive and ransomware expert in major hack on agents' data
The FBI arrested a Canadian cybersecurity executive and ransomware expert as part of the investigation of a damaging hack that exposed the sensitive data of current and former FBI employees, according to court documents and people familiar with the investigation.
Video above: FBI Director Kash Patel defends policies during congressional hearing
Edward Dubrovsky was arrested in the Philadelphia area in recent days and appeared in federal court there Thursday, where a magistrate judge appointed a federal public defender to represent him. Dubrovsky is facing charges related to extortion and making threats. He has been transferred to Texas’s Eastern District for a scheduled detention hearing, according to court records and a law enforcement official.
FBI Director Kash Patel announced the arrest on Friday but did not disclose where it occurred or what role the man is suspected of playing in the hack. Patel also didn’t name Dubrovsky, but CNN confirmed the defendant is believed to be tied to the FBI hack through multiple people familiar with the investigation.
“Earlier this week, our agents in the field arrested another suspected co-conspirator” of the cybercriminal group believed to be responsible for the hack, Patel said on Friday.
A federal law enforcement official confirmed the spelling of Dubrovsky’s name. In original court documents, his last name was misspelled.
An investigation is ongoing into other people believed to be involved in the hack, the sources said.
Dubrovsky did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Friday night, nor did the public defender’s office in Philadelphia.
A LinkedIn profile under Dubrovsky’s name lists years of experience in the Canadian cybersecurity industry and describes Dubrovsky as a “globally recognized cybersecurity expert.” An Ed Dubrovsky is also the author of a book on handling ransomware negotiations with cybercriminals.
The arrest comes after one of the most serious breaches of the bureau’s data in years. A prolific cybercriminal group known as ShinyHunters last month claimed responsibility for breaking into an FBI jobs portal and gaining access to the personal data on thousands of current and former FBI employees. The identities of FBI personnel working in sensitive units on China and Russia were exposed, according to people who have seen the data.
Independent journalist Brian Krebs earlier reported Dubrovsky’s alleged connection to the investigation into the hack of the FBI.
The FBI declined to comment on Friday night when CNN asked about Dubrovsky’s arrest.
The FBI has pursued other suspects in the investigation. Last week, the FBI announced that Dutch authorities arrested “one of the alleged leaders” of ShinyHunters.
Aftermath of the FBI hack
ShinyHunters used their dark-web site to demand that the FBI amend a previous advisory issued about the group, before the hack, saying it was “offended” over how the agency described its alleged tactics for extorting victim organizations. Many in the cybersecurity industry took the demand as a tacit threat that ShinyHunters would leak the stolen data. The hackers later claimed that was never their intention.
Some FBI employees felt underwhelmed by the security resources being offered to victims of the breach, CNN previously reported.
Amid the internal criticism and media scrutiny, Patel and a senior FBI cyber official, Brett Leatherman, put out a series of public statements and video messages with updates on the investigation. Some were addressed to the cybercriminals.
“Arrests have a way of changing who is willing to talk and seized infrastructure has a way of showing us who is left,” Leatherman said in a video posted after the arrest by Dutch authorities.
“The longer you stay in this, the more we learn about you. You know how to find us, and we know how to find you. I suggest you reach out first while the choice is still yours.”
There has also been an inquest at the FBI over how such a critical security lapse happened. The FBI determined that a contractor managing the bureau’s jobs portal failed to update software “explicitly issued to secure the platform,” Leatherman said last week. The FBI has “removed the contractor,” he said.
The software in question is a human-resources platform made by Oracle, ShinyHunters has said.
The hackers previously used a flaw in the software to attack targets in the education sector in May and June, according to Google’s Threat Intelligence Group. But months later, the FBI contractor apparently still had not applied a security patch that was available for the software.

title: Strawberry farmer hopes steam holds the key to healthy soil and a better crop
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Strawberry farmer hopes steam holds the key to healthy soil and a better crop
Long-time strawberry farmer Rod Koda has rows of plants on his California farm that are still producing fruit well after the harvest would typically end.
The fields brimming with green near the Pacific Coast have produced nearly twice the amount of organic strawberries this year as other plots thanks to steam, he said. The bountiful plots were treated with steam before Koda planted his organic strawberries as part of a project aimed at finding an alternative to chemical fumigants used to kill soil-borne diseases and weeds.
"It's a very noticeable difference," Koda said.
Steam has been used for decades in greenhouses, and researchers in California have been working to adapt the technology to the fields where strawberries, one of the state's key crops, are grown near the Pacific Coast. It's part of a broader push to help organic farmers become more productive and reduce the use of chemicals that environmental advocates say pose a health risk to farmworkers and those who live near the fields.
Rick Tomlinson, president of the California Strawberry Commission, said researchers have been working on steam for more than a decade and are tinkering with the technology so it can be applied to fields faster. The industry has also been working on other alternatives to chemical fumigants, including cutting off oxygen to kill soil disease and developing more resistant plants, he said.
"Fundamentally, there's this disease in the soil, and if you don't have some solution, you're just rolling the dice and one of the years you're going to end up bankrupt," Tomlinson said, "because it can wipe out the entire field."
Nine out of 10 strawberries grown in the United States come from California. The berry, which is grown on 35,000 acres, was one of the state's top 10 commodities in 2025.
Strawberry growers have long relied on chemical fumigants because the fruit is grown close to the ground and is soft and fleshy, making it susceptible to disease, farm experts said. Using a machine to inject steam into the soil before planting can kill key soil-borne diseases and weeds and improve crop productivity, said Jenny Broome, a University of California, Santa Cruz researcher working on the project.
Four growers in California participated in the trials last fall, Broome said. On Koda's farm, the steam-treated plots produced more berries and also suffered less damage from fusarium wilt, a fungal disease, she said.
Steam might also work on fields used for lettuce, carrots and other high-yield crops, she said. A challenge is making steam cost-effective for farmers, and proponents of the technology are trying to speed up the machines used in the process so they can cover more terrain faster.
"We're going back to the future, where we're looking back at an older technology but we're finding more ways to engineer more efficiently and use it," Broome said.
David Andrews, chief science officer for the Environmental Working Group, welcomed the push for an alternative to traditional fumigants, noting farmworkers in the fields and their families are the ones who have been exposed to the chemicals. He said the technology has improved while concerns about the impact of fumigants have risen.
"The economics are shifting," Andrews said.

title: Thankful Maine is without the death penalty
text:
This is in reference to the news report on the botched execution in Tennessee. I fervently hope that anyone who is on the fence about whether to oppose or support this evil, unnecessary practice of the death penalty will now see it for what it is and oppose it.
The reasons go on and on: that it is arbitrary and targets far more Black folks and other minorities; that it is actually more expensive to execute than to sentence to life without parole; that the United States is the only country in the Western world that uses it.
I grew up and lived in Iowa for many years, a state without the death penalty. I met folks from Nebraska, which has the death penalty. They continue to work to defeat it.
Through these folks, I met and became friends with a death row inmate. The state killed him. The night before, he called to say goodbye.
It was horrifying to know this was the last time I would speak with him. This was a man who had been redeemed by good folks. There was no reason to kill him, except for vengeance.
I am so grateful that Maine does not have the death penalty. I would not live here if it did.
Barbara Doughty
Portland

title: Anthropic's Claude AI submits a false tip on a Philadelphia unsolved homicide case
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — An Anthropic artificial intelligence model submitted a false tip to a Philadelphia police website about an unsolved homicide case, authorities and Anthropic said.
It’s the latest example of AI models acting in unintended ways and manipulating government and other websites during tests. In a report Friday, Anthropic also disclosed a separate incident when its AI model submitted forms to an undisclosed government website instead of stopping before submission.
The incident in Philadelphia occurred on July 18 when the AI model Claude Haiku 4.5 was tasked with generating and performing example tasks on randomly selected webpages, Anthropic said.
Claude filled out a form on police site PhillyUnsolvedMurders.com indicating it might have information regarding an unsolved murder listed on the site.
Philadelphia Police said in a statement they were unaware of the incident until Anthropic notified them on Wednesday. Then they found the submission in the website’s tip records and confirmed it was marked spam and never forwarded to police.
There are rising concerns about AI companies’ unchecked AI agents meddling with everything from U.S. government websites to healthcare data. Critics have been calling for more regulation.
In September, another AI company, OpenAI, disclosed six reports of “unexpected or concerning” behavior in artificial-intelligence models.
“Unsolved cases involve real victims, grieving families and investigators working to secure answers,” the Philadelphia Police Department said in a statement. “Technology companies must take all appropriate steps necessary to prevent their systems from submitting false information to law enforcement.”
Anthropic said in its report that most of the reported behaviors are forms of what it calls “persistence” — “in which Claude, when it cannot complete a task as given, works around a restriction instead of stopping.”
The company said it was modifying its training to “reduce the likelihood of further misbehavior.”
Anthropic said it briefed the White House on cases that involved U.S. government agencies at the federal, state and local levels, and notified each agency involved.

title: Stetson looks back at how the cowboy hat helped shape America
text:
GARLAND, Texas (Gray DC) - As America continues to celebrate its 250th birthday, the company behind the modern cowboy hat is reflecting back on how it helped shape the country into what it is today.
“I think Stetson played a pretty vital role over the period of its history,” said Robert Dundon, CEO of the Stetson hat company. ”Particularly in the first 25 or 30 years with the expansion, to provide something that just didn’t exist at the time."
The “Boss of the Plains” Stetson was the first cowboy hat, invented by John B. Stetson in Colorado in 1865. The entrepreneur created the wide-brimmed hat to protect pioneers from the elements, just as westward expansion in the U.S. was beginning to accelerate.
“So the expansion was dangerous conditions, harsh weather. People were really in perilous places,” Dundon said. “So the hat was a tool really to provide them with protection from the elements, from the rain and the harsh conditions that they were facing.”
Before the Stetson was invented, most headwear brims would fall down when wet because they were made with raccoon skin or wool.
“Nobody had a big hat with a big brim, something to protect. So then he created this, and then he sold the first piece for $5, and it was a cowboy hat shape,” said Devin Marcum, the president of HatCo, which manufactures Stetson hats.
The hats quickly became popular after Stetson built his first factory in Philadelphia. By 1888, the company was the largest hat manufacturer in the world and it was turning into an American icon.
“It’s been one of these quintessential American pieces that has found its way into all sort of walks of life and use for for people who are hat wearers,” Dundon said.
Throughout the 20th and 21st centuries, Stetsons have been worn by ranchers, members of law enforcement, celebrities, rodeo riders and several U.S. presidents, including Ulysses S. Grant, Harry S. Truman, Dwight D. Eisenhower, Lyndon B. Johnson, Ronald Reagan, George W. Bush and Donald Trump.
Interest in cowboy hats has increased significantly in recent years, especially during the COVID-19 pandemic.
“All of a sudden we had orders flying through for cowboy hats,” Marcum said. “That came from a lot of things. I think people were now venturing out of cities and towns and being in more outdoor areas, being in more ranches, different things. And so the cowboy coolness really took over.”
The brand’s story continues to live on in Garland, Texas, where HatCo has been making Stetsons, after the Philadelphia factory was closed in 1970.
“There’s a lot of third and fourth generational families that have worked here,” Marcum said. “So I think it has something to do with the culture that we have here, the products that we get to build, the sense of pride that, when they’re working with building the Stetson brand hats, it’s something that they get to go home about, brag about.”
And even 161 years after the Stetson was first created, Dundon said the hats continue to be a popular way to express American identity.
“The cowboy hat is uniquely American,” he said. “...It reflects back to a time in our history where this ruggedness, this individual pursuit for an American way of life. I think the cowboy hat encapsulates a lot of that.”

title: Hundreds of thousands without power after Isaias slams the Florida Panhandle and Alabama
text:
Hundreds of thousands without power after Isaias slams the Florida Panhandle and Alabama
Hundreds of thousands of people in Alabama and the Florida Panhandle were without power early Saturday after Isaias crashed into the U.S. Gulf Coast as a dangerous hurricane and left flooded roads and downed trees in its wake as it moved inland.
Video above shows storm surge in Destin, Florida, as Hurricane Isaias makes landfall
The storm made landfall Friday as a Category 2 hurricane, then quickly moved north through Alabama as its wind speeds dropped sharply. But the possibility of life-threatening storm surges still loomed for parts of the Florida Panhandle, along with heavy rain and potential flooding for much of the Southeast over the weekend.
Forecasters also warned that conditions could stir up tornadoes across parts of the Florida Panhandle and into Georgia and the Carolinas.
Isaias made landfall near Destin, Florida, as the first hurricane of the Atlantic season. Hurricane-force winds lashed the Gulf shoreline in the low-lying coastal area known for powdery white-sand beaches dotted with vacation homes, waterfront bars, and seafood shacks.
"The storm is here. Buckle down at this point. Don't be getting out on the roads," Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said at a news conference Friday.
Roads in Destin were flooded, while in nearby Pensacola, police warned residents to stay off the streets because of debris across roadways. While the extent of the damage was not immediately known, many area residents posted pictures online of downed trees and power lines, and one social media video, below, showed a roof being ripped off an inn in Pensacola.
Some Panhandle counties temporarily suspended emergency response Friday night because of dangerous conditions.
Video above: Heavy wind and rain in Destin, Florida, as Isaias makes landfall
More than 726,000 customers in Florida and Alabama were without power early Saturday, according to poweroutage.com.
Tim Mowry, who rode out the storm from his home in Pensacola, said the wind was so intense it sounded like a train whistle as it whipped through a crack in his patio door. He lost power around 4:30 p.m. but was able to rely on a generator. Standing water also covered his backyard, and parts of his fence were ripped down, but overall he said the storm wasn't as bad as he expected.
"As far as Pensacola-wise, we really got fortunate," Mowry said.
Mowry said his son, who lives about 15 minutes away, tried to drive to his home after losing power but had to turn around because downed trees and power lines blocked the roads.
Despite weakening, heavy rain is forecast as Isaias moves inland, with 4 to 8 inches (10 to 20 centimeters) or even more expected through the weekend from southern Alabama, the Florida Panhandle and Big Bend, and southwest Georgia.
The storm also grounded most Friday flights at several Panhandle airports, including all flights into and out of Destin-Fort Walton Beach Airport. President Donald Trump, meanwhile, scrapped his plans to attend Saturday's football game between the University of Georgia and the University of Alabama in Tuscaloosa. He said he didn't want to disrupt emergency response efforts.
Meanwhile, in the Pacific, Simon strengthened into a Category 4 hurricane as it approached Mexico's coast.
Tropical Storm Rachel was also expected to bring heavy winds and rain to northern Mexico and Southern California over the weekend.

title: Freeze and Frost alerts issued for parts of Maine Sunday

Freeze and Frost alerts issued for parts of Maine Sunday
Freeze Warning and a Frost Advisory from 2 a.m. to 8 a.m.
Freeze and Frost alerts issued for parts of Maine Sunday
Freeze Warning and a Frost Advisory from 2 a.m. to 8 a.m.
Residents across portions of Maine and New Hampshire should prepare for freezing temperatures and frost early Sunday morning, October 11. The National Weather Service in Gray, Maine, has maintained a Freeze Warning and a Frost Advisory from 2 a.m. to 8 a.m. EDT Sunday.
Temperatures could drop as low as 30 degrees in parts of Maine, creating conditions that could damage or kill sensitive outdoor plants. Residents are encouraged to take precautions Saturday evening to protect vegetation before temperatures fall overnight.
A Freeze Warning remains in effect for central interior Cumberland and Androscoggin counties in Maine. Temperatures as low as 30 degrees are expected between 2 a.m. and 8 a.m. Sunday, increasing the risk of damage to uncovered plants and gardens.
The warning includes the communities of Gorham, New Gloucester, Auburn, Livermore Falls, Greene, Turner, North Windham, Sabattus, Wales, Lewiston, Gray and Minot.
A Frost Advisory is also in effect from 2 a.m. to 8 a.m. Sunday for portions of south-central and southwestern Maine, along with central and southern New Hampshire. Temperatures falling into the mid-30s could lead to frost formation, which may harm sensitive outdoor vegetation.
Residents should cover tender outdoor plants with sheets or frost-protection fabric before temperatures begin to drop. Potted plants should be moved indoors or placed in a sheltered location whenever possible. Taking these precautions before bedtime can help reduce the risk of damage from frost and freezing temperatures.

title: The United Auto Workers tries to reassert political power in Michigan as it faces internal divisions
text:
SHELBY TOWNSHIP, Mich. (AP) — Walter Usakowski was mowing his lawn in a northern suburb of Detroit when three canvassers from the United Auto Workers approached.
“I don’t even need to talk to you,” Usakowski said. As a retired member, he was already supporting the union’s slate of Democratic candidates in the Nov. 3 midterms.
But he is not sure how many of the other “guys in the shop” will vote for Democrats. He worked at Ford Motor Co.’s Sterling Axle Plant for more than 45 years, and he knows many members who backed Republican President Donald Trump.
The election-year canvassing was one part of the UAW’s efforts to reassert its political power in Michigan, a premier political battleground. Although the union generally backs Democrats, its membership is more divided over which party best represents working-class interests. It also is reckoning with past corruption scandals, a drop in membership and a lack of transparency that has eroded trust within its ranks.
“It’s not going to be an overnight thing,” said JJ Jewell, who is part of the UAW’s Community Action Program executive committee. “Even if this election goes fantastically, that’s not mission accomplished. That means we’re 1% of the way done.”
Internal divisions and distrust pose challenges
Jewell and others made the rounds on a recent sunny Saturday in Macomb County, where Trump won by nearly 14 percentage points in 2024. Many of the union members they met in a neighborhood of well-kept suburban houses were retirees, and while most said the cost of living was their top concern, they did not agree on whether Democrats or Republicans would better address it.
One resident, who said she blamed billionaires for the country’s problems, planned to vote for Democrats. Another street over, a couple said they both supported Trump and declined to take a flyer of the UAW-endorsed candidates.
In a microcosm of broader political rifts, union voters remain politically divided. Union voters have traditionally been seen as a Democratic-leaning constituency, but Trump made direct appeals to them with his anti-elite rhetoric and promises to overhaul international trade agreements that sapped factory jobs. In 2024, voters who were union members or were in a household with a union member split between Trump and Democratic nominee Kamala Harris, with more than half voting for the then-vice president and 44% for Trump.
Betty Anderson, a UAW member, thinks the organization is on the right track, but she is not confident about bridging internal political divisions. She said she is angry with members who voted for Trump, whom she sees as selling out the working class.
“I don’t think those people are ever going to be on our side,” Anderson said. “They think they have an opportunity to be in an elite class.”
Leaders hope to rebuild trust with transparency
Since 2017, more than 10 UAW officials have pleaded guilty in a corruption investigation that found millions of dollars of union dues were stolen. Members also faulted leaders for closed-door contract negotiations that they said destroyed trust in the UAW.
Shawn Fain was elected UAW president in 2023 on a platform of transparency, and victories in labor disputes with Detroit’s three major automakers bolstered member support. Leaders hope this will translate into votes for its candidates.
“I think the UAW members now are starting to fall a little more in line,” said Usakowski, the retired axle plant worker.
Mark DePaoli, director for one of the UAW’s southeast Michigan regions, said the union hosted forums with candidates where any member could ask questions. The UAW endorsed progressive Democrat Abdul El-Sayed in the U.S. Senate primary even though rival Haley Stevens, a four-term congresswoman, worked as chief of staff on an auto bailout task force during the Great Recession, a position she frequently cited while campaigning.
“I don’t think anybody expected us to endorse him,” DePaoli said. In its announcement, the union referenced El-Sayed’s support for universal healthcare and criticism of corporate money in politics. El-Sayed wore a UAW pin during the first Senate debate with his Republican opponent, former U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers.
“The UAW’s backing of Abdul was critical in winning a historic primary despite being outspent by tens of millions of dollars, and will be just as critical in winning” next month, El-Sayed spokesperson Cole Wozniak said in a statement.
Rogers is emphasizing his opposition to controversial federal regulations under Democratic President Joe Biden that would have required automakers to ramp up production of electric vehicles, which some feared would lead to factory closures.
“Mike knows the challenges our autoworkers face, and he’ll be their champion in the U.S. Senate,” Rogers spokesperson Alyssa Brouillet said in a statement. “The same can’t be said for Abdul and UAW national leadership.”
The union needs to turn out the vote to be politically relevant
Robert Bruno, a professor in the School of Labor and Employment Relations at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, said the UAW’s strength relies on its ability to mobilize voters.
“You don’t win campaigns off of your endorsements,” Bruno said. “You win campaigns at the door, or at the bar, or at the union hall.”
In the 1980s, there were more than 600,000 active and retired UAW members in Michigan, according to the union. Today, that number hovers around 350,000. The UAW is still the largest union in the state.
UAW leaders are optimistic after a primary election campaign drive and what they see as better, more transparent leadership. The union said about 113,000 of its members voted early during Michigan’s August primary, and it has volunteers canvassing and calling voters before Election Day.
In September, the UAW hosted a conference of its Michigan political arm for the first time since 2018. Fain, who claimed reelection Friday based on preliminary results in the voting, told reporters at the Lansing event that the organization wants members to drive the direction of the union, focusing on issues like affordability.
“We are as active as we can be right now,” Fain said.
___
GaNun is a corps member for The Associated Press/Report for America Statehouse News Initiative. Report for America is a nonprofit national service program that places journalists in local newsrooms to report on undercovered issues.

title: Isaias weakens but flooding threats persist as hundreds of thousands grapple with power outages
text:
GULF BREEZE, Fla. (AP) — Isaias weakened overnight and was no longer considered a hurricane but flash flooding threats and the potential for tornadoes persisted Saturday as the storm moved inland across Alabama.
The storm, now considered a post-tropical cyclone, made landfall Friday as a Category 2 hurricane, then quickly moved north through Alabama as its wind speeds dropped sharply to 35 mph (55 kph). But the possibility of life-threatening storm surges still loomed for parts of the Florida Panhandle, along with a potential for 4 to 8 inches (10 to 20 centimeters) of rain across southern Alabama, the Florida Panhandle and Big Bend over the weekend.
Early Saturday, Isaias was about 25 miles (40 kilometers) south-southwest of Montgomery, Alabama and nearly 105 miles (170 kilometers) south of Birmingham, Alabama, with maximum sustained winds of 35 mph (55 kph), the NHC said Saturday. It is expected to move into the Tennessee Valley later Saturday and Sunday.
All tropical storm and storm surge warnings have been discontinued. But forecasters warned that conditions could stir up tornadoes across parts of the Florida Panhandle and into Georgia and the Carolinas.
Isaias made landfall near Destin, Florida, as the first hurricane of the Atlantic season. Hurricane-force winds lashed the Gulf shoreline in the low-lying coastal area known for powdery white-sand beaches dotted with vacation homes, waterfront bars, and seafood shacks.
“The storm is here. Buckle down at this point. Don’t be getting out on the roads,” Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said at a news conference Friday.
Roads in Destin were flooded, while in nearby Pensacola, police warned residents to stay off the streets because of debris across roadways. While the extent of the damage was not immediately known, many area residents posted pictures online of downed trees and power lines, and one social media video showed a roof being ripped off an inn in Pensacola.
Some Panhandle counties temporarily suspended emergency response Friday night because of dangerous conditions.
Parts of southern Alabama also were flooded, with officials in Mobile reporting downed trees and power lines. Roads in Houston County, which is in the southeastern corner of the state, were closed because of similar conditions.
More than 911,000 customers in Florida, Alabama and Georgia were without power early Saturday, according to poweroutage.com.
Tim Mowry, who rode out the storm from his home in Pensacola, said the wind was so intense it sounded like a train whistle as it whipped through a crack in his patio door. He lost power around 4:30 p.m. but was able to rely on a generator. Standing water also covered his backyard, and parts of his fence were ripped down, but overall he said the storm wasn’t as bad as he expected.
“As far as Pensacola-wise, we really got fortunate,” Mowry said.
Mowry said his son, who lives about 15 minutes away, tried to drive to his home after losing power but had to turn around because downed trees and power lines blocked the roads.
Isaias, the first hurricane to hit the eastern U.S. since Milton tore up the Gulf Coast of Florida in 2024, is also expected to bring heavy rain and potential flooding to much of the Southeast over the weekend, then to parts of the Midwest and Northeast into Monday.
The storm also grounded most Friday flights at several panhandle airports, including all flights into and out of Destin-Fort Walton Beach Airport. President Donald Trump, meanwhile, scrapped his plans to attend Saturday’s football game between the University of Georgia and the University of Alabama in Tuscaloosa. He said he didn’t want to disrupt emergency response efforts.
Meanwhile, in the Pacific, Simon strengthened into a Category 4 hurricane as it approached Mexico’s coast.
Tropical Storm Rachel was also expected to bring heavy winds and rain to northern Mexico and Southern California over the weekend.
___
Megnien reported from Panama City, Florida, Golden reported from Seattle, and Seewer reported from Toledo, Ohio. Seth Borenstein and Collin Binkley in Washington; Rio Yamat in Las Vegas; Gerald Herbert in Pensacola, Florida; Dave Collins in Hartford, Connecticut; Sarah Raza in Sioux Falls, South Dakota; Kim Chandler in Montgomery, Alabama; and Laura Turbay in Little Rock, Arkansas contributed to this report.

title: I’m all for Bowdoinham’s new four-way stop
text:
Jeremy Cluchey lives in Bowdoinham.
To borrow the words of conservative commentator David Frum, stop signs are not “the first step on a slippery slope to the abolition of motion.”
Somebody needs to tell the folks in Bowdoinham’s community Facebook group.
For the past few weeks, there’s been a collective meltdown over a new four-way stop being tested out at the village’s lone intersection. After decades of only having to stop when traveling north or south, the addition of an east-west halt is generating a frankly stunning level of criticism, condemnation and ire.
Of course, if you’ve spent any time on the internet over the past 20 years, it shouldn’t be stunning to see people get wrapped around an axle over something as seemingly minor as new stop signs. Every town in America has its own version of the great four-way stop Facebook debate at this point. It may be the one modern experience that unites us all.
It can be funny, at first, to see how worked up people get over a little old stop sign. But over time, it’s become clear that there are real casualties to these virtual feeding frenzies. Town staff, local officials and volunteers working to improve their communities get caught in the crossfire, burn out from all the thankless negativity and end up opting to step away from civic life rather than be targeted on social media every day. We’ve lost a lot of good folks in the Great Keyboard Wars.
Has it always been like this? A few years ago, I was talking with a town manager in a small central Maine municipality who referred to the local, vocal critics of a particular project as “cavepeople.” When I expressed surprise that he’d characterize his residents that way, he explained that “C.A.V.E.” is an acronym — it stands for “Citizens Against Virtually Everything.”
Community contrarians have always been around, but social media has turned them into local influencers. In the good old days, a loud complainer was just a grumpy Gus who occasionally made a good point; now he has a digital megaphone for his gripes and a platform for others to pile on. Conflict researcher Amanda Ripley calls these folks “conflict entrepreneurs” — people who intentionally inflame disputes, reduce complex questions to simple binaries and delight in the drama.
All this incessant pot-stirring makes it harder than ever for people to improve their communities. Change is scary — but at a moment when even the most ardent contrarians agree that things could be a fair sight better than they are right now, isn’t it also necessary? At least a little? And if we’re going to try a little change, what better place to start than with a couple new stop signs in downtown Bowdoinham?
Yes, that’s right, I am hereby announcing my loud, proud support for Bowdoinham’s new four-way stop. It slows traffic through the village, it’s safer for pedestrians, and it gives me a chance to downshift my 1984 Chevy before I turn up the big hill on Main Street when I’m loaded down with recycling. Stalling out on that hill is literally one of my biggest fears in life, and now I don’t have to worry about it. Thank you, Bowdoinham stop signs!
I realize this hot take may get me flayed in my hometown Facebook group. It’s a risk I’m willing to take. And maybe, after we have our fill of the comments section, we’ll decide that today is a good day to step out of our respective caves, meet up at our town’s newly calm intersection and complain about the world together, in person, the way God intended.

title: High school golf rankings gave players a new perspective this season
text:
VASSALBORO — Colin Mitchell saw the rankings. The Lincoln Academy junior didn’t agonize over them, but yeah, he checked them out.
Sixth in Class B, 16th in the state, according to the Maine high school golf rankings that made their debut this fall.
“I kind of saw it as an opportunity to prove myself,” Mitchell said after winning the Class B individual state title Saturday afternoon at Natanis Golf Club. “I’m sixth. I’ve got nothing to lose, really.”
The idea for a statewide ranking had percolated in Brian Bickford’s brain for a while. How could Maine Golf, the state’s governing body for the sport, make it happen?
“I always was intrigued by Heal points,” Bickford said, referring to the system by which the MPA ranks teams to seed the tournament in most high school sports. “For me, it kind of brings the state together.”
How does a player from Fort Kent compare with a player from York when they’ve played entirely different courses all season, in different conditions? This ranking system helps quantify what had been unquantifiable.
Bickford, the executive director for Maine Golf, who also coaches the University of Southern Maine golf team, enlisted Alex Grant in the endeavor. A 2024 Nokomis High grad and a member of the USM golf team, Grant worked on creating the ranking system.
An information technology major, the project was right in Grant’s wheelhouse. The rankings include the player’s score, course slope and course rating. To put it in basic terms, the better a player shoots on a tougher course, the higher he or she will rank.
It goes beyond the eye test and score comparisons. Taking a course’s rating into account gives a more accurate measure of a player. A plus-2 on a more challenging course has to be considered more impressive than an even-par round on an easier one, right?
“I wish it was something I had when I was in high school, whether I was ranked 1,000 or first,” Grant said.
Winthrop junior Kaydence Allarie knew entering her round Saturday that she was the top-ranked girl in Class C. She was a little nervous, especially with 18 holes to play rather than the typical nine played in the regular season.
Allarie probably had the healthiest attitude toward the rankings.
“Anything can happen,” she said. “You pretty much just play and do your best. I just wanted to stay consistent and not worry about everyone else. Just be me.”
The more rounds played, the more accurate the rankings should be. Anyone can have a bad day, the kind that makes you want to give your putter a Viking funeral. Anyone can have a great day, too, when every tee shot finds the middle of the fairway and you read every green perfectly.
The rankings work as a complete picture, Grant said. As the season moved from late August to early October, the minimum number of matches required to be ranked increased.
“The more the merrier. It gave you a better ranking,” Grant said.
The rankings, available for viewing at mainegolf.org, rank individual players in each class, as well as teams. Going into Class B state championship, Mitchell and his Lincoln Academy teammates figured through the ranking that Freeport and Fryeburg Academy would be their top competition for the team title.
In Class C, the top-ranked team was Winthrop, ahead of Dexter and Calais.
To the MPA’s credit, they love it.
“I feel a little guilty. People keep thanking me and congratulating me, and I had little to nothing to do with it,” said Todd Sampson, the MPA assistant executive director.
To the MPA, submitting results for the rankings was strictly voluntary this fall. The MPA doesn’t have any plans to use the rankings in determining which golfers play with whom at the state championships. Maybe that’ll change in a few years, when there’s more data to analyze and any kinks or bugs have been ironed out.
Sampson said a few athletic directors have expressed interest in using the rankings as a barometer for choosing all-conference players, since it covers a player’s complete season of work if data is entered dilligently after each match.
For this debut season, the rankings gave high school golfers something to talk about. And for some, maybe a little motivation.

title: Maine State Police investigating fatal crash on I-95 in Gray
text:
Maine State Police are investigating a car crash that killed one passenger and injured two drivers and an additional passenger Friday night on I-95 in Gray.
Police say 31-year old Megan Stuart, of Auburn, was northbound in a 2010 Honda Fit near mile marker 60 at around 11:47 p.m. on Friday when she swerved to avoid a deer, striking a guardrail and spinning into oncoming traffic. The vehicle crashed head-on into a northbound 2016 Chevy Malibu.
Stuart’s passenger, 38-year-old Soda Mao, of Auburn, was killed in the collision. Stuart was transported to Maine Medical Center with non-life-threatening injuries, and the driver and passenger of the Chevy Malibu suffered minor injuries.
The Falmouth Fire Department and Cumberland County Sheriff’s Office assisted at the scene. Authorities shut part of the Maine Turnpike down for approximately 20 minutes to clear the scene and closed lane 1 for two hours.
The crash remains under investigation, according to Maine State Police.

title: CMP shares northern Maine transmission route with legislators
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The Maine Republican Caucus got the first look this week at a proposed transmission line route designed to move electricity from Aroostook County to the New England grid.
The Central Maine Power/Avangrid 1,200-megawatt transmission line, connecting northern Maine to the regional grid through substations in Haynesville and Pittsfield, is part of the planned Northern Maine Renewable Energy Development Program.
The 108-mile route already has some Mainers concerned about how it will affect their homes, farms, and northern Maine’s abundant wildlife and wilderness.
The discussion with legislators was one of many that will take place over the coming weeks and months as engineering, environmental review, permitting and other planning activities move forward, CMP officials said.
“We have begun briefing stakeholders, including elected officials, about the project, and those conversations will continue as development advances and additional details are refined,” CMP spokesman Jonathan Breed said.
In August, the Maine Public Utilities Commission chose CMP from an undisclosed list of bidders to enter into contract negotiations for the development and construction of the project’s transmission line portion.
The utility’s proposal for a transmission line from Pittsfield to Haynesville was the best for the state, commissioners said, citing CMPs planned use of existing transmission corridors.
“By following existing corridors and rights-of-way where transmission infrastructure already exists, we can minimize community impacts, reduce environmental disturbance, and limit uncertainty as the project moves forward,” Breed said.
The regulators also chose Clearway Energy Group LLC, headquartered in San Francisco, for an 800-megawatt onshore wind project that will generate electricity for transmission to the grid.
The procurement is a multistate effort that also involves Massachusetts, Connecticut, Vermont and Rhode Island. With five New England states sharing in regional transmission project costs, Maine ratepayers could pay much less of the overall cost for a northern project, according to clean energy experts.
The commission’s selection is an important milestone, but the project remains at the beginning of a multiyear development process, Breed said. Before construction can begin, work will include engineering, environmental review, permitting, agency coordination and stakeholder engagement.
Timeline
CMP aims for a “transparent process” that will include input from communities, landowners, local officials, tribes and other stakeholders, he said. The project will address constraints that have limited northern Maine’s connection to the regional grid.
Rep. Mathew McIntyre, R-Lowell, attended this week’s meeting with CMP. From what he could see on the map, a portion goes through his district, House District 18, he said.
McIntyre said he is cautiously optimistic and sees a potential benefit, but has many questions and wants to make sure the project will actually benefit Maine ratepayers.
“I believe Maine is facing an energy crisis that we must address,” he said. “The decisions that are being made in Augusta, and not just the legislative branch but executive branch, have resulted in the condition that we are currently in.”
He is sensitive to the concerns of rural Mainers who do not want an energy project near their homes and those who struggle to pay escalating power bills, he said.
“This project is designed to facilitate moving power out of the state and I want to make sure that whatever the end result is that there is a tangible benefit to Maine ratepayers,” he said. “This contract award is in such infancy, the project recipients still have to navigate layers and layers of gateways, permitting processes and financing that go into a project.”
The PUC declined a Bangor Daily News request for all the bids submitted to the regulator for the generation and transmission portions of the project, citing a 10-year-old precedent.
According to a new state law, beginning Jan. 1, 2026, all records and documents regarding the competitive bidding process, including question-and-answer summaries, evaluation team packets and award decision letters, are public documents.
This is the commission’s second attempt to solicit bids for generation and transmission from northern Maine to the New England power grid under a 2021 state law, following the failed King Pine Wind and LS Power project.
The King Pine and LS Power project was plagued by a complicated contracting process, long delays and cost increases. State regulators reopened the project’s bid window in April only after taking measured steps to avoid a similar fate.
“The map released [this week] shows the location of the Haynesville substation only as a square,” Tanya Blanchard of Landowner’s Voice said. “It does not provide a site plan or indicate how much land the new substation will occupy. We don’t yet have the current design details.”
As the development moves forward, CMP will work closely with communities, landowners, and stakeholders to ensure the project is planned and delivered responsibly and transparently, Breed said.
A group of Haynesville residents, concerned that their way of life will be drastically altered with the addition of the project’s substation, have formed the Haynesville Maine Residents MPUC-Avangrid Substation Awareness Group.
In this Aroostook County town of 97, there are no stores and no gas stations — and some residents said they like it that way.
“That’s why we are here. It’s a recluse’s paradise,” resident Alan Trudeau said. “There’s nothing but wilderness and abundant wildlife.”
The Haynesville group, which started meeting last month, has presented to the select board a signed petition for a new ordinance related to energy development. The ordinance calls for a pause on substation activity, new transmission lines, wind farms, solar farms and data centers, said Trudeau, the document’s creator.
“The moratorium is only temporary, up to 180 days, and we can vote to extend it for another 180 days,” he said. “It’s a beautiful place and to have a substation of this magnitude come into this town is scary. It’s something that we don’t want but it sounds to me like we have no choice. We are hoping it will come up at the Tuesday select board meeting.”
The Haynesville Select Board meeting is at 6 p.m. Tuesday at the town office on Danville Road.

title: Maine cannot afford to lose Susan Collins’ bipartisan voice in Washington
text:
KC Johnson is a professor of history at Brooklyn College and lives in Scarborough.
By now, most of us have seen the ad dozens of times. Four (identified) female narrators castigate Sen. Susan Collins for never standing up to President Trump.
The narrators focus on three issues: the Iran war, Medicaid cuts and the Supreme Court’s reversal of Roe v. Wade. They cite four votes by Collins: against a measure to invoke the War Powers Resolution on the Iran war, in favor of a measure to allow Senate debate on Trump’s major funding bill last year and to confirm Brett Kavanaugh and Neil Gorsuch, two of the five justices who voted to overturn Roe.
The ad doesn’t mention that Collins (along with 2nd District Democrat Jared Golden,
whose votes followed a similar path) subsequently voted in favor of invoking the
War Powers Resolution on Iran. Or that she voted against passing the Trump 2025
spending bill.
Most misleadingly, the ad does not note that Collins has voted to confirm all three pro-choice justices on the Court (Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan and Ketanji Brown Jackson). Nor does it reveal that she broke from Trump to oppose the 2020 confirmation of Amy Coney Barrett, who provided the fifth vote necessary to reverse Roe. In fact, if the Court consisted solely of justices who earned Collins’ support, it seems likely that Roe would still be the law of the land.
The thrust of the ad, funded by a group called WinSenate, seems to be that independence or open-mindedness is a bad thing in a senator. Two of the narrators place independence in air quotes as they describe Collins. And the three issues chosen — Iran, the 2025 spending bill and Trump’s Supreme Court nominees — are ones where Collins has taken independent positions from the president.
Perhaps such a claim is unfair to WinSenate. Their ads identify a website — winsenate.org — where Maine voters can go to learn more about the group’s positions, which is funded by a super PAC affiliated with Senate Democrats.
I visited the website to try to get more information on why the organization seems so hostile to an independent approach in the Senate, and in particular what justification the group could have to attribute the reversal of Roe to Collins, given her opposition to Barrett’s confirmation.
The website consists solely of a photograph of the American flag. It provides no statement of principles about the group’s mission, no rationalization for its hostility to a senator who doesn’t always vote a party line and no explanations to bolster its claims.
The two WinSenate ads about Collins analyzed by the fact-checking website PolitiFact
are rated “false” and “mostly false.”
As someone who voted for Joe Brennan in the 1996 Senate race, Chellie Pingree in
2002, Tom Allen in 2008 and even Shenna Bellows (who lost by a greater than 2-1 margin to Collins) in 2014, I understand the impulse to vote against Collins. But 2026 is not 1996, nor even 2014.
With Collins chairing the Appropriations Committee, her demonstrated clout on behalf of the state highlights her importance to the state.
Perhaps more importantly, at a time when American politics is more polarized than it’s been in decades, it’s critical to maintain one of the Senate’s few bipartisan voices — especially since the Democrats’ replacement nominee, Troy Jackson, seems likely to be little more than an automatic vote for whatever position Bernie Sanders or Elizabeth Warren take, rather than an independent vote for Maine.
A 2026 vote for Collins provides a way to resist the two parties’ race to ideological extremes — and, perhaps, also a way to reject misleading ads that, as here, quite literally wrap themselves in the American flag and hope that voters don’t look too closely into their underlying claims.

All this incessant pot-stirring makes it harder than ever for people to improve their communities. Change is scary — but at a moment when even the most ardent contrarians agree that things could be a fair sight better than they are right now, isn’t it also necessary? At least a little? And if we’re going to try a little change, what better place to start than with a couple new stop signs in downtown Bowdoinham?
Yes, that’s right, I am hereby announcing my loud, proud support for Bowdoinham’s new four-way stop. It slows traffic through the village, it’s safer for pedestrians, and it gives me a chance to downshift my 1984 Chevy before I turn up the big hill on Main Street when I’m loaded down with recycling. Stalling out on that hill is literally one of my biggest fears in life, and now I don’t have to worry about it. Thank you, Bowdoinham stop signs!
I realize this hot take may get me flayed in my hometown Facebook group. It’s a risk I’m willing to take. And maybe, after we have our fill of the comments section, we’ll decide that today is a good day to step out of our respective caves, meet up at our town’s newly calm intersection and complain about the world together, in person, the way God intended.

title: Knicks champion Karl-Anthony Towns opens up about grief for World Mental Health Day
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — Karl-Anthony Towns has been traded from Minnesota, lost the conference finals and won the NBA title for his childhood team — and still feels he is in the period of grief that began six years ago.
Just 10 days before the New York Knicks’ banner-raising celebration, the All-Star big man marked World Mental Health Day by sharing his ongoing emotional journey following the death of his mother to complications from COVID-19.
Entering the first game of this year’s NBA Finals, he said he felt “this very big calm” wash over him. He was taken back to amateur youth games with crowds so small he could spot his mom from anywhere.
“I felt like it was kinda just me, her and the game of basketball,” he told the audience gathered Saturday by the nonprofit Project Healthy Minds. “I was able to be like an artist out there. I was able to have my paint brush and have a canvas with the court. And I was able to just paint a beautiful picture for her about the love I have for the game. The love I have to show the world because of her.”
There was a time when he had lost that love for the game. Towns, whose bright smile became a constant image of the Knicks’ championship run, said basketball “felt hollow” after his mother’s death. “I didn’t know if I wanted to do it anymore,” he said.
But Towns found some solace in Arnie Kander, a well-known strength and wellness coach.
“Just to be heard, to be able to talk to someone you can trust, be able to really unload all that pain onto it and allow them to understand your feelings and articulate your feelings the right way, it makes life much lighter,” he said. “And I felt myself getting lighter every time we kept talking.”
Athletes embrace mental health
Project Healthy Minds hopes Towns’ example will inspire others to seek mental health care. The tech nonprofit runs a free online marketplace for finding therapy, psychiatry, support groups and other services. Its annual World Mental Health Day festival in New York offers an all-day schedule of yoga, art therapy and speakers.
Speaking Saturday with Towns was Boardroom CEO Rich Kleiman, the longtime manager for NBA superstar Kevin Durant and a new member of Project Healthy Minds’ board.
Kleiman told The Associated Press that these sorts of conversations are growing more prevalent among athletes. DeMar DeRozan and Kevin Love kick-started the conversation eight years ago when DeRozan tweeted about depression and Love then published a first-person essay about anxiety. Kleiman recalled trading stories about anxiety attacks with Love for several hours one night shortly afterward.
Most players won’t feel that comfortable constantly telling their story, Kleiman said. Mental health isn’t a topic of discussion in the locker room. But he said players are certainly more aware of its impact.
“They just carry so much weight and speak to so many people,” Kleiman told The Associated Press before the panel. “I think it says a lot that Karl Towns is feeling comfortable enough right before the season starts to be able to be so open about it.”
Another panel brought together former NFL wide receiver Brandon Marshall and Gotham FC forward Midge Purce for a conversation about finding purpose outside of performance. Marshall, a six-time Pro Bowl player who publicly shared his borderline personality disorder diagnosis in 2011, said therapy showed him how to “connect with his brain.” He even started taking his therapy sessions in the cafeteria to normalize it for others.
Purce discussed her evolving definition of “tough.” Raised by her dad, she said she grew up believing toughness meant “no tears.” But she credited her teammates with teaching her “it’s OK to feel sad and upset.”
“I think tough is being able to feel all those things that are touching you and touching your heart, but still finding that resilience to go forward while living all of it,” she told the crowd.
Using sports to show emotional strength
Saturday’s sports focus offers a glimpse into Project Healthy Minds’ future programming.
The nonprofit relies on cultural figures to introduce its platform to their audiences. It partnered this summer with the Broadway play “Every Brilliant Thing,” a one-person show whose narrator — originally played by Daniel Radcliffe, then Mariska Hargitay and, finally, Tracee Ellis Ross — presents his struggling mother with a list of reasons to live.
Soon-to-be-announced initiatives will lean further into sports as the nonprofit tries to inspire more communities to seek mental health care. With interest in women’s sports growing and live sports remaining a powerful convener in an otherwise fragmented media landscape, Project Healthy Minds CEO Phil Schermer finds that athletes are well suited to bring their message to the masses.
Athletes, according to Schermer, also shape the American public’s notions of strength. It makes sense to him that they could then model that “it is strong to talk about your emotions.”
“There need to be more men — and more men who are archetypes of strength — being vulnerable,” Schermer told AP. “Being willing to talk about these things. And role modeling that it can serve as fuel for your greatest success.”
The Knicks championship run became a rare moment of monoculture, Schermer suggested. The title chase also offered the in-person socialization that young people are demanding, according to Rachel Janfaza, the founder of the Gen Z research firm The Up and Up.
Speaking with “The Anxious Generation” author Jonathan Haidt and The TAG Movement CEO Alexa Arnold, Janfaza said young people used the Knicks and the World Cup to create the in-real-life community they missed during the pandemic.
“We’re seeing this swing,” she said, “and it’s really incumbent upon schools and employers and anyone who has a vested interest in helping this generation thrive to actually celebrate this.”
___

title: Robert Indiana’s foundation donates Vinalhaven working waterfront property
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
VINALHAVEN — The Star of Hope Foundation has donated a working waterfront property to the Vinalhaven Land Trust.
The land trust announced in a news release the donation of 3 Clamshell Alley, the former site of the Sail Loft in Carvers Harbor, which includes a pier, parking area and open space along Main Street.
“For generations, the area has served as an active part of Vinalhaven’s commercial fishing heritage. Working waterfront access is increasingly rare along the Maine coast, and its preservation is critical to sustaining the state’s fishing economy and way of life. This donation ensures that the property will remain available for commercial fishing use, protected from residential or commercial redevelopment. It also ensures waterfront views for the wider community, as well as future seating for public use,” trust officials said in a news release.
They also said that with financial support from The Star of Hope Foundation, art-related environmental programming will be offered by the land trust in the future.
“Donating this property to the land trust ensures it remains in working hands, serving the island and its residents,” said Emily Lane, board president of the Star of Hope Foundation.
“This generous gift will enable VLT to bring new life to a largely underutilized site. We are particularly excited to support Vinalhaven’s working waterfront while creating a space that benefits the entire community. The Land Trust is very grateful to the Star of Hope Foundation for their vision and generosity,” said Elizabeth Swain, president of the land trust’s board.
The property will be managed to support active commercial fishing operations with potential for other publicly beneficial uses. The land trust will work with local business owners, fishermen and town officials to ensure continued use consistent with Vinalhaven’s maritime traditions.
The Star of Hope Foundation was created from the estate of the late artist Robert Indiana.
This story appears through a media partnership with Midcoast Villager.

title: Missile strikes passenger terminal at Riyadh airport and many are wounded, official says
text:
Missile strikes passenger terminal at Riyadh airport and many are wounded, official says
The airport in the capital city of Riyadh has been targeted multiple times this week
Missile strikes passenger terminal at Riyadh airport and many are wounded, official says
The airport in the capital city of Riyadh has been targeted multiple times this week
The airport in the Saudi Arabian capital, Riyadh, was attacked again on Saturday and evacuated, two regional officials said, two days after three Saudi citizens, including a pilot, were killed as the kingdom faces an extraordinary series of assaults on the new front in the Iran War.
Related video above: President Trump announces the US will not strike Iran before the November midterm elections
A missile struck a passenger terminal and many people were wounded, one of the officials said. They spoke on condition of anonymity because they weren't authorized to speak to the media. Ambulances were seen rushing toward the airport.
Flights to Riyadh diverted elsewhere, the Flightradar24 tracker said, almost four hours after the last flight landed at 2:05 p.m. Kuwait Airways said it was canceling flights because the airport had closed. Canada's embassy advised citizens to avoid all travel to the airport, noting "ongoing military activity."
King Khalid International Airport has been targeted multiple times in the week since a Saudi-led coalition launched a major military offensive against Iran-backed Houthi rebels in neighboring Yemen. The Houthis claimed responsibility for the earlier attacks, including one Wednesday that killed a Sudanese national.
A resident said he heard explosions in Riyadh
There was no immediate Houthi statement Saturday. The Saudi government-run Center for International Communication, which oversees foreign media in the kingdom, didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.
A Riyadh resident, Ahmed Sayed, told The Associated Press he heard at least two loud explosions that rocked the capital.
The airport issued a terse alert telling passengers to check their flight status with airlines before heading to the airport. At least 225 flights at the airport had been canceled over the past 24 hours, according to flight-tracking site FlightAware.
Fighting in Yemen between the Houthis and Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces has escalated, with the Saudi-led coalition providing air support for government forces in an attempt to reverse recent Houthi gains along the Red Sea.
The rebels' gains gave them better surveillance of shipping on a corridor that's a crucial alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, where Iran has been attacking ships.
Though the Houthis have told the AP and others they are only targeting Saudi shipping as part of a blockade in retaliation for one imposed on them, concerns about wider attacks persist. The Houthis previously attacked other ships after the war in Gaza began, calling it solidarity with Palestinians. A U.S. bombing campaign ended that.
Trump 'not happy' but no sign of new support
The Saudis have sought support from the U.S. and other allies as its airports, military facilities and oil infrastructure have come under attack. Officials said U.S. assistance has included intelligence sharing, target identification and planning for the latest offensive.
On Friday, as he left the White House, U.S. President Donald Trump was asked about the attacks on the Riyadh airport and told reporters, "It's not good" and "I'm not happy." But there has been no immediate sign of U.S. military support to respond to the attacks.
The Saudi and Omani foreign ministers spoke by phone about the importance of "supporting diplomatic solutions to de-escalate tensions" in the region, the kingdom said Saturday. Oman, which lies across the Strait of Hormuz from Iran, has played a mediator role at times in the region.
Meanwhile, Saudi authorities warned the public this week that "filming, publishing or sharing information related to countering missiles and drones and their impact sites exposes you to legal liability."
Flight disruptions are growing
This week, the Houthis warned global airlines "for the last time" about the potential consequences of operating in Saudi airspace, which they described as a theater for their military operations.
Air India, FlyDubai, Lufthansa Group and Pakistan International Airlines have been among the airlines suspending flights to and from Riyadh and other Saudi airports for the next few days.
The European Union Aviation Safety Agency has expanded its guidance on Saudi airspace, noting the Houthis' ability to strike targets deeper inside the kingdom, including Riyadh, and a "greater focus on aviation infrastructure."
The missile and drone attacks and interception efforts "create an increased risk of misidentification of civil aircraft," it said.
In Thursday's attack, the Saudi national carrier said one of its aircraft was damaged while it was on the ground, with no passengers on board.
Associated Press writers Victoria Eastwood in Cairo, Cara Anna in Jerusalem and Sally Abou AlJoud in Beirut contributed to this report.

title: Deputy injured by falling tree during Hurricane Isaias response
text:
DALE COUNTY, Ala. (WSFA/WTVY/Gray News) — A sheriff’s deputy in Alabama was injured Friday night while responding to storm damage from Hurricane Isaias.
Dale County Sheriff Mason Bynum said one of his deputies was responding to the scene of a rollover vehicle crash with a downed tree on U.S. Highway 231 in Newton.
A car struck the tree, causing it to fall. Multiple other vehicles then hit the tree, Bynum said.
While deputies were on scene, another tree fell, landing on one of the involved vehicles and entrapping the driver.
The tree struck one of Bynum’s deputies as it fell. Bynum confirmed the injuries were “minor.” The deputy was taken to an area hospital.
The driver was extricated from the vehicle. Bynum said the driver is OK.
Sheriff urges drivers to stay off roads
Bynum said there were numerous trees down in his jurisdiction and urged residents to stay off the roads.
“It’s a very dangerous situation, very fluid situation. We just urge people to please stay off the roadways right now,” Bynum said.

CMMC asks labor board to review nurses' union case
Central Maine Medical Center is asking the National Labor Relations Board to review its challenge to the hospital's newly certified nurses' union after its initial request to block the election was denied.

Central Maine Medical Center is asking the National Labor Relations Board to review its challenge to the hospital's newly certified nurses' union.
In September, nurses at the Lewiston hospital voted overwhelmingly to unionize in hopes of negotiating for improved working conditions and benefits.
Before the vote was certified, CMMC asked the National Labor Relations Board's regional director to block the election results. That request was denied.
The hospital has now filed a request asking the full labor board to review the case, arguing it was not given an explanation for why its original motion was rejected.
A lawyer representing the nurses' union responded this week, calling the hospital's appeal "a bad-faith waste of the Board's time and resources."
The National Labor Relations Board has not yet ruled on the hospital's latest request.

title: Officer arrested for alleged sexual assault of minor also facing separate rape charge
text:
LIVINGSTON PARISH, La. (WAFB/Gray News) - A police officer who was previously arrested for indecent behavior with a juvenile is now facing second-degree rape in a separate incident, according to Louisiana authorities.
Hayden McKenzie, 23, was taken into custody and booked on indecent behavior with a juvenile on October 5 in Walker. Deputies say the investigation into McKenzie began in August following a sexual assault complaint for an incident that occurred in April 2025.
“Detectives were notified that this incident occurred in Livingston Parish. At the time, the victim was a 13-year-old juvenile,” said Sheriff Jason Ard.
The Walker Police Department says McKenzie was suspended with pay following his arrest.
“Upon learning of McKenzie’s arrest, and pursuant to our policies and procedures, McKenzie was suspended with pay pending the outcome of an administrative investigation and the disposition of the sheriff’s office charge. We are prohibited by our policies and procedures from commenting further at this time.”
Following that arrest, the Livingston Parish Sheriff’s Office says they were contacted by an adult woman regarding an alleged sexual assault that happened in April 2024.
“Based on evidence uncovered by our team, this investigation resulted in this new charge,” said Sheriff Ard.
McKenzie is being processed back into the Livingston Parish Detention Facility on second-degree rape after he initially bonded out.
The investigation is ongoing.

title: Lightsaber Darth Vader used in 'Empire Strikes Back' goes up for auction
text:
Lightsaber Darth Vader used in 'I am your father' duel in 'Empire Strikes Back' goes up for auction
In July, a lightsaber with Luke Skywalker's severed hand from "The Empire Strikes Back" sold for $3.75 million at auction, the highest price ever fetched for a prop used in a "Star Wars" film, according to the auction house.
Video above: Darth Vader speaks in "support" of Flock cameras
Now, someone can buy the saber that did the severing.
A Darth Vader lightsaber used in the climactic duel in Cloud City where he tells Skywalker "I am your father" is among the highlights of the Ultimate Star Wars Auction to be held by Heritage Auctions on Nov. 12.
The Vader saber, also used in "Return of the Jedi," is expected to fetch at least $1 million. It is one of more than two dozen lightsaber props that will be up for sale at the auction that spans "Star Wars" Episodes I through IX and other films and TV shows from the galaxy George Lucas created.
Others include dueling lightsabers forcefully wielded by Ewan McGregor's Obi-Wan Kenobi and Hayden Christensen's Anakin Skywalker in "Revenge of the Sith" that are expected to go for at least $10,000 apiece.
An EE-3 carbine blaster wielded by Boba Fett throughout "The Empire Strikes Back" is estimated to bring in more than $100,000.
Also included are a Yoda puppet hand used by Frank Oz in the character's original appearance in "The Empire Strikes Back," C-3PO actor Anthony Daniels' signed, personal third-draft screenplay for the original 1977 "Star Wars," and a TIE Fighter pilot helmet from "Rogue One: A Star Wars Story."

title: Hearts of Pine allow another stoppage time goal in loss to AC Boise
text:
PORTLAND — It looked like the Portland Hearts of Pine were about to buck a season-long trend.
Instead, the problem that has haunted the USL League One team for most of the season did them in again.
For the 12th time this season, Portland allowed a late goal that flipped an outcome from positive to negative. This time, Thomas Ang’s goal in the 93rd minute gave Athletic Club Boise a 2-1 win at Fitzpatrick Stadium. It was the 10th goal allowed by the Hearts in the 90th minute or later in 30 USL1 matches.
“I think that’s the 20-some odd point we’ve dropped in the last 10 minutes of games,” Portland coach Bobby Murphy said. “My frustration is, they play their hearts out, they do so much good, and then we don’t respect the moments that it takes to get something from the game.”
Overall, Portland has given up 26 potential points when a tie turned to a loss, or a would-be win became a tie or loss. With the loss of one point Saturday, Portland has squandered 21 points in the final 10 minutes of matches.
Portland (7-13-10, 31 points) was officially eliminated from the playoffs on Wednesday. If half of those 26 points had gone their way, the Hearts would be a single point out of playoff contention with two matches remaining.
“We’re still trying to ask ourselves why, and why it happens to us,” said right back Mo Mohamed. “Today, it felt like we had the game for the majority of it and momentum especially toward the end, and for them to score that goal, it’s kind of like heartbreaking.”
Boise (15-8-7) moved up a spot in the standings and is now in fourth place, in line for a quarterfinal home game.
HOME STRUGGLES
Portland played before the franchise’s 38th consecutive sellout (6,318 fans) at Fitzpatrick Stadium. But the fan support has not translated into much success. Portland is 5-7-3 at home this season.
After an evenly played first half with few chances for either team, Boise opened the scoring in the 54th minute on a strike by 32-year-old Tumi Mosobane after a long throw-in to the box caromed out away from the pack.
It was the eighth time in 15 home matches that Portland has conceded the first goal. Portland is 1-6-1 in those games, 0-6 the last six times it has happened.
After Diego Gonzalez took a Diogo Barbosa pass, then turned and rifled a shot into the right-third of the goal in the 74th minute, it began to feel like Portland was going to be the team to get the late winning tally.
Aboubacar Camara had the best chance in the 84th minute when he got behind the Boise defense but popped a short-range shot over the net.
RISK, NOT REWARD
Boise’s winner was a sharp shot by Amang from about 12 yards that zipped past keeper Hunter Morse (three saves) and inside the right post.
Murphy said the issue started with a “diagonal goal kick into Diego’s head, which he’s not going to be able to do anything with.”
Then it was Boise’s Denys Kostyshyn winning a ball from Barbosa and quickly passing to the right sideline to Jonathan Ricketts, who had several steps on left back Josh Drack. With Drack chasing and Barbosa closing, Ricketts slid a pass to his left that Amang one-timed through traffic.
“At the end, we had a couple moments where were trying to get too much from situations where there was nothing to be gained, really,” Murphy said. “The game comes down to moments, and in those moments, we’ve fallen short far too often.”
Portland is at Forward Madison next Saturday and finishes its season hosting current league-leader Charlotte Independence on Oct. 24.
NOTES
National Soccer Hall of Famer Landon Donovan was in the house after a holiday weekend of Maine-oriented activities. It was not the four-time U.S. Player of the Year’s first connection to the Hearts of Pine. Donovan modeled the Hearts’ “lighthouse” jersey for a video and photo shoot at West Quoddy Lighthouse when the team announced the alternate kit.
Best chant: “Our potatoes are better.” … Mid-year signing Felipe Rodriguez Gentile, who scored his second goal in Portland’s 3-3 tie at Spokane, started at the left wing spot normally held down by injured Ollie Wright.

title: Thankful Maine is without the death penalty
text:
This is in reference to the news report on the botched execution in Tennessee. I fervently hope that anyone who is on the fence about whether to oppose or support this evil, unnecessary practice of the death penalty will now see it for what it is and oppose it.
The reasons go on and on: that it is arbitrary and targets far more Black folks and other minorities; that it is actually more expensive to execute than to sentence to life without parole; that the United States is the only country in the Western world that uses it.
I grew up and lived in Iowa for many years, a state without the death penalty. I met folks from Nebraska, which has the death penalty. They continue to work to defeat it.
Through these folks, I met and became friends with a death row inmate. The state killed him. The night before, he called to say goodbye.
It was horrifying to know this was the last time I would speak with him. This was a man who had been redeemed by good folks. There was no reason to kill him, except for vengeance.
I am so grateful that Maine does not have the death penalty. I would not live here if it did.
Barbara Doughty
Portland

title: Letter: Vote for Troy Jackson to rein in Donald Trump
text:
Sen. Susan Collins enters her re-election campaign with some strong plusses, including good constituent service and helping bring federal resources into Maine. Her opponent, Troy Jackson, is less well-known and can come across as inarticulate and uncharismatic. In another election year I think Collins might be the better choice. But not so this year.
What’s different this year is the congressional Republicans’ passivity and complicity as President Donald Trump dismantles the norms and institutions that make America great. Collins’ re-election would likely result in maintaining the Republican majority in the Senate, giving Trump free rein for two more years. I believe a Republican majority will assure that Trump’s corrupt self dealing won’t be challenged or investigated; legal immigrants will continue to be arrested and deported; health and welfare programs will continue to be gutted; wars and tariffs will continue to drive up costs; Trump’s perceived enemies will be persecuted; and his attacks on free and fair elections will continue.
Collins will probably express “concern ” at some of Trump’s actions, but I believe her re-election and the resulting Republican Senate majority will further the nation’s descent into authoritarian oligarchy.
If Jackson wins and Democrats control the Senate, they would be able to investigate and shine light on unwise and illegal executive branch actions and block destructive legislative proposals.
I think voting for Jackson is less a rejection of Collins than a rejection of the national Republican Party and its damage to the nation’s ideals and institutions. I believe electing Jackson and a Democratic Congress is to start the healing, beginning the work of making America great again.
Stephen McKay
Orono
