title: Lincoln Academy gets its turn, wins first Class B golf championship
text:
VASSALBORO — For years, with players like Bailey Plourde and Kellen Adickes coming through the program, the Lincoln Academy golf team had seen individual success at the Class B state championships.
Team success, however, kept eluding the Eagles. It was always another team’s time, another team’s turn at the top.
Until Saturday, that is. With medalist Colin Mitchell leading the way with a 2-over 74, Lincoln won its first state championship, shooting 317 to hold off Freeport (326), Yarmouth (334), Cape Elizabeth and Fryeburg Academy (both 341) in the Class B tournament at Natanis Golf Course.
“It was a huge goal of ours. We won KVACs, which was nice, but we knew that this was a bigger goal on our minds,” Mitchell said. “We knew it was definitely doable. … We knew if we played well, we would have a fighting chance.”
Freeport’s Ryan Savona finished second to Mitchell with a 76. He was followed by Henry Stone of Gray-New Gloucester and Caden Chretien of Nokomis at 77, and Declan Hickey of Yarmouth at 78.
Carla Ferraris of Fryeburg Academy and Kathryn Peterson of Lake Region tied for girls medalist honors at 90.
Lincoln Academy finished ninth the last two seasons and had only one top-five finish the previous four years while failing to qualify twice. But after winning the KVAC B qualifier by 15 strokes, the Eagles had the answers this year.
“It’s been on my mind for a couple of years,” coach Todd Brackett said. “This team has a lot of potential. They’re young, and we’ve seen it coming up.
“They’ve had some great (individual) performances, but just never put it all together. Obviously, it came together today.”
In addition to Mitchell, the Eagles got a 79 from Brody Day, an 80 from Drew Nichols and an 84 from Max Blake — all juniors. The medalist honors were particularly sweet for Mitchell, who shot a 91 in the tournament last year and began making frequent trips to Natanis in the spring to ensure he’d be ready in October.
“This is one of the first courses to open in the spring. It’s kind of far from my house, but it’s worth the trip,” he said. “(Then) I’d play every day in the summer, like four to five hours a day, if not more.”
The work paid off Saturday. Mitchell got his round going with birdies on the fourth and sixth holes, and after bogeys on the eighth, ninth and 11th, he played his final seven holes at even par to maintain his lead.
“I felt like I was still swinging it good, so I just had to trust that,” he said. “It’s easy to drift out of focus a little bit. … I definitely checked back in mentally.”
Savona’s 76, combined with Liam Nihill’s 81, Will Obrin’s 84 and Charlie MacDonald’s 85, kept Freeport close. Savona opened with a birdie, then got two more on the 11th and 17th while playing the back nine at 1 under.
“It got kind of scrappy for a little bit, but I felt like I held it together well,” he said. “I made a couple of double (bogeys) out there, and my mentality was (that) it wasn’t even a bad double, I hit a couple of bad shots. I still feel solid about my game.”
Yarmouth also got an 82 from Lucas D’Alessandro, an 86 from Rory Truesdell and an 88 from Charles Hughes. Cape Elizabeth was led by an 82 from Charlie Lampman. Fryeburg’s Sergio Trejo shot an 81.
Lake Region’s Shane Plummer also finished in the top 10 with an 80 that tied him with Lincoln Academy’s Nichols for seventh.

title: What to do if you encounter wild animals after a major storm
text:
PANAMA CITY, Fla. (WJHG/WECP/Gray News) - Wildlife may be more visible after a major storm, especially in flooded areas.
The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission advises people to keep their distance and give animals space.
The FWC says:
- Alligators and snakes: Keep away. You may see more after a storm. Report concerns about an alligator to the Nuisance Alligator Hotline at 866-392-4286.
- Manatees and sea turtles: Rough weather can strand manatees or wash sea turtle hatchlings ashore. Report a stranded, injured or dead manatee, or a hatchling found tangled in seaweed or somewhere it doesn’t belong, by calling the Wildlife Alert Hotline at (888) 404-3922.
- Bears: Secure food that could attract bears. If spoiled food is in storm debris, keep it separate from other debris. Report conflicts to FWC regional offices during business hours or call the Wildlife Alert Hotline at (888) 404-3922 after hours.
More information is available at Wildlife and Storms and in FWC’s Storm Safety with Wildlife video.

title: Democrats appear to be our only hope on healthcare
text:
I think I speak for many as I age, requiring more encounters with our healthcare system.
I used to speak of our need for a single-payer healthcare system in the U.S. I reminded people I knew about the fact that we are the only industrialized nation in the world that doesn’t provide healthcare for its citizens. I worked to encourage my political representatives to make the changes needed to bring about that end. Was it all for nothing? Now that I truly need healthcare, where am I?
Maine hospitals are cutting departments or closing down for various reasons — Medicaid cuts, nurse shortages, etc. Nursing homes, birthing centers and even local medical practices, especially in our more rural areas, are suffering as well. We read about this crisis almost every day in our newspapers. And we hear many explanations. OK, now what?
I have friends who have looked for solutions — from seeking alternative medicine locally to traveling to specialized treatment centers in other states and even to using eye surgeries, dental care and joint replacement in other countries. I’m not likely to do any of those things. I’m simply hoping for my government to provide the healthcare we all need.
One thing I do know — the government we have now won’t come to my aid. I believe the only hope for the changes we need will come under a government led by Democrats.
Betsy Braunhut
Deer Isle

title: Lapierre Scores Five as County Soccer Offenses Erupt Friday
text:

Goals came in bunches across Aroostook County on Friday, with Emily Lapierre turning in one of the biggest individual performances of the fall.

title: Let’s deny Maine’s 12% gift to Donald Trump
text:
Dan Rabata of Cape Elizabeth is a retired U.S. Air Force lieutenant colonel.
A September New York Times/Siena poll found that “in Maine, 12% of voters who said they preferred Democrats to control the Senate also said they planned to support
Ms. Collins.”
With both the Maine Senate race and control of the Senate rated as toss-ups by the Cook Political Report, that split may be decisive in handing Senate control to Donald Trump — again.
Sen. Susan Collins understandably wants us not to pretend that Trump is on the ballot. That ship has sailed. He is the issue, the elephant in the room. Given Trump’s plummeting popularity and negative polling on every major issue, Collins has no choice but to tear up the Trump signs on her lawn.
Trump desperately needs to retain Senate control. Losing it opens up all kinds of difficulties for him. No more confirmations of unqualified hacks. Release of all the Epstein files. Investigations of corruption. Subpoena power. Control of legislation. Votes to end his war. Accountability. Trump knows he is in serious hurt if Collins loses her seat and with it the Senate majority.
What cards can she play to distance herself from Trump? That’s tricky.
She could cite roll-call data showing that she has cast the deciding vote 56 times against her own party. Not particularly impressive against the 144 times when she cast the deciding vote in line with her Republican majority. And not impressive at all against how those same 200 votes would have gone with a Democratic senator in her seat.
How about her high-profile stances against Trump’s nominees? Hasn’t her “moderation” served to rein in some of the worst excesses of Trump/MAGA? Even though she voted for Brett Kavanaugh, Neil Gorsuch and Robert F. Kennedy Jr., didn’t she stand up against Pete Hegseth, Amy Coney Barrett and Todd Blanche? She did. Did it matter? No, all were confirmed by a Republican-controlled Senate.
Are her occasional positions against unpopular GOP priorities genuine or “independent only when it doesn’t make a difference”? Does it matter? Not much, since the outcome is almost always the same: her opposition does not carry the day. When it does, it is usually damage control to mitigate the chaos created by her own party.
Example: First come the Trump-initiated and deeply unpopular Canadian tariffs. Then follow a couple of exceptions to avoid complete disaster, leaving behind a Maine more negatively affected than nearly all other states. Even if her moderate, bipartisan impact is minimal, isn’t it better than nothing? Shouldn’t we applaud it as an example encouraging other Republicans to move in that direction?
Unfortunately, the contrary evidence is clear. Even GOP incumbent Sens. Cassidy and Cornyn, who rarely departed from the party line, have suffered primary losses to significantly more “MAGA” challengers. In this hyperpartisan climate of bend-the-knee fidelity to the Trump agenda — one that is decidedly unfriendly to Maine interests — Susan Collins’ ability to influence what happens in today’s Senate is greatly diminished.
Given the enormous stakes, the strategic imperative is to flip the Senate. Anything less is a lost opportunity. I urge the 12% to reconsider. They may achieve a costly Pyrrhic victory — one that wins a lesser objective but overlooks and loses the greater objective.
We can’t have it both ways. A vote for Susan Collins (regardless of what she does in her individual capacity) endorses continued Republican control of a Trump-compliant Senate. One may even admire her for her past efforts but a vote for her — however well-intentioned — is a vote for the very Trump-controlled agenda of chaos, cruelty and corruption that the 12% despise.

title: Weekend Crossword: Hard Fall Frost
Auburn school comes together for a canine cause, motivated by its comfort dog Luna
text:
Every Monday, Wednesday and Friday since the start of the school year, students and faculty at Auburn’s Franklin Alternative School have run — or walked — in the surrounding High Street neighborhood to prepare for a 5K race. The event not only supported a favorite school cause but ended up bringing them together and teaching lessons in ways they never expected.
“So many of our students face barriers when it comes to being part of their community. Sometimes they are tangible — poverty, abuse, instability — and sometimes in their heads — anxiety, depression — but all of those barriers send the message to kids that they don’t belong. A 5K is such a simple thing but it’s an event that has a strong sense of community,” said Principal Melissa McLeod.
Despite the rigors of a 5K, the students didn’t need much convincing right from the start, McLeod said, because the 5K benefited the organization behind the school’s beloved comfort dog, Luna.
And as far as McLeod was concerned, it didn’t matter that there ended up being more walking then running as training for the 5K progressed, because it was all about the effort and the cause.
“A lot who wanted to run are now walking,” McLeod joked last week, before eight school staff and 22 students lined up Oct. 4 for Moxie’s Memorial 5K in Oxford.
Franklin School is an alternative learning environment that students at risk of not graduating can choose to attend. It serves about 100 students from Lewiston and Auburn. In the eight years McLeod has served as principal, the school has always had a wait list, she said.
The school secured a $125,000 grant two years ago from The John T. Gorman Foundation, a philanthropic organization in Maine, to pilot trauma-informed programming that can bolster academic achievement and social outcomes.
McLeod said the school implemented an aerobic movement program three times a week as part of the wellness side of the grant. She explained that academic research shows that movement not only helps regulate a person’s nervous system, but can help improve academic performance.
The addition of training for a 5K felt like a perfect way to implement that exercise, she said. And the staff idea to do the Moxie’s Memorial 5K was a great motivator: The event raises funds for the nonprofit that brought Franklin Alternative’s comfort dog Luna into the school’s life.
Every student and staff member who could participate, did, and they were out of the building every Monday, Wednesday and Friday to train. The staff had a lot of fun with it, McLeod said, and some even started lifting weights.
“One thing I emphasized to staff is that if we are going to get the kids to do this, we have to show enthusiasm, and there ended up being a lot more than we thought,” she said.
Luna has become a staple to Franklin Alternative School. She has a distinctive personality and free reign through the school’s hallway. McLeod said Luna helps the students immensely. If students, or even staff, are having a difficult day, they can spend some time cuddling with Luna to lift their spirits. At the end of the day, Luna goes home to McLeod and her family.
Luna has also made an impact on the greater Auburn school community. McLeod jokes that if she goes anywhere with Luna, it will take twice as long because everyone wants to pet her.
Luna came to Franklin School from Mission Working Dogs, which hosts the Moxie’s Memorial 5K in Oxford. The organization breeds, raises and trains service dogs for disabled veterans and civilians who are suffering from post-traumatic stress disorder, or mobility issues, while also providing comfort dogs to hospitals and schools.
Christy Gardner, an Auburn Edward Little High School graduate, was injured in 2006 while serving as a sergeant in the U.S. Army Police Military in Asia. After returning to Maine, Gardner adopted her service dog, Moxie, in 2010 and in 2020 founded Mission Working Dogs.
Auburn Police Department’s comfort dog, Benny-Bud, also came from Mission Working Dogs.
Gardner said after the 5K event Oct. 4 that it was “awesome” to have the Franklin students and Luna participate in the race.
“They brought great attitudes and smiles to the event. We love our partnership with their school and the difference therapy dog Luna brings to the environment there,” Gardner said.
McLeod said she knows it sounds cliché, but participating with students and staff in an event like the one this past weekend reinforces the feeling of family that the school has.
Often, students at Franklin Alternative School arrive needing more than just academics, they need a support system. The combination of physical movement training for the recent 5K and the new statewide cellphone ban have strengthened that bond, McLeod said.
“We have these kids who are always walking around the city, but now they’re forced to walk with adults and other kids. They are all talking to each other, and they’re still at school so they can’t have their phones. It’s forcing the kids to be more social with adults and it’s been great, just walking around chatting,” she said.
Several teachers, including Stevie Dunton, a special education teacher, got involved in the 5K. He said he is not a runner, but he wanted to show his students that they could do whatever they put their minds to.
Melissa Anderson, a social worker, said Luna is an integral part of the support system at Franklin. Anderson herself is a new member of the “Franklin family” and being a part of the training for the 5K and seeing the success of the students was meaningful to her.
“The conversations that grew out of morning walks and the confidence built through this opportunity were truly wonderful to observe and be a part of,” said Anderson.
Moving forward, staff at Franklin Alternative School will continue to remind their students that they have a sense of belonging in the community, whether they are training together or bonding in the classroom with Luna, especially in the light of conversations around youth and the gun violence Lewiston is experiencing.
“Kids who are told that they don’t have value and don’t belong in their communities have no incentive to protect their streets or contribute in positive ways. They also have no incentive to hold each other accountable. We will continue to encourage our kids at Franklin to be a part of their world and will open any doors we can to get them passage into their community,” McLeod said.

title: Medicaid cuts strip refugees and other legal immigrants of their health coverage
text:
New restrictions have stripped Medicaid coverage from certain legal immigrants, including refugees and victims of human trafficking, as part of broader federal changes to the health insurance program that are expected to force millions off their coverage.
The change effective Oct. 1 cut from Medicaid what is estimated to be hundreds of thousands of people who legally immigrated to the United States, many of whom work and pay taxes, in the latest Trump administration policy to target foreigners.
The move is part of sweeping changes to Medicaid under President Donald Trump’s 2025 tax cut and policy law, with many set to take effect early next year. The Medicaid changes are projected to result in 7.5 million fewer people with health insurance, according to the Congressional Budget Office’s 2025 estimate.
Advocates say that without Medicaid, people will not be able to afford private insurance and will either delay care or end up in emergency rooms, adding pressure to a strained health system. For immigrants, the cuts could be felt more acutely, compounding the effects of other administration efforts to restrict their access to public assistance as part of a broader immigration crackdown.
“This is about telling every immigrant in the United States that they are not welcome here and that they should leave,” said Ben D’Avanzo, a senior strategist at the National Immigration Law Center, which has pursued litigation against the Republican administration over its immigration agenda.
Refugees, asylum seekers, victims of human trafficking and domestic violence are among those who have lost coverage. Green-card holders were not impacted.
Lauren Bis, a White House spokesperson, said in a statement that “immigrants must be able to support themselves without taking from overburdened benefits programs paid for by hard-working American taxpayers.”
D’Avanzo said many people who have lost coverage will likely only realize when they need medical care. But for some, the change has been felt immediately.
Dwindling supplies of lifesaving medication
In Tucson, Arizona, María Chacon has been caring for her son Jesus for almost five years since a car accident at 17 left him unable to breathe on his own. He requires a ventilator, a feeding tube and daily medication, and must be turned once every two hours to stop sores from forming. Chacon said he sometimes opens his eyes.
The family is originally from Mexico and entered the U.S. on a T visa, offered to victims of human trafficking, in 2018.
Chacon said Medicaid has helped cover almost $25,000 per month of care for her son, which includes a small stipend for her and her husband as compensation for being long-term caregivers. She said doctors have explained that even if they both worked 24 hours a day, they would not be able to cover the cost of his care.
“Since that day I haven’t been able to sleep. We haven’t been able to eat or anything. We’re wondering what we’re going to do?” Chacon said.
Jesus takes medication that Chacon estimates costs $7,000 a month. The supply runs out in mid-October. Without coverage, she does not know how her son is going to survive.
Chacon found out just days before the cuts that she was losing care. She called the state’s Medicaid offices to appeal. Although she is in the process of obtaining a green card, Medicaid coverage would only kick in five years after she is approved.
Steven Camarota, research director for the Center for Immigration Studies, a right-leaning think tank that seeks less immigration, said the administration “is trying to nibble around the edges” with the Oct. 1 cuts, finding piecemeal ways to curb immigration into the U.S.
Camarota believes the government should screen legal immigrants for income potential and education, reducing the number who might rely on public benefits once they cross the border.
“You need immigrants who are unlikely to need welfare,” he said, or those with high educational attainment.
The administration recently revived a federal rule that could deny green cards to immigrants who use public benefits that could include food stamps, Medicaid, housing vouchers and others.
Chacon believes the cuts to Medicaid coverage are part of the administration’s clampdown on immigrants. She said her son is in no condition to travel.
“I know that’s what he’s doing, but, as my son is, I couldn’t go to Mexico,” Chacon said.
Millions more will be dropped from Medicaid
Medicaid, jointly funded by states and the federal government, has become a political focal point during Trump’s second term. The president has pushed to root out what he describes as fraud in the program. In July, the administration deferred over $1 billion in Medicaid payments to California and Minnesota, claiming there was suspected fraud; critics argued the move targeted Democratic-led states.
As more people are cut from Medicaid, the federal government is predicted to reduce program spending by $911 billion, according to healthcare research nonprofit KFF.
In Arizona, officials said 29,000 legal immigrants were cut from Medicaid rolls on Oct. 1. In Florida, estimates are closer to 177,000. Overall, more than 281,000 immigrants from nine states and the District of Columbia are estimated to lose Medicaid coverage, according to KFF.
As more states implement various restrictions to coverage, 7.5 million people are expected to lose coverage by 2034, according to analysis by the Congressional Budget Office.
Without coverage, people will turn to emergency rooms for care. When people delay seeing a doctor, conditions can worsen and become even more expensive to treat.
“At the end of the day, it does raise the cost for the states because once you get these people in for something that could have been prevented, they could not go to the doctor because they were uninsured; they most likely will end up at a hospital in an emergency room,” said Carmen Feliciano, the vice president of policy and advocacy at UnidosUS, a Latino civil rights organization.
UnidosUS partners with community organizations to help provide medical care, but Feliciano said they already are overwhelmed and would not be able to support the number of people who are going to lose medical coverage in the coming months.
“We are not going to have the capacity to serve all the people who need it,” Feliciano said.

title: Colby football starts slow, falls to Wesleyan
text:
Colby fell behind by 14 points in the first half and couldn’t recover in a 21-7 NESCAC football loss to Wesleyan on Saturday in Middletown, Connecticut.
The Mules (0-4) pulled within seven when Jagger Matera threw a 4-yard touchdown pass to Sean Trinder with 5:19 remaining, but Wesleyan (4-0) answered less than two minutes later on a 69-yard pass from Matt Fitzsimons to Blake Newcomb.
Fitzsimons scored on 1-yard runs in the first and second quarter. He completed 22 of 28 passes, with a touchdown and three interceptions.
Colby managed just 155 yards and nine first downs.
WILLIAMS 34, BATES 0: The Ephs (3-1) held the Bobcats (0-4) to 84 yards and seven first downs and cruised to a NESCAC win in Williamstown, Massachusetts.
Drew Weiler, Brady Stahelski and Aiden Clark each had a rushing touchdown in the second quarter as Williams took a 21-0 lead. Leonardo Maiuolo kicked a 34-yard field goal in the third quarter and a 21-yarder in the fourth. Quinn Rucker added a 4-yard scoring run.
NORWICH 28, MAINE MARITIME ACADEMY 7: Jahmir Dixon caught 11 passes for 228 yards and a touchdown to lead the Cadets (2-3) past the Mariners (0-5) in Castine.
MMA quarterback Harris Stone completed 21 of 37 passes for 214 yards, with one touchdown and one interception.
Will Patenaude scored on touchdown runs of 6, 8 and 57 yards for Norwich.

title: Cause of death revealed for two Ole Miss students in court
text:
OXFORD, Miss. (WMC/Gray News) - The cause of death was revealed for two Ole Miss students in court proceedings.
In court, one of the defense attorneys for two men charged with selling narcotics said one student died from a combined use of various substances, including cough syrup.
The other student died from inhalation asphyxiation.
The two students, 18-year-old Aidan Hamilton and 20-year-old Robert Strang, died on Monday, Sept. 21.
Investigators allege that Puffs Vape, Tobacco and Beer Store in Oxford, where both Moslehs worked, sold Hamilton the pills twice in the days before his death.
While officials believe it was Puffs that sold Hamilton the narcotics found in his system, they say Strang bought his pills from a different store outside the county 20 miles away.
After the deaths, Lafayette County Metro Narcotics agents sent a confidential informant into Puffs Vape, Tobacco and Beer Store in Oxford to investigate the alleged sales of illegal substances, according to the arrest affidavit.
The informant asked if the store sold “7-OH Kratom-based pills.”
Records show the clerk said yes before warning the informant to “be careful taking the pills, because people are dying from them.”
Oxford police then executed a search warrant at the store, and 500 units of kratom and kratom-like products were seized. An assortment of “THC cartridges, gummies, pre-rolls, and other suspected THC substances” was also recovered.
During the raid, detectives found the same brand of Smax Mango Breeze MGM-15, with identical packaging, ingredients and a $39.99 price tag with a smudge on the 9, at the store that had been found near Hamilton.
According to court records, a toxicology report, which has not been made publicly available, shows both victims had the same three substances present — Mitrogynine, MGM-15 and MGPI — which are all featured in the Smax Mango Breeze pills.
The victims’ families provided law enforcement with photocopies of bank records. According to Easter, victim one spent $87.18 at Puff’s Vape on Sept. 20.
Victim two spent $43.59 at Puff’s Vape also on Sept. 20, according to Easter. Both purchases were made the day before the two students’ deaths.
In closing, federal prosecutors stated, “this case comes from several tragic overdose cases of students here in Oxford... evidence supports the detention… victims died of conditions consistent to overdoses.”
Prosecutors stated that the defendants were aware of their actions selling the illegal drugs.
The judge determined Yahya Mosleh will remain behind bars as the case plays out. Islam, his son, will be released on a $20,000 unsecured bond with conditions.

title: Christa Pike discharged from hospital after surviving execution attempt
text:
Christa Pike discharged from hospital after surviving execution attempt
Christa Pike, who survived Tennessee’s attempt to execute her by lethal injection, has been moved back to prison, her attorneys said Saturday.
Pike, 50, was discharged from the hospital and is back at the Deborah K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center, the women’s prison where she was housed for 30 years, her attorneys said in a written statement.
“She is grateful to the first responders and her medical team for their care in these extraordinary circumstances. She is continuing to receive medical care at the prison, and we will continue to track her recovery,” the statement said.
Pike had been hospitalized since surviving two doses of pentobarbital as the state attempted to execute her on Sept. 30 for the 1995 beating and stabbing death of classmate Colleen Slemmer. At one point she was on a ventilator and her attorneys did not expect her to survive. However, they said Pike woke up and began talking and walking with assistance.
The Death Penalty Information Center says Pike is the first person to survive after receiving lethal injection drugs during an execution.
The Tennessee Department of Correction has not said what went wrong in the execution. Medical and lethal injection experts have focused on whether a problem with the IV line caused the drug to pool in her tissue instead of entering her bloodstream. Pike’s attorneys wrote in a court filing that “apparently at no point did any member of the execution team realize that the IV lines were not correctly placed.”
The failed execution brought renewed scrutiny to how Tennessee carries out death sentences.
Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee has since postponed the state’s only other scheduled execution this year and ordered a review of what went wrong. The state’s prison chief resigned in the wake of the failed execution
As the process got underway Pike was asked if she had a final statement, and she spoke of being at peace. About five minutes later, she raised her head and said her arm hurt. Later, she appeared to lose consciousness but could be heard breathing heavily until media witnesses were escorted from the witness room nearly 90 minutes into the execution. An ambulance took her to a hospital.

title: Frigid Sunday morning ahead of possible late evening showers
text:
Frigid Sunday morning ahead of possible late evening showers
Remnants of Isaias could bring showers to Maine late Sunday.
Frigid Sunday morning ahead of possible late evening showers
Remnants of Isaias could bring showers to Maine late Sunday.
A frost advisory is in effect from 2 AM to 8 AM Sunday.
Tonight will be partly cloudy, with patchy fog and areas of frost after midnight. Lows will be in the mid-30s with light winds.
Sunday will be partly sunny in the morning, becoming mostly cloudy later. Frost is possible early. Highs will reach the low 60s, with southwest winds of 10 to 15 mph and gusts up to 25 mph.
Sunday night will be cloudy with rain likely. Lows will be in the upper 40s, with a 90% chance of rain.
Monday (Columbus Day) will start mostly cloudy with a chance of morning showers, then become mostly sunny. Highs will reach the upper 60s. Monday night will turn cloudy, with a slight chance of showers after midnight. Lows will be in the low 40s.
Tuesday will bring likely showers and highs in the mid-50s. Rain will continue Tuesday night, with lows in the upper 40s.

title: Letter: Paul LePage wasn’t a friend of Maine’s 2nd District as governor
text:
Once again Paul LePage has pulled out that old half dollar his dad gave him when he assaulted him and sent him to the hospital. How many times do we have to hear that same story? It’s a shame his father was abusive to him, but LePage isn’t the only kid who grew up hard during the late 1950s and early ‘60s. Perhaps his hope is for a big sympathy vote by waving that coin at us again.
I believe LePage was no friend to the citizens of the Second Congressional District when he was governor. He blocked Medicaid expansion several times. He cut funding for Meals on Wheels and many other social services critical to seniors in central and northern Maine.
Paul LePage has moved to Florida at least twice and basically returned to Maine only when he thinks the voters will elect him to a political position. I think he has traveled Interstate 95 so often they should change it to the LePage Thruway.
If elected to Congress, I believe LePage will be no more than a bench warmer. I think he will follow the orders given him by Speaker Mike Johnson and likely offer no bills of his own to help the citizens of Maine. He would be the one of oldest people ever sworn in to Congress for their first term if elected.
I believe Matt Dunlap offers a much better opportunity for Maine to be heard and represented in Washington than the opportunist LePage.
Bill Osborne
Bangor

title: Officer arrested for alleged sexual assault of minor also facing separate rape charge
text:
LIVINGSTON PARISH, La. (WAFB/Gray News) - A police officer who was previously arrested for indecent behavior with a juvenile is now facing second-degree rape in a separate incident, according to Louisiana authorities.
Hayden McKenzie, 23, was taken into custody and booked on indecent behavior with a juvenile on October 5 in Walker. Deputies say the investigation into McKenzie began in August following a sexual assault complaint for an incident that occurred in April 2025.
“Detectives were notified that this incident occurred in Livingston Parish. At the time, the victim was a 13-year-old juvenile,” said Sheriff Jason Ard.
The Walker Police Department says McKenzie was suspended with pay following his arrest.
“Upon learning of McKenzie’s arrest, and pursuant to our policies and procedures, McKenzie was suspended with pay pending the outcome of an administrative investigation and the disposition of the sheriff’s office charge. We are prohibited by our policies and procedures from commenting further at this time.”
Following that arrest, the Livingston Parish Sheriff’s Office says they were contacted by an adult woman regarding an alleged sexual assault that happened in April 2024.
“Based on evidence uncovered by our team, this investigation resulted in this new charge,” said Sheriff Ard.
McKenzie is being processed back into the Livingston Parish Detention Facility on second-degree rape after he initially bonded out.
The investigation is ongoing.

title: High school golf rankings gave players a new perspective this season
text:
VASSALBORO — Colin Mitchell saw the rankings. The Lincoln Academy junior didn’t agonize over them, but yeah, he checked them out.
Sixth in Class B, 16th in the state, according to the Maine high school golf rankings that made their debut this fall.
“I kind of saw it as an opportunity to prove myself,” Mitchell said after winning the Class B individual state title Saturday afternoon at Natanis Golf Club. “I’m sixth. I’ve got nothing to lose, really.”
The idea for a statewide ranking had percolated in Brian Bickford’s brain for a while. How could Maine Golf, the state’s governing body for the sport, make it happen?
“I always was intrigued by Heal points,” Bickford said, referring to the system by which the MPA ranks teams to seed the tournament in most high school sports. “For me, it kind of brings the state together.”
How does a player from Fort Kent compare with a player from York when they’ve played entirely different courses all season, in different conditions? This ranking system helps quantify what had been unquantifiable.
Bickford, the executive director for Maine Golf, who also coaches the University of Southern Maine golf team, enlisted Alex Grant in the endeavor. A 2024 Nokomis High grad and a member of the USM golf team, Grant worked on creating the ranking system.
An information technology major, the project was right in Grant’s wheelhouse. The rankings include the player’s score, course slope and course rating. To put it in basic terms, the better a player shoots on a tougher course, the higher he or she will rank.
It goes beyond the eye test and score comparisons. Taking a course’s rating into account gives a more accurate measure of a player. A plus-2 on a more challenging course has to be considered more impressive than an even-par round on an easier one, right?
“I wish it was something I had when I was in high school, whether I was ranked 1,000 or first,” Grant said.
Winthrop junior Kaydence Allarie knew entering her round Saturday that she was the top-ranked girl in Class C. She was a little nervous, especially with 18 holes to play rather than the typical nine played in the regular season.
Allarie probably had the healthiest attitude toward the rankings.
“Anything can happen,” she said. “You pretty much just play and do your best. I just wanted to stay consistent and not worry about everyone else. Just be me.”
The more rounds played, the more accurate the rankings should be. Anyone can have a bad day, the kind that makes you want to give your putter a Viking funeral. Anyone can have a great day, too, when every tee shot finds the middle of the fairway and you read every green perfectly.
The rankings work as a complete picture, Grant said. As the season moved from late August to early October, the minimum number of matches required to be ranked increased.
“The more the merrier. It gave you a better ranking,” Grant said.
The rankings, available for viewing at mainegolf.org, rank individual players in each class, as well as teams. Going into Class B state championship, Mitchell and his Lincoln Academy teammates figured through the ranking that Freeport and Fryeburg Academy would be their top competition for the team title.
In Class C, the top-ranked team was Winthrop, ahead of Dexter and Calais.
To the MPA’s credit, they love it.
“I feel a little guilty. People keep thanking me and congratulating me, and I had little to nothing to do with it,” said Todd Sampson, the MPA assistant executive director.
To the MPA, submitting results for the rankings was strictly voluntary this fall. The MPA doesn’t have any plans to use the rankings in determining which golfers play with whom at the state championships. Maybe that’ll change in a few years, when there’s more data to analyze and any kinks or bugs have been ironed out.
Sampson said a few athletic directors have expressed interest in using the rankings as a barometer for choosing all-conference players, since it covers a player’s complete season of work if data is entered dilligently after each match.
For this debut season, the rankings gave high school golfers something to talk about. And for some, maybe a little motivation.

title: Who is Katie Zacharia? What to know about the next White House press secretary
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump announced Friday that Katie Zacharia, a communications adviser for his media company, will succeed Karoline Leavitt as White House press secretary.
Trump revealed his selection of Zacharia on his Truth Social platform, where he often makes political and official announcements. Zacharia is a conservative commentator for Trump Media & Technology Group, which operates the social media site.
In naming Zacharia, Trump described her as “a loyal and brilliant supporter, right from the beginning.”
In a social media post, Zacharia thanked Trump and called it the “honor of a lifetime.” She added that Trump’s leadership is “a blessing to this country.”
“The work ahead is to continue delivering strong results for our Country and communicating to the American people the major wins that this Administration is making every single day,” she wrote on X.
Zacharia briefly worked as a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security earlier this year and has been a commentator for Fox News and Newsmax. Trump said Zacharia had been involved in his presidential campaigns, notably in swing states.
A request for comment left with Zacharia was not immediately answered. A LinkedIn profile noted that she earned a law degree from Pepperdine University.
Leavitt announced her departure Aug. 12 and left the position Aug. 27.
She will serve as an on-air contributor on Fox News Channel beginning Nov. 1, the network said Monday.
Leavitt became press secretary in January 2025, and left the position, she said, to spend more time with her young children. Prior to serving in the White House, Leavitt was national press secretary for Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign.

title: A mainly sun filled weekend with chilly overnights. Rain possible early next week
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - There will be few if any clouds visible across the state today as it yet another gorgeous fall day out there today. Some clouds may filter in overnight as the remnants of Isaias stay off to our south later Sunday but it will still be a very comfortable fall day. Monday will be mainly clear before another system moves in Tuesday that may bring our first wintry precip to northern locations.
Today: A cool, breezy day filled with sun
It will be yet another absolutely top notch fall day today will sunshine all around, though temps will be a bit cooler than average and it will be a bit breezy with winds from the NW gusting as high as 25 mph or so. A few clouds may arrive by late in the evening for southern portions of the state but they will be few and far between. Highs will mainly be in the 50s and a few spots in the far north may not get out of the 40s even with the sun.
Tonight: A chilly but clear night
The wind will die off substantially and go basically calm and without the clouds temps will drop easily in the 30s for most. Some of the coldest areas may even drop into the 20s once again.
Sunday: Sun and clouds mixed with warmer temperatures
The winds will swing around to the SW and bring a warmer day with them. More clouds will move into the region as well with the remnants of Isaias which will eventually slide out to sea to our south but may bring a few showers later in the day on Sunday especially for southern regions of the state. Highs will fall mainly in the 60s. Winds will again be somewhat gusty perhaps as high as 25 mph or so.
Sunday night: Slight chance of a weak shower, otherwise overcast
There is a slight chance for a stray shower Sunday night but it will otherwise be mainly overcast and warmer than previous nights. Lows will only probably drop into the 40s for most with some areas further south barely getting below 50. Winds will be light out of the SW at 5-10 mph.
Monday and beyond: A very pleasant, partly sunny day Monday... Rain or even a wintry mix far north Tuesday
The work week will start off comfortably with highs in the 60s and very little wind. Temps will drop quickly Monday evening into the 40s and 30s and a developing low may slide into the region early Tuesday and bring some cold Canadian air with it and there is a possibility some of the coldest spots may see some wintry mix early on Tuesday. But a cold rain is possible for most on Tuesday.
Today: Sunny and breezy with highs in the 50s for most. Winds NW at 10-20 mph.
Tonight: Chilly and clear with lows in the middle to low 30s. Winds light.
Sunday: Partly sunny with highs back into the 60s. Winds SW at 10-15 mph.
Sunday night: More clouds and a slight chance of a shower. Winds SW at 5-10 mph
Monday: Warmer with a few breaks of sun. Winds light.
Monday night: Chance of showers move in and chilly. Lows in the 30s and 40s.

title: ‘Deeply disturbing’: 9 dead in Pennsylvania shooting, police chief says
text:
ERIE, Pa. (WICU/WSEE) — Nine people are dead after a shooting Friday night, authorities said.
Police said the suspected shooter died of a self-inflicted gunshot wound.
Witnesses said the suspect was seen firing a weapon before entering a house.
Police respond to scene
Police arrived at the scene near 7th and Perry streets, and tried to get the man to surrender. Additional gunshots were then heard from inside the home.
“At this time we can confirm that the suspect is deceased. Based on the information currently available to us, there is no ongoing threat to the public,” Erie Police Chief Rick Lorah said.
There is no word yet on a possible motive. The identities of the victims have not been released.
“I want to be candid with our community. This is one of the most difficult and heartbreaking scenes our officers and investigators have ever encountered. The loss of life is devastating, and the circumstances we are working through are deeply disturbing,” Lorah said.
An investigation into the matter is ongoing.

title: Park service could remove more than 500 trees at historic golf course Trump wants to redesign
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The National Park Service has begun a new round of tree-cutting at a historic golf course near the National Mall as the Trump administration proceeds with a plan to renovate the East Potomac Golf Links into a championship-level course.
More than 500 trees “that do not contribute to the historic landscape will be removed” as part of the rehabilitation project, the National Park Service said in a court filing Friday. “No healthy trees that are contributing features of the historical golf course” — including historic cherry trees — will be removed as part of the project, the park service said.
A total of 169 trees will be removed starting Saturday, with another 90 trees slated for removal later, the agency said.
The tree removals come as President Donald Trump has moved to turn the course into a world-class golf venue — part of his grand vision for Washington, D.C., where he has torn down storied structures, remade or renamed others and deployed the National Guard for more than a year.
Some residents fear the planned changes to the golf course — where Trump has visited with a cabinet member, a well-known golf course architect and blueprints — risk altering the character of a place that has served Washingtonians of all income levels for more than a century. Turning the park into an upscale golf course will mean costlier fees and a likely loss of public space.
“The National Park Service is finally implementing a 7-year-old plan to address tree overgrowth at East Potomac Golf Course,” the Interior Department said in a statement Saturday. The department oversees the park service and other agencies that manage federal lands.
The renovation work will include selective tree and vegetation work to restore the course, the Interior Department said, adding that the work is intended to “help restore the course’s historic character and reopen views toward landmarks, including the Washington Monument, National War College, Potomac River and Washington Channel.”
The park service “recognizes the importance of trees to the park and its visitors. This carefully planned work is part of our required stewardship of the park,” the statement said.
The golf course will remain open to the public throughout the renovation effort, although individual holes may temporarily close while work is underway, the agency said.
The 106-year-old public course has been embroiled in a lawsuit since February. Plaintiffs including the DC Preservation League say the Trump administration’s reconstruction would violate the congressional act that created the park in 1897. The group sought an emergency stop-work order this spring because of concerns that work was expected to begin immediately on the course.
Trump, an avid golfer, has posted about the course on social media, “When completed, this Course will have the ability to host Major Golf Tournaments, including The U.S. Open, The Ryder Cup, The PGA Championship, and other top PGA Tour events,” he wrote in late June.
It’s unclear when the course could host any major tournaments, as locations are chosen several years ahead of the events.

title: Maranacook golf holds off Winthrop for Class C title
text:
VASSALBORO — Maranacook senior Jack Fontaine has come through in plenty of big moments on the basketball court.
Saturday, he came through on the golf course.
Fontaine shot a 1-over 73 to take the Class C individual boys title and help the Black Bears win the team title on the Arrowhead course at Natanis Golf Course.
“It feels amazing. I did not expect this,” said Fontaine. “It’s just a hobby, really. I just play for fun.”
Maranacook finished with a score of 317 to beat Winthrop by one shot. It’ i’s the third state title for the Black Bears, who also won in 2022 and 2024. Calais (328), Dexter (332) and Houlton (336) rounded out the top five.
“This year was definitely different,” said Maranacook coach Ryan Meserve. “We didn’t play as well as we wanted to all throughout the (regular) season. We knew that if we could just get through one (good) day, we’ve got guys who have won state championships before … The team is super resilient, like each other as a team. We knew we needed just one good day.”
Winthrop’s Kaydence Allarie shot 83 to win the Class C girls title. Mattanawcook Academy’s Skylar Bard was second with a 90.
“It feels really good,” said Allarie, a junior. “I definitely knew that I could do it. I just needed to stay consistent and play my game.”
In addition to Fontaine’s round, Grady Hreben shot 79, Josh Herzing carded an 80 and Sam Dunton had an 85 for Maranacook.
Drew Mertzel, who won medalist honors last year, led Winthrop with a 76. Also for the Ramblers, Sam Corgan shot 79 and Lincoln MacArthur finished with an 80.
Fontaine has only played competitive golf for three years and wasn’t thinking about winning the title entering play Saturday. He had birdies on the fourth, 12th and 13th holes.
“Today is just (the mindset) of you versus you,” Fontaine said. “You’re competing against yourself.”
Ryan Farnsworth of Dexter was the boys runner-up with a 74. Mertzel, Beckett Peabody of Houlton and Chris Johnson of Kents Hill tied for third at 76.
Allaire said she struggled on the back nine, but her putting helped her out.
“The whole front nine, I felt pretty good about my game,” Allarie said. “I think that definitely helped, because I got my numbers a little lower.”

title: UMaine hockey rallies to upend No. 6 Quinnipiac
text:
The University of Maine rallied from a 3-2 deficit to edge sixth-ranked Quinnipiac 5-3 at Alfond Arena on Saturday night.
UMaine is now 2-2 while Quinnipiac fell to 3-1.
The teams split their series as Quinnipiac triumphed 2-1 on Friday night.
Quinnipiac erased a pair of one-goal deficits in the first period and took a 3-2 lead just 1:04 into the second period when senior left wing and captain Mason Marcellus scored his fourth goal of the season.
He is one of just two players in the country with goals in each of his first four games.
But junior defenseman and Bemidji State transfer Isa Parekh tied it at the 2:20 mark, his second of the season, and junior right wing and UMass Lowell transfer Lee Parks scored 2:33 later to supply the Black Bears with their third one-goal lead of the night.
It was Parks’ third of the season and extended his goal-scoring streak to three games.
Nobody scored the rest of the period so UMaine took a one-goal lead into the third period.
UMaine protected the lead and Sully Scholle added an empty-net goal.
UMaine sophomore defenseman Loic Usereau opened the scoring with his first at the 7:42 mark. But the lead was short-lived as senior center and Holy Cross transfer Jack Stockfish responded just 1:13 later with his second of the campaign.
Sophomore right wing and Arizona State transfer Sam Alfano restored the lead while the Black Bears were on a five-minute power play resulting from a major charging penalty and game misconduct on Alex Kostov at the expense of Chris Romaine, who had to be helped off the ice and didn’t return.
It was Alfano’s first of the season.
But freshman defenseman Jan Golicic potted his first career goal to tie it.
Usereau collected his first goal of the season, wristing the puck through a crowd during a scramble.
Stockfish tied it by jamming home a rebound before Alfano fired home a rebound at the 13:48 mark. Golicic equalized with a wrist shot from the right point that may have hit a Black Bear on its way in.
Marcellus converted a nice pass from Ethan Wyttenbach with a quick one-timer after sprinting down the left wing.
But Parekh equalized with a wrister from the middle of the slot off an Owen Fowler feed and an unattended Parks scored what proved to be the game-winner from the low slot at the far post off a well-placed cross-ice pass from Will Gerrior.
“It was a great play. A great pass,” said Parks, who has been best friends with Gerrior since eighth grade.
“Over the years, we built chemistry from summer skates and stuff like that. It has been a lot of fun to play with him so far,” said Parks. “He is more of a shooter, actually, but he has been setting me up.”
Gerrior had set up Parks with a similar pass for Friday night’s UMaine goal.
UMaine head coach Ben Barr said the game “wasn’t as pretty as last night. We looked a little jittery which can be expected because (Friday night) was an emotional game.
“It was good to see some guys step up and make plays when we needed it which is something we hadn’t had the prior two games. Max Scott’s line with Will Gerrior and Lee Parks was awesome. Loic Usereau was way better tonight, Sammy Alfano got his first goal and Isa Parekh played really well, too,” added Barr.
Center Scott had three assists, Parks had a goal and an assist and Gerrior had two assists.
Fowler had two assists.
Wyttenbach and Dylan Edwards each had two assists for Quinnipiac.
UMaine outshot Quinnipiac 29-23.
Albin Boija made 20 saves for UMaine and Rorke Applebee finished with 24 for Quinnipiac.
“Albin was a really good in the second and third periods,” said Barr. “He was a little shaky in the first period but he rebounded which was really good to see. We needed it because they had a lot of good looks in the second and the third.”
Parekh said earning the win was “crucial.”
“You see how hard we all work out there. We didn’t want to go 1-3. We needed this win bad and we did it,” said Parekh.
Parks said he felt the entire team played “great” on Friday night but the “bounces didn’t go out way. That’s how it goes.
“We knew we had to come out tonight and find a way and that’s what we did,” added Parks.
UMaine has next weekend off before hosting Colgate on Oct. 23-24. Game times are 7 each night.
Quinnipiac visits Penn State for one game next Friday night.

title: Letter: Alternatives to jail must be more fully considered
text:
Residents of Penobscot County will be asked to cast a vote next month on an issue of critical importance: whether to locate a proposed new county jail outside the city of Bangor. But this is about much more than where a building should be located.
Before the taxpayers of Penobscot County are asked to shoulder more financial burden, I believe there needs to be a vigorous, open conversation about continued commitment to an incarceration system that fails all of us.
A majority of those in Penobscot County jail have not yet been convicted of a crime. Many lack adequate money for bail. Large majorities have substance use/addiction and/or mental health issues and are low income. Many suffered trauma as children. Some may wait as long as six months for a trial. While they wait they may lose jobs, housing and access to needed healthcare. Their families are adversely affected.
The costs to provide basic healthcare to inmates are shouldered by county taxpayers. That’s in addition to the custodial costs of incarceration. Why aren’t we using those dollars more wisely?
There’s little evidence that jailing people actually keeps our communities safer.
Diversion programs that would link those arrested with the services they could actually benefit from are one alternative to incarceration that has been employed successfully here and elsewhere.
The current system is of questionable value. Let’s pause and plan a more humane, efficient, cost-effective way forward.
Deb Leon
Holden

title: A US-brokered ceasefire was supposed to end the Israel-Hamas war. A year later, progress has stalled
text:
A US-brokered ceasefire was supposed to end the Israel-Hamas war. A year later, progress has stalled
It's been a year since a ceasefire deal brokered by U.S. President Donald Trump and Arab allies promised to end the war in Gaza, and Israel is still launching deadly strikes on the devastated territory.
Previous video coverage above: Israeli soldiers share rare accounts from Gaza, describing ongoing killings despite ceasefire
The agreement halted major military operations, freed all remaining hostages and increased humanitarian access. But it has failed to deliver on promises of a new Palestinian administration aided by international forces, the disarmament of Hamas and an end to Israel's control over more than half the territory. Almost nothing has been rebuilt.
Israel has tied any progress on the other issues to Hamas' complete disarmament, while the militant group — and the Trump administration — say they should happen simultaneously. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu hardened his stance over the summer, openly defying Trump, his most important ally, ahead of Israeli elections later this month.
The wrangling has left Gaza's 2 million Palestinians in limbo. Most are sheltering in rodent-infested tent camps, the rubble of their former neighborhoods or war-damaged buildings at risk of collapse.
The 20-point ceasefire agreement, reached after months of negotiations under the Biden and Trump administrations, ended major military operations and led to the return of all the remaining hostages taken in Hamas' Oct. 7, 2023, attack that ignited the war.
Hamas-led militants killed some 1,200 people that day and abducted 251. Israel responded with massive bombardment and a ground invasion that has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, according to the Gaza Health Ministry.
The ministry, part of the Hamas-run government, maintains detailed records and is seen as generally reliable by U.N. agencies and independent experts. It does not distinguish between civilians and militants in its toll but says women and children make up around half the dead.
After the deal was announced, Trump called for a new era of harmony in the Middle East. "We have a once-in-a-lifetime chance to put the old feuds and bitter hatreds behind us," he said at a summit marking the deal.
Video below: Trump announces deal for Hamas to disarm and Israeli forces to withdraw from Gaza
The agreement called for Hamas to hand over power to a committee of Palestinian administrators vetted by the Board of Peace, a new body chaired by Trump and charged with implementing the ceasefire.
The militants officially dissolved their government in July but left the civil service intact and remain the dominant power in the roughly 40% of Gaza not controlled by the Israeli military. Israel has meanwhile barred the new Palestinian administration from entering Gaza via Egypt.
The formation of an International Stabilization Force was announced in February but has yet to materialize. Indonesia, which pledged the largest troop contingent — 8,000 soldiers — put those plans on hold last spring as the world's focus shifted to the Iran war.
Israel was supposed to withdraw from Gaza but has instead seized more territory, pushing the so-called yellow Line of Control westward toward the Mediterranean Sea. It has also carried out regular strikes on individuals it accused of violating the ceasefire, approaching the yellow line or having taken part in the Oct. 7 attack — strikes that have often killed civilians.
Israeli strikes have killed over 1,400 Palestinians since the ceasefire took effect, according to the Gaza Health Ministry. Sporadic attacks have killed five Israeli soldiers in Gaza in the same period.
In July, Trump announced a deal to disarm Hamas, portraying it as a breakthrough in the long-stalled process.
That deal, an extension of the original ceasefire, called for Hamas to disarm "in a gradual, sequential and time-bound manner" that is "linked to an Israeli withdrawal, in phases." Hamas confirmed for the first time that it had agreed to disarm, also linking it to Israel halting its strikes and withdrawing from Gaza.
Days later, Netanyahu announced that Israel would not withdraw from any part of Gaza until after Hamas has been completely disarmed, explicitly rejecting the agreement announced by Trump.
The rare instance of friction between the two allies came as Netanyahu seeks to shore up his nationalist base ahead of Oct. 27 elections that could end his nearly unbroken 17-year rule, the longest in Israel's history.
Netanyahu has come under fire over security and intelligence failures leading up to the Oct. 7 attack, with opponents accusing him of having been soft on Hamas. That gives him little space to make even minor compromises on Gaza, at least until a new government is formed, which could take months.
In the meantime, virtually nothing has been rebuilt in Gaza, Hamas is weakened but still in power, and a return to fighting cannot be ruled out.

title: Colby football starts slow, falls to Wesleyan
text:
Colby fell behind by 14 points in the first half and couldn’t recover in a 21-7 NESCAC football loss to Wesleyan on Saturday in Middletown, Connecticut.
The Mules (0-4) pulled within seven when Jagger Matera threw a 4-yard touchdown pass to Sean Trinder with 5:19 remaining, but Wesleyan (4-0) answered less than two minutes later on a 69-yard pass from Matt Fitzsimons to Blake Newcomb.
Fitzsimons scored on 1-yard runs in the first and second quarter. He completed 22 of 28 passes, with a touchdown and three interceptions.
Colby managed just 155 yards and nine first downs.
WILLIAMS 34, BATES 0: The Ephs (3-1) held the Bobcats (0-4) to 84 yards and seven first downs and cruised to a NESCAC win in Williamstown, Massachusetts.
Drew Weiler, Brady Stahelski and Aiden Clark each had a rushing touchdown in the second quarter as Williams took a 21-0 lead. Leonardo Maiuolo kicked a 34-yard field goal in the third quarter and a 21-yarder in the fourth. Quinn Rucker added a 4-yard scoring run.

MMA quarterback Harris Stone completed 21 of 37 passes for 214 yards, with one touchdown and one interception.
Will Patenaude scored on touchdown runs of 6, 8 and 57 yards for Norwich.

title: Despite weakening, Isaias still poses threat to Southeast
text:
CRESTVIEW, Fla. (WEAR) — Isaias is now a post-tropical storm but remains a threat as it drenches the Southeast.
The National Hurricane Center said in its final advisory that the storm’s sustained winds fell to 35 miles per hour.
The storm made landfall on Florida’s Panhandle on Friday, Oct. 9, as a Category 2 hurricane.
At least four storm-related deaths have been reported, two in Florida and two in Alabama.
Hundreds of thousands of customers are without power across the Southeast.
Homes and businesses were damaged across the region, with the roof of at least one gas station getting shredded to pieces.
Much of the Southeast is still at risk of flash flooding as the storm continues to weaken.
The area will also experience strong wind gusts as well as the threat of spin-up tornadoes.

title: How to better plan your fall foliage outings in Maine
text:
This story was originally published in September 2020.
A dazzling time of year, fall foliage season marks the end of summer with a fiery display that transforms the Maine landscape. The spectacular show lasts just a few weeks. If you drag your feet, you just might miss it.
To truly embrace the season, many people plan special outings to find the most vibrant colors. Whether you’re visiting Maine for the first time or you’ve lived here for many years, leaf peeping is a fun activity that brings joy to all ages. To help you get the most out of the experience, here are a few tips.
Time it right
To learn when leaves are changing color in different parts of the state, check out the Maine Fall Foliage Report, which is issued weekly by the Maine Department of Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry. The report tracks the color progress across the state using a network of observers, including Maine forest rangers and forest pathologists.
The report is updated on Wednesday afternoons, typically starting mid-September and running through October, until most of the leaves have fallen from the trees or faded to brown. To view the full reports, including color-coded maps that divide the state up into different zones, visit mainefoliage.com. You can also sign up for the weekly report to be sent to you via email on the website.
Extend the season
Maine is a big state that varies in temperature from south to north, and from the coast to inland areas. This matters when it comes to fall foliage because temperature is one of the main factors for when leaves change color. Generally, leaves change color in colder regions first. Therefore, in Maine, fall foliage progresses from north to south. Leaves also tend to change color in inland mountainous regions before they do along the coast.
With this in mind, you can sometimes enjoy peak fall foliage for a few weeks by planning trips to different regions of Maine. For example, in mid-September, the leaves might be mostly green in southern Maine, but in Aroostook County, color could be popping up all over the landscape.
Spot color early
Views of fall foliage in Maine. Credit: Aislinn Sarnacki / BDN
One trick for spotting colorful trees early in the season is visiting areas where trees are facing less than ideal growing conditions. When stressed, trees sometimes tap out early in the season and stop producing green chlorophyll. As this natural pigment breaks down, the leaves’ fall colors are revealed.
A prime example of this is when trees along roadways turn color before trees that are deeper in the forest. Roadside trees are sometimes stressed by road salt, dust and lack of water. Another example is when trees change color early in regions experiencing drought.
In addition, some of the trees that grow around wetlands, such as silver and red maple, tend to change color earlier. So if you’re in an area that is still largely green, seek out a road or trail that travels by a bog.
Seek out certain trees
When it comes to fall color, certain tree species outshine the rest. In Maine, some of our most colorful trees are sugar maples and red maples. Their leaves often bleed into bright orange, blood red and even peach and purple. Less common black gum trees are also known to be among the showiest fall trees, with their leaves turning bright red and sometimes orange.
Oak trees also put on a show, with leaves transitioning to orange and gold late in the season. Birch trees often display yellows, as do aspen trees. And beech leaves tend to turn a rusty orange and cling to branches well into the winter.
Some understory plants can also turn bright colors. Hobblebush, for example, is a broad-leafed shrub found in shady, wet woods throughout Maine, and its leaves often turn bright reddish purple. And blueberry plants are known for turning bright red. Visit one of Maine’s many blueberry fields and see for yourself. Blueberries also grow atop many of the state’s mountains, including mountains in Acadia National Park.
In general, seek out areas with plenty of deciduous trees rather than conifer forests. The only Maine conifer that changes color in the fall is the tamarack, which has soft needles that turn golden and fall off, just like leaves, to grow back again the following spring.
Plan for chilly weather
Fall in Maine is a time for flannels, fleece and at times, wool hats. Though summer was only yesterday, the temperature drops quickly during this time of year, especially in the evening. While enjoying the beautiful fall foliage, stay cozy by packing plenty of warm clothing layers. A thermos of hot cider can also significantly improve your leaf peeping experience.
Leave the road behind
Viewing the fall colors from the comfort of a car can be a lot of fun, but stepping out into the cool autumn air can really add to the experience. The rich scent of decaying leaves, while it doesn’t sound particularly appealing, is actually quite nice.
One way to spend time outside while leaf peeping is to select a well-marked and maintained trail. Do a little research ahead of time to select a trail that fits your needs, whether that’s a wheelchair-accessible path or a rugged hiking trail that leads to the top of a mountain. Some trails are known for being particularly good for viewing fall foliage. But whatever trail you choose in Maine, as long as it’s not in the thick of an evergreen forest, should lead you to plenty of colorful trees.
Another way to view fall foliage is by train. Maine is home to the Downeast Scenic Railroad and the Belfast and Moosehead Lake Railroad, both of which offer scenic day trips in open air coaches and have made changes to follow state and Centers for Disease Control and Prevention guidelines for safety during the COVID-19 pandemic.
Traveling by boat is another excellent way to view fall colors. There’s something especially beautiful about colorful trees reflecting in the water. Fall paddling can be more dangerous than summer paddling because the water is quickly becoming colder (which can cause paddlers to develop hypothermia faster if they fall in). It’s especially important to wear a life jacket and stick to paddling trips within your skill level. Or you could seek out a guided tour or boat cruise.
Look out for storms
Keep an eye on the weather forecast. If you see predictions for heavy rain or wind, you’ll want to get out there and enjoy the fall foliage beforehand. Wind and rain can bring a swift end to fall foliage season in Maine by knocking the already fragile leaves to the ground.

title: High schools Saturday: Sanford football earns first win with last-minute TD
text:
Adam Cote Jr.’s fourth touchdown of the game — a 2-yard run with 17.8 seconds remaining — gave Sanford a 44-36 win over Scarborough in a Class A South football game Saturday afternoon in Scarborough.
Scarborough (0-6) tied the game midway through the fourth quarter on a 28-yard run by Aiden Carpenter and a conversion pass from Oscar Goss to Quinncy Colvin.
After an exchange of punts, Sanford (1-5) took over at its own 34 with less than two minutes left. Cote kept the possession alive when he connected with Oakley O’Keeffe for a 39-yard gain on third-and-5. Later, on first-and-goal from the 2, he kept the ball himself, went around left end and dove into the end zone.
The teams combined for 58 points in the first half, which ended with Sanford ahead 30-28.
Cote had TD runs of 23 and 17 yards in the first quarter and 65 yards in the second.
Scarborough answered with three second-quarter touchdowns — a 39-yard pass from Goss to Brandon Brady, and scoring runs of 85 and 14 yards by Ozzie Bodah. Bodah’s first TD came immediately after an interception by Goss and put Scarborough ahead 21-16. Tyson Kimball, though, returned the ensuing kickoff 77 yards, setting up a 9-yard touchdown run by Logan Sevigny.
Sevigny and Carpenter each finished with two TD runs.
MARSHWOOD 45, CHEVERUS 6: Greg Castoras rushed for four touchdowns for the second week in a row, leading the Hawks (6-0) to a Class B South win over the Stags (1-5) in Portland.
Castoras reached the end zone twice on Marshwood’s first six plays. First, he broke free for a 51-yard touchdown. Then, after a 69-yard run by Jack O’Brien, Castoras went in from the 3 and added a 2-point conversion to make it 14-0.
Marshwood, ranked No. 4 in the Varsity Maine Top 10, extended its lead to 28-0 in the second quarter. Parker Ferrer caught a 5-yard TD pass from Michael Sbrizza, and Castoras plunged in from the 1 for his third touchdown.
Cheverus, meanwhile, was held without a first down in the first half. The Stags used a bit of trickery to score on the opening possession of the second half, as Jackson Holmes caught a short pass from Colton Jewett and flipped the ball to Kevin True, who went the distance for a 45-yard touchdown.
Castoras quickly answered with a 50-yard run. Then, after Cheverus forced a Marshwood fumble just outside its own goal line, Jewett was tackled in the end zone for a safety that made it 38-6.
The final TD was a 1-yard run by Jon Buttrick early in the fourth quarter.
BOYS SOCCER
WESTBROOK 3, BONNY EAGLE 0: Mechac Boyilimpo, Mustafa Saker and Ryan Garber scored for the Blue Blazes (7-5) against the Scots (1-9) in Westbrook.
Ryan Garber added a goal. Westbrook keepers Ahmed Al Obaidi and Ethan Brewer combined for 12 saves.
Asa Proctor made nine saves for Bonny Eagle.
LEWISTON 4, MT. ARARAT 0: Khalil Ibrahim and Yussuf Ali scored in the first half and Daniel Dimandja added two second-half goals for the Blue Devils (11-1) in a win over the Eagles (3-8-1) in Lewiston.
GIRLS SOCCER
GARDINER 1, MEDOMAK VALLEY 0: The Tigers (10-1-1) scored on an own goal in the second half to beat the Panthers (1-10-1) in Gardiner.
Adela Ricker stopped three shot for Gardiner, while Lilly Hills made five saves for Medomak Valley.
FIELD HOCKEY
THORNTON ACADEMY 4, NOBLE 0: Vanessa Dyer and Olivia Lamey each scored one goal and set up another, and the Golden Trojans (8-3) broke open a close game with three third-quarter goals against the Knights (7-5) in North Berwick.
Kinsleigh Plummer and Camila Sibille each added a goal in the third quarter after Thornton led 1-0 at halftime.
MOUNTAIN VALLEY 4, POLAND 0: Melina Byam recorded two goals and two assists to propel the Falcons (7-3) to a win over the Knights (3-8-1) in Rumford.
Addie Libby added a goal and two assists, and Emma Williamson also scored for Mountain Valley.
Bella Dupuis made one save for Mountain Valley.
Izzie Billings stopped 24 shots for Poland.
TELSTAR 3, TRAIP ACADEMY 0: Quinn Coolidge had two goals and an assist as the Rebels (1-10) beat the Rangers (0-9) in Bethel.
Idella Cooley also scored and Kallie Buck had an assist.
Madelyn Cooley earned the shutout with four saves. Traip’s Madison Evans stopped five shots.
MT. BLUE 4, FRYEBURG ACADEMY 0: Elyse Mastine scored and added an assist as the Cougars (7-5) defeated the Raiders (2-7) in Farmington.
Kilee Merrill, Catherine Ferriter and Reese Nye were the other goal scorers. Tabby Hesseltine finished with two assists.
Sophia Carone made six saves for Fryeburg.

title: Horrified by Maine Library Commission proposal
text:
I was horrified to read that the Maine Library Commission is trying to limit tiny volunteer libraries (“Maine’s volunteer libraries thrive with tight budgets. State rules could make that harder,” Oct. 5). Really? That makes me very sad and angry for the small towns with limited resources.
My grandmother and mother were both teachers and instilled the love of reading and researching in me. I grew up frequenting the library regularly — and I still do as an adult. Our library in Gray is a friendly place to meet fellow book lovers and attend various groups, talks and more.
The ability to borrow books via interlibrary loans is fabulous and the opportunity to use the computers available when I have a power outage at home is invaluable. Certainly even a library that is open only a few days a week is better than no library.
Jan Strout
Gray

title: Needle exchanges save lives
text:
My dad died in 2003, just before his 58th birthday. Since before I was born he had been an alcoholic and a heroin user. He died of liver cancer brought on by hepatitis C. He likely contracted that hepatitis from a shared needle.
I don’t know if there were needle exchange services where he was then. Probably not; it was the 1970s, when even having “drug paraphernalia” was criminalized in the United States. Criminalization did not stop people from using. Those who ran clean needle services were usually activists, risking imprisonment in their attempts to halt the spread of diseases.
Dad was a Navy veteran. He’d complained of abdominal pain and loss of appetite for years. By the time he was diagnosed by a Veterans Affairs doctor in 2002, his cancer was terminal. He said his earlier attempts to have his pain addressed were probably dismissed as “drug-seeking behavior.”
It can be uncomfortable to be around people who use street drugs. Just because someone uses does not mean that they deserve to catch a deadly illness. I don’t pretend to know why Dad started using. But I’m reasonably confident that people use drugs for reasons that are very real to them; they stop for their own reasons too.
Addiction is complicated. I know people who were given powerful pain medicines during hospitalization and quickly became addicted to them.
Helping people avoid reusing needles is good. One needle not getting shared can mean one person not getting hepatitis or HIV that day. That’s why it’s called “harm reduction.” That person might be someone’s dad, mom, brother, sister, daughter, spouse or friend. Everyone is someone’s something.
Siiri Cressey
Lewiston

title: Man seen riding out Hurricane Isaias in boat as storm surged in Gulf
text:
DAUPHIN ISLAND, Ala. (WALA/Gray News) - A man was reportedly on a boat off the east end of an Alabama island as Hurricane Isaias drew closer to landfall.
Police said they had been in contact with the boater on Dauphin Island earlier on Thursday. Officials said the boater is a local man who wanted to be on his boat.
Police said the man is aware of the dangers of being aboard the boat during the storm and was willing to take the risk.
The hurricane was expected to make landfall around 9:30 p.m. near Pensacola, about 95 miles away.
Maximum sustained winds were recorded up to 120 miles per hour by Thursday evening, dropping down to about 110 mph an hour before expected landfall.
A storm surge of up to 4 to 6 feet was expected for Dauphin Island, and 4 to 8 inches of rain were expected across the southern part of Alabama.

title: Cause of death revealed for two Ole Miss students in court
text:
OXFORD, Miss. (WMC/Gray News) - The cause of death was revealed for two Ole Miss students in court proceedings.
In court, one of the defense attorneys for two men charged with selling narcotics said one student died from a combined use of various substances, including cough syrup.
The other student died from inhalation asphyxiation.
The two students, 18-year-old Aidan Hamilton and 20-year-old Robert Strang, died on Monday, Sept. 21.
Investigators allege that Puffs Vape, Tobacco and Beer Store in Oxford, where both Moslehs worked, sold Hamilton the pills twice in the days before his death.
While officials believe it was Puffs that sold Hamilton the narcotics found in his system, they say Strang bought his pills from a different store outside the county 20 miles away.
After the deaths, Lafayette County Metro Narcotics agents sent a confidential informant into Puffs Vape, Tobacco and Beer Store in Oxford to investigate the alleged sales of illegal substances, according to the arrest affidavit.
The informant asked if the store sold “7-OH Kratom-based pills.”
Records show the clerk said yes before warning the informant to “be careful taking the pills, because people are dying from them.”
Oxford police then executed a search warrant at the store, and 500 units of kratom and kratom-like products were seized. An assortment of “THC cartridges, gummies, pre-rolls, and other suspected THC substances” was also recovered.
During the raid, detectives found the same brand of Smax Mango Breeze MGM-15, with identical packaging, ingredients and a $39.99 price tag with a smudge on the 9, at the store that had been found near Hamilton.
According to court records, a toxicology report, which has not been made publicly available, shows both victims had the same three substances present — Mitrogynine, MGM-15 and MGPI — which are all featured in the Smax Mango Breeze pills.
The victims’ families provided law enforcement with photocopies of bank records. According to Easter, victim one spent $87.18 at Puff’s Vape on Sept. 20.
Victim two spent $43.59 at Puff’s Vape also on Sept. 20, according to Easter. Both purchases were made the day before the two students’ deaths.
In closing, federal prosecutors stated, “this case comes from several tragic overdose cases of students here in Oxford... evidence supports the detention… victims died of conditions consistent to overdoses.”
Prosecutors stated that the defendants were aware of their actions selling the illegal drugs.
The judge determined Yahya Mosleh will remain behind bars as the case plays out. Islam, his son, will be released on a $20,000 unsecured bond with conditions.
