title: Stetson looks back at how the cowboy hat helped shape America
text:
GARLAND, Texas (Gray DC) - As America continues to celebrate its 250th birthday, the company behind the modern cowboy hat is reflecting back on how it helped shape the country into what it is today.
“I think Stetson played a pretty vital role over the period of its history,” said Robert Dundon, CEO of the Stetson hat company. ”Particularly in the first 25 or 30 years with the expansion, to provide something that just didn’t exist at the time."
The “Boss of the Plains” Stetson was the first cowboy hat, invented by John B. Stetson in Colorado in 1865. The entrepreneur created the wide-brimmed hat to protect pioneers from the elements, just as westward expansion in the U.S. was beginning to accelerate.
“So the expansion was dangerous conditions, harsh weather. People were really in perilous places,” Dundon said. “So the hat was a tool really to provide them with protection from the elements, from the rain and the harsh conditions that they were facing.”
Before the Stetson was invented, most headwear brims would fall down when wet because they were made with raccoon skin or wool.
“Nobody had a big hat with a big brim, something to protect. So then he created this, and then he sold the first piece for $5, and it was a cowboy hat shape,” said Devin Marcum, the president of HatCo, which manufactures Stetson hats.
The hats quickly became popular after Stetson built his first factory in Philadelphia. By 1888, the company was the largest hat manufacturer in the world and it was turning into an American icon.
“It’s been one of these quintessential American pieces that has found its way into all sort of walks of life and use for for people who are hat wearers,” Dundon said.
Throughout the 20th and 21st centuries, Stetsons have been worn by ranchers, members of law enforcement, celebrities, rodeo riders and several U.S. presidents, including Ulysses S. Grant, Harry S. Truman, Dwight D. Eisenhower, Lyndon B. Johnson, Ronald Reagan, George W. Bush and Donald Trump.
Interest in cowboy hats has increased significantly in recent years, especially during the COVID-19 pandemic.
“All of a sudden we had orders flying through for cowboy hats,” Marcum said. “That came from a lot of things. I think people were now venturing out of cities and towns and being in more outdoor areas, being in more ranches, different things. And so the cowboy coolness really took over.”
The brand’s story continues to live on in Garland, Texas, where HatCo has been making Stetsons, after the Philadelphia factory was closed in 1970.
“There’s a lot of third and fourth generational families that have worked here,” Marcum said. “So I think it has something to do with the culture that we have here, the products that we get to build, the sense of pride that, when they’re working with building the Stetson brand hats, it’s something that they get to go home about, brag about.”
And even 161 years after the Stetson was first created, Dundon said the hats continue to be a popular way to express American identity.
“The cowboy hat is uniquely American,” he said. “...It reflects back to a time in our history where this ruggedness, this individual pursuit for an American way of life. I think the cowboy hat encapsulates a lot of that.”

title: Medicaid cuts strip refugees and other legal immigrants of their health coverage
text:
New restrictions have stripped Medicaid coverage from certain legal immigrants, including refugees and victims of human trafficking, as part of broader federal changes to the health insurance program that are expected to force millions off their coverage.
The change effective Oct. 1 cut from Medicaid what is estimated to be hundreds of thousands of people who legally immigrated to the United States, many of whom work and pay taxes, in the latest Trump administration policy to target foreigners.
The move is part of sweeping changes to Medicaid under President Donald Trump’s 2025 tax cut and policy law, with many set to take effect early next year. The Medicaid changes are projected to result in 7.5 million fewer people with health insurance, according to the Congressional Budget Office’s 2025 estimate.
Advocates say that without Medicaid, people will not be able to afford private insurance and will either delay care or end up in emergency rooms, adding pressure to a strained health system. For immigrants, the cuts could be felt more acutely, compounding the effects of other administration efforts to restrict their access to public assistance as part of a broader immigration crackdown.
“This is about telling every immigrant in the United States that they are not welcome here and that they should leave,” said Ben D’Avanzo, a senior strategist at the National Immigration Law Center, which has pursued litigation against the Republican administration over its immigration agenda.
Refugees, asylum seekers, victims of human trafficking and domestic violence are among those who have lost coverage. Green-card holders were not impacted.
Lauren Bis, a White House spokesperson, said in a statement that “immigrants must be able to support themselves without taking from overburdened benefits programs paid for by hard-working American taxpayers.”
D’Avanzo said many people who have lost coverage will likely only realize when they need medical care. But for some, the change has been felt immediately.
Dwindling supplies of lifesaving medication
In Tucson, Arizona, María Chacon has been caring for her son Jesus for almost five years since a car accident at 17 left him unable to breathe on his own. He requires a ventilator, a feeding tube and daily medication, and must be turned once every two hours to stop sores from forming. Chacon said he sometimes opens his eyes.
The family is originally from Mexico and entered the U.S. on a T visa, offered to victims of human trafficking, in 2018.
Chacon said Medicaid has helped cover almost $25,000 per month of care for her son, which includes a small stipend for her and her husband as compensation for being long-term caregivers. She said doctors have explained that even if they both worked 24 hours a day, they would not be able to cover the cost of his care.
“Since that day I haven’t been able to sleep. We haven’t been able to eat or anything. We’re wondering what we’re going to do?” Chacon said.
Jesus takes medication that Chacon estimates costs $7,000 a month. The supply runs out in mid-October. Without coverage, she does not know how her son is going to survive.
Chacon found out just days before the cuts that she was losing care. She called the state’s Medicaid offices to appeal. Although she is in the process of obtaining a green card, Medicaid coverage would only kick in five years after she is approved.
Steven Camarota, research director for the Center for Immigration Studies, a right-leaning think tank that seeks less immigration, said the administration “is trying to nibble around the edges” with the Oct. 1 cuts, finding piecemeal ways to curb immigration into the U.S.
Camarota believes the government should screen legal immigrants for income potential and education, reducing the number who might rely on public benefits once they cross the border.
“You need immigrants who are unlikely to need welfare,” he said, or those with high educational attainment.
The administration recently revived a federal rule that could deny green cards to immigrants who use public benefits that could include food stamps, Medicaid, housing vouchers and others.
Chacon believes the cuts to Medicaid coverage are part of the administration’s clampdown on immigrants. She said her son is in no condition to travel.
“I know that’s what he’s doing, but, as my son is, I couldn’t go to Mexico,” Chacon said.
Millions more will be dropped from Medicaid
Medicaid, jointly funded by states and the federal government, has become a political focal point during Trump’s second term. The president has pushed to root out what he describes as fraud in the program. In July, the administration deferred over $1 billion in Medicaid payments to California and Minnesota, claiming there was suspected fraud; critics argued the move targeted Democratic-led states.
As more people are cut from Medicaid, the federal government is predicted to reduce program spending by $911 billion, according to healthcare research nonprofit KFF.
In Arizona, officials said 29,000 legal immigrants were cut from Medicaid rolls on Oct. 1. In Florida, estimates are closer to 177,000. Overall, more than 281,000 immigrants from nine states and the District of Columbia are estimated to lose Medicaid coverage, according to KFF.
As more states implement various restrictions to coverage, 7.5 million people are expected to lose coverage by 2034, according to analysis by the Congressional Budget Office.
Without coverage, people will turn to emergency rooms for care. When people delay seeing a doctor, conditions can worsen and become even more expensive to treat.
“At the end of the day, it does raise the cost for the states because once you get these people in for something that could have been prevented, they could not go to the doctor because they were uninsured; they most likely will end up at a hospital in an emergency room,” said Carmen Feliciano, the vice president of policy and advocacy at UnidosUS, a Latino civil rights organization.
UnidosUS partners with community organizations to help provide medical care, but Feliciano said they already are overwhelmed and would not be able to support the number of people who are going to lose medical coverage in the coming months.
“We are not going to have the capacity to serve all the people who need it,” Feliciano said.

title: Deputy injured by falling tree during Hurricane Isaias response
text:
DALE COUNTY, Ala. (WSFA/WTVY/Gray News) — A sheriff’s deputy in Alabama was injured Friday night while responding to storm damage from Hurricane Isaias.
Dale County Sheriff Mason Bynum said one of his deputies was responding to the scene of a rollover vehicle crash with a downed tree on U.S. Highway 231 in Newton.
A car struck the tree, causing it to fall. Multiple other vehicles then hit the tree, Bynum said.
While deputies were on scene, another tree fell, landing on one of the involved vehicles and entrapping the driver.
The tree struck one of Bynum’s deputies as it fell. Bynum confirmed the injuries were “minor.” The deputy was taken to an area hospital.
The driver was extricated from the vehicle. Bynum said the driver is OK.
Sheriff urges drivers to stay off roads
Bynum said there were numerous trees down in his jurisdiction and urged residents to stay off the roads.
“It’s a very dangerous situation, very fluid situation. We just urge people to please stay off the roadways right now,” Bynum said.

title: 2 killed by fallen trees since Hurricane Isaias made landfall on Gulf Coast, authorities say
text:
BIRMINGHAM, Ala. (WBRC/Gray News) - Alabama authorities say a person has died after a tree fell on a home in Birmingham Saturday morning.
According to Birmingham Fire and Rescue, crews were called to the home on Monterey Drive after midnight regarding two people being trapped inside.
The person was pronounced dead once rescuers were able to check the scene. There was no immediate word given on the condition of the second person.
Hurricane Isaias moved through parts of Alabama during the overnight hours Friday and into Saturday morning after making landfall hours earlier in the Florida panhandle.
Isaias made landfall as a Category 2 hurricane and then quickly moved north through Alabama, bringing strong winds and periods of heavy rain across the state.
The Escambia County Sheriff’s Office in Florida has also confirmed a fatality since Isaias’ landfall, stating that a downed tree has taken the life of a resident.

title: Therapy dogs bring calm and joy to students following shooting at Colorado high school
text:
EVERGREEN, Colo. (AP) — With wagging tails and kind eyes, the four-legged staff members at Evergreen High School welcome students each morning, walk the halls and visit classrooms to offer a loving, calming presence and moments of joy to a student body still processing a school shooting.
Norene and Polenta, two golden Labs, joined the high school southwest of Denver to help students relieve stress and stay focused as they heal from last year’s trauma after a student shot and wounded two of his peers before shooting himself.
“Every morning after I get off the bus, I have to say hi to these two. It’s my first thing I do every day,” said Fisher Helbraun, a junior at Evergreen High School. “Every single time I see one, I always have a smile on my face. I always get either some puppy kisses or I get some nice pets.”
Norene, a calm, young dog who loves attention, and Polenta, her spunky and rambunctious colleague, started at the school in March and August, respectively. They are part of program run by Canine Companions, a nonprofit based in California that provides trauma support dogs free of charge. The dogs are the first to be matched with a school following a shooting on campus.
The shooting left ‘a lot of sorrow’
In September 2025, a 16-year-old student opened fire with a revolver at the school during lunch hour, wounding two students before shooting himself. The suspect later died. Evergreen High School Principal Skyler Artes sheltered in the main office with students and staff and remained at the school until the last person had left.
After the shooting “everybody was devastated, a lot of sorrow, a lot of grief, a lot of uncertainty about how to proceed,” Artes said
Some of the nonprofit’s dogs provided support at a family reunification site.
Artes decided to train with Canine Companions to be a support dog handler after seeing the positive impact the animals had on the students and staff.
The dogs were crowned prince and princess at homecoming
Volunteers with Canine Companions continued to bring dogs to the school in the days following the shooting, and Artes decided support dogs should be a permanent presence at the school.
“The fact that they are calm, that they’re generally peaceful and attentive makes them good at providing that ongoing, consistent, stable source of support, affection and quiet when people need it most,” she said.
Even though the dogs are a relatively new presence at the school in the foothills of the Rocky Mountains, they were crowned prince and princess at the homecoming football game last week and donned royal capes and crowns as they paraded through the football field.
“The second that I see them in the hallway, or I go out of my way to come see them, it just brightens my day, it makes it so much better,” said Maddie Cornwell, a senior. “That kind of innocent joy and love that they have to share, they just give it to humans so easily and it just makes you so happy to see them play and run around.”
Artes is Norene’s handler, and Polenta is assigned to lead counselor Amy Wells, who is also a volleyball coach and brings Polenta to practices. Wells also completed the handler training at Canine Companions.
Students make a point to see the dogs daily
The organization starts training support dogs from the time they are puppies when they start learning dozens of tasks, from following simple commands like sitting and staying, to more refined skills, including how to respond to students or teachers going through a difficult moment. They also learn how to be a stable presence in areas of the school that could trigger trauma, said Paige Mazzoni, chief executive of Canine Companions.
“What’s really powerful about dogs in this type of work is that they have a lot of heart, they have high intelligence, they respond very well to people and to forming a partnership, and it’s really the power of the human-canine bond,” she said.
Quinn McEvers, a senior, said she makes it a point to see the dogs or pet them each school day because it always puts her in a good mood.
Having “these dogs in the school is amazing because when we have tests, when there’s a stressful moment, when the weather’s bad, when, honestly, anything puts our mood kind of down, the dogs are there,” McEvers said.
“I would think people do a lot better in school when they’re actually in a good mood or when they’re excited about going to school,” she added.
Research shows that shootings at schools can lead to lower test scores and declines in students’ ability to concentrate and focus but Evergreen saw the opposite, Artes said.
“We saw our AP test scores go up,” she said. “We also had a 100% graduation rate in a year that was extraordinarily difficult.”
After a dog is assigned to a facility, they stay there for eight to 10 years, when the animal retires.
Artes said she plans to get more support dogs once Norene and Polenta leave their posts.
“Having a steady presence, an animal that doesn’t really care what’s going on and loves you anyway,” she said, “that unconditional love and support, that is valuable no matter what’s going on.”
____
Rodriguez reported from San Francisco.

title: Isaias weakens but flash flooding threat persists as hundreds of thousands grapple with power outages
text:
PANAMA CITY BEACH, Fla. (AP) — Isaias roared onto the Florida Panhandle, ripping roofs off homes and condominiums, before it moved north Saturday, bringing torrential rain and the threat of flash floods and tornadoes across the Southeast.
Two people were killed by fallen trees and about 800,000 customers were without power, mostly in Florida and Alabama.
Isaias came ashore as a Category 2 hurricane on Friday near Destin, Florida, a popular Gulf Coast vacation spot filled with high-rises and quirky tourist shops. The storm weakened overnight and was downgraded to a post-tropical cyclone but remained a threat.
“The risk of flooding is still high,” Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said Saturday morning. “Sometimes these things happen a day or two days after the storm goes through. So the flooding story is not over.”

title: 12-year-old girl dies after drinking Twix milkshake, reports say
text:
(Gray News) - A 12-year-old girl died after drinking a Twix milkshake, according to multiple reports.

EN ESPAÑOL | Reportan la muerte de una niña de 12 años luego de tomar una malteada Twix
She visited the cafe with her aunt and sister in London in August 2023.
CCTV evidence captured the moment cafe operator Baris Yucel made the drink in a blender that hadn’t been washed after its previous use.
Her aunt said Mia, who had a hazelnut allergy, had consumed some of a Twix milkshake “which had been cross-contaminated with hazelnut residue from a Kinder Bueno milkshake previously prepared.

In a case brought by Southwark Council, the café’s food business operator, Baris Yucel, pleaded guilty to six charges.
Southwark Council said in a release that the charges included not making allergen advice available or visible to consumers, failing to manage allergen contamination during the food production process, and serving food that contained an allergenic ingredient that was not supposed to be present.

title: 'Horrific scene': Multiple people dead in Pennsylvania shooting
text:
9 people dead, including children, after shooting in Erie, Pennsylvania, sources say
Nine people were found dead after a shooting Friday night at a home in Erie, Pennsylvania. Local sources reported that two were children.
Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro said nine people had died, and Erie News Now said the shooter was among the dead.
Erie Police Chief Rick Lorah said the number of lives lost on the 700 block of Perry Street was devastating and that the crime scene was by far the worst one he has ever seen in his law enforcement career.
"This is one of the most difficult and heartbreaking scenes our officers and investigators have ever encountered," he said. "The loss of life is devastating, and the circumstances we are working through are deeply disturbing."
Reports from Erie
The first reports made to police were of two women who had been shot outside a home on Perry Street, according to WJET.
Witnesses then told police the gunman had run into a nearby house.
The city of Erie released a statement clarifying the events, saying investigators determined that all nine deaths happened before police arrived.
"The deaths were not the result of any prolonged standoff or delay in police action," the city said. "No additional gunshots were fired after police arrived. Sounds heard during the police response that may have been mistaken for gunfire were flash bangs associated with law enforcement's tactical response."
According to local media, once inside, police found multiple bodies in different areas of the home.
Erie County Coroner Lyell Cook said two children were found dead inside the home.
“Our hearts are with the victims, their families and everyone affected by this tragedy. There are no words that can be adequately expressed the magnitude of the loss of life here,” Lorah said.
The city will hold a press conference at 4 p.m., livestreamed today on its Facebook page and YouTube channel.
In the press release, the city said it will "clarify several important facts in response to inaccurate information circulating about the incident."
'Horrific scene'
"It’s a horrific scene,” Lorah said. “There was a large loss of life inside that residence and outside that residence.”
Lorah went on to say, “I can’t confirm or deny the amount of individuals that were involved here. I can tell you that this is a tragic, tragic situation.”
Lorah told WJET the suspect is dead from what appeared to be a self-inflicted gunshot wound.
An investigation into what led to the shooting is ongoing. It is unclear whether any of the victims and the shooter knew each other.
Erie is a city of 94,831 people on the shore of Lake Erie. It is about 80 miles from Buffalo, 90 miles from Cleveland, and 120 miles from Pittsburgh.

title: Pope Leo declares death penalty 'inadmissible' as his native US plans to livestream execution
text:
ROME (AP) — Pope Leo XIV on Saturday declared capital punishment ”inadmissible” as he marked the World Day Against the Death Penalty and his native United States announced plans to livestream an execution by firing squad.
In a post on X, the American pope quoted the revised Catholic teaching on capital punishment ushered in by Pope Francis that the death penalty attacks the inherent dignity of a human being.
“The common good can be safeguarded and the requirements of justice can be met without recourse to capital punishment,” read the post under Leo’s official handle, @Pontifex. “Effective systems of detention have been developed that protect citizens while at the same time do not completely deprive those who are guilty of the possibility of redemption.”
The post ended with the hashtag #NoDeathPenalty.
The U.S. Defense Department announced Thursday that the firing squad execution of Nidal Malik Hasan, convicted of a 2009 shooting at the Fort Hood military base, will be livestreamed. Hasan, scheduled to be executed at Fort Hood on Dec. 3, was convicted of killing 13 people and wounding 32 others.
Leo didn’t refer specifically to the planned execution, or the botched lethal injection in Tennessee earlier that has revived debate over the death penalty in the United States. Saturday is World Day Against the Death Penalty, and it is common for the pope’s official social media accounts to post messages marking such commemorations.
But Leo’s post came just hours after his top deputy, Cardinal Pietro Parolin, the Vatican secretary of state, said explicitly that the planned U.S. public execution was “unacceptable.”
Pope Francis declared capital punishment ‘inadmissible’
Pope Francis in 2018 amended official Catholic teaching to declare capital punishment “inadmissible” in all circumstances.
Previously, the Catechism of the Catholic Church, the official compendium of church teaching, said the church didn’t exclude recourse to capital punishment “if this is the only possible way of effectively defending human lives against the unjust aggressor.”
Past popes had upheld that position, though St. John Paul II began urging an end to the practice and stressed that guilty people were just as deserving of dignity as innocent ones.
Like Francis before him, Leo has made visiting prisons a key part of his papal travel in a bid to give a message of hope to inmates and underscore their inherent dignity, that God loves them and that there is always a chance for redemption.
“If any of you fear being abandoned by everyone, know that God will never abandon you, and that the church will stand by your side,” Leo told inmates at the notorious Bata prison in Equatorial Guinea during his visit in April. Leo is to visit a prison in Buenos Aires during his upcoming tour through Latin America.
Speaking specifically about the United States, Cardinal Pietro Parolin, the Vatican secretary of state, said the planned livestreamed execution was “truly incomprehensible” and “unacceptable to turn death into a spectacle.”
“The Church’s position is one of total opposition to the death penalty; it is incompatible with human dignity and serves as no deterrent…,” Parolin said in comments carried by Vatican News. “It is truly incomprehensible that anyone would want to use this system today — I don’t know for what purpose. It is certainly unacceptable to turn death into a spectacle; even if the person is guilty, of course, there are other methods.”
The head of the U.S. bishops conference, Archbishop Paul Coakley, expressed “shock” and “great sorrow” at the Pentagon’s plans.
“In no way can Hasan’s actions be condoned but this decision is a barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered,” he said in a statement Friday. “The public execution even of one who has done grave harm will only further undermine the moral fabric of our nation and be a blight on the conscience of its people.”

title: Christa Pike is discharged from a hospital after surviving execution attempt, her attorneys say
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (AP) — Christa Pike, who survived Tennessee’s attempt to execute her by lethal injection, has been moved back to prison, her attorneys said Saturday.
Pike, 50, was discharged from the hospital and is back at the Debra K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center, the women’s prison where she was housed for 30 years, her attorneys said in a written statement.
“She is grateful to the first responders and her medical team for their care in these extraordinary circumstances. She is continuing to receive medical care at the prison, and we will continue to track her recovery,” the statement said.
Pike had been hospitalized since surviving two doses of pentobarbital as the state attempted to execute her on Sept. 30 for the 1995 beating and stabbing death of classmate Colleen Slemmer. At one point she was on a ventilator and her attorneys did not expect her to survive. However, they said Pike woke up and began talking and walking with assistance.
The Death Penalty Information Center says Pike is the first person to survive after receiving lethal injection drugs during an execution.
The Tennessee Department of Correction has not said what went wrong in the execution. Medical and lethal injection experts have focused on whether a problem with the IV line caused the drug to pool in her tissue instead of entering her bloodstream. Pike’s attorneys wrote in a court filing that “apparently at no point did any member of the execution team realize that the IV lines were not correctly placed.”
The failed execution brought renewed scrutiny to how Tennessee carries out death sentences.
Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee has since postponed the state’s only other scheduled execution this year and ordered a review of what went wrong. The state’s prison chief resigned in the wake of the failed execution
As the process got underway Pike was asked if she had a final statement and she spoke of being at peace. About five minutes later, she raised her head and said her arm hurt. Later, she appeared to lose consciousness but could be heard breathing heavily until media witnesses were escorted from the witness room nearly 90 minutes into the execution. An ambulance took her to a hospital.
___
An earlier version mispelled the name of the prison. It has corrected to Debra K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center, instead of Deborah K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center.

title: 'Total betrayal of Ukraine': Lawmakers react to Trump's diesel deal with Russia
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
'Total betrayal of Ukraine': Lawmakers react to Trump's diesel deal with Russia
Lawmakers on both sides of the aisle are voicing concerns after President Donald Trump struck a diesel deal with Russia, his latest push to lower prices ahead of the midterm elections.
'Total betrayal of Ukraine': Lawmakers react to Trump's diesel deal with Russia
Lawmakers on both sides of the aisle are voicing concerns after President Donald Trump struck a diesel deal with Russia, his latest push to lower prices ahead of the midterm elections.
President Donald Trump is striking a diesel deal with Russia in an effort to lower fuel prices ahead of the midterm elections, a move some lawmakers described as a "total betrayal of Ukraine."
The announcement marks a significant shift, as the U.S. has not imported Russian oil or gas since Moscow invaded Ukraine in 2022, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration.
What's in the deal?
Trump announced the agreement on Friday on social media, following what he described as "a highly successful discussion" with Russian President Vladimir Putin. He said Russia agreed to immediately supply over 300,000 tons of diesel "to the American and Global Marketplace," with 500,000 tons to follow in November, and another 1 million tons "immediately thereafter."
"Additionally, based on the condition of their Diesel Refineries, Russia will then deliver, within a short period of time, 3,000,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel," Trump added. "Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority."
In an exchange with reporters later Friday, Trump thanked Putin and didn't respond to shouted questions about criticism from the Ukrainian President, Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
Zelenskyy said on social media that any easing of sanctions against Russia without an agreement to de-escalate fighting is "an obvious weakness."
"It plays into Russia’s hands – allowing it to kill more, wage war for longer, have even less respect for America, and inflict even greater losses and damage on the world," Zelenskyy said.
Despite those concerns, the U.S. Treasury Department moved to ease sanctions for six months, allowing Russian diesel to be supplied to the global market.
The White House didn't immediately respond to questions about when the diesel would become available, who would pay for it, and whether Trump made any concessions in exchange.
How are US lawmakers reacting?
Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer, along with Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, who is the top Democrat on the Foreign Relations Committee, and Sen. Elizabeth Warren, the ranking Democrat on the Banking Committee, called the deal "a total betrayal of Ukraine, our European allies and American national security."
"After launching a war with Iran that has spiked gas and diesel prices for every American, the President is resorting to desperate ‘deals’ with a murderous dictator to attempt to clean up his own mess," the senators added in a joint statement.
Republican Sen. Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, urged the president to reverse course and use the tools outlined in a bipartisan law that Trump signed last month to choke off Russia's oil and gas revenues. The law was championed by the late Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham, one of Trump's closest allies on Capitol Hill, before his unexpected death earlier this year.
"The President should be using those authorities instead of allowing Russia to export diesel, rake in revenues, and continue its catastrophic war in Ukraine," Murkowski said. "We can discuss Russia’s return to global energy markets once the war is over, but in the meantime, we need to cut off everything fueling it."
Will the deal lower prices?
Trump has repeatedly pointed to Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil refineries as a reason that diesel prices remain near record highs. Russia has banned diesel exports since July as it has struggled to meet demand at home.
Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis for GasBuddy, said the deal "may be difficult to achieve," but predicted a short-term price dip of 10 cents to 20 cents per gallon.
"The psychological impact may reduce prices temporarily, but it’ll take more time to determine if Russia has such ability," De Haan wrote on social media.
In a statement, Putin said the deal would have a "positive impact on the entire global economy" and confirmed Russia's "readiness to supply oil and oil products to the American and global markets."
Trump claimed diesel prices "will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!"
Where do peace talks stand?
Trump's announcement Friday came as his team was meeting with Ukrainian and European officials in Miami, Florida, about strategies to end the Russia-Ukraine war.
No major breakthroughs were reported, but Trump's envoy, Steve Witkoff, described the talks as productive on social media.
Zelenskyy said on Friday that Ukraine is ready to take "symmetrical de-escalatory steps."
"Ukraine will not set Russian oil refineries on fire if Russia does not destroy our energy infrastructure. This is the kind of agreement we are proposing to America, and we believe the United States has enough power to achieve such a compromise," Zelenskyy said.

title: 84-year-old woman dead after vehicle falls from parking garage
text:
HONOLULU (HawaiiNewsNow/Gray News) - An 84-year-old woman was pronounced dead after her vehicle fell from a high-rise parking garage in downtown Honolulu Friday afternoon.

Investigation underway
Hotel Street was temporarily closed between Bishop and Bethel streets as police investigated.
Authorities have not yet determined if speed, drugs or alcohol were factors in the crash.
This is the fourth non-traffic fatality on Oahu this year, compared with zero at this time in 2025.

title: Medicaid cuts strip refugees and other legal immigrants of their health coverage
text:
New restrictions have stripped Medicaid coverage from certain legal immigrants, including refugees and victims of human trafficking, as part of broader federal changes to the health insurance program that are expected to force millions off their coverage.
The change effective Oct. 1 cut from Medicaid what is estimated to be hundreds of thousands of people who legally immigrated to the United States, many of whom work and pay taxes, in the latest Trump administration policy to target foreigners.
The move is part of sweeping changes to Medicaid under President Donald Trump’s 2025 tax cut and policy law, with many set to take effect early next year. The Medicaid changes are projected to result in 7.5 million fewer people with health insurance, according to the Congressional Budget Office’s 2025 estimate.
Advocates say that without Medicaid, people will not be able to afford private insurance and will either delay care or end up in emergency rooms, adding pressure to a strained health system. For immigrants, the cuts could be felt more acutely, compounding the effects of other administration efforts to restrict their access to public assistance as part of a broader immigration crackdown.
“This is about telling every immigrant in the United States that they are not welcome here and that they should leave,” said Ben D’Avanzo, a senior strategist at the National Immigration Law Center, which has pursued litigation against the Republican administration over its immigration agenda.
Refugees, asylum seekers, victims of human trafficking and domestic violence are among those who have lost coverage. Green-card holders were not impacted.
Lauren Bis, a White House spokesperson, said in a statement that “immigrants must be able to support themselves without taking from overburdened benefits programs paid for by hard-working American taxpayers.”
D’Avanzo said many people who have lost coverage will likely only realize when they need medical care. But for some, the change has been felt immediately.
Dwindling supplies of lifesaving medication
In Tucson, Arizona, María Chacon has been caring for her son Jesus for almost five years since a car accident at 17 left him unable to breathe on his own. He requires a ventilator, a feeding tube and daily medication, and must be turned once every two hours to stop sores from forming. Chacon said he sometimes opens his eyes.
The family is originally from Mexico and entered the U.S. on a T visa, offered to victims of human trafficking, in 2018.
Chacon said Medicaid has helped cover almost $25,000 per month of care for her son, which includes a small stipend for her and her husband as compensation for being long-term caregivers. She said doctors have explained that even if they both worked 24 hours a day, they would not be able to cover the cost of his care.
“Since that day I haven’t been able to sleep. We haven’t been able to eat or anything. We’re wondering what we’re going to do?” Chacon said.
Jesus takes medication that Chacon estimates costs $7,000 a month. The supply runs out in mid-October. Without coverage, she does not know how her son is going to survive.
Chacon found out just days before the cuts that she was losing care. She called the state’s Medicaid offices to appeal. Although she is in the process of obtaining a green card, Medicaid coverage would only kick in five years after she is approved.
Steven Camarota, research director for the Center for Immigration Studies, a right-leaning think tank that seeks less immigration, said the administration “is trying to nibble around the edges” with the Oct. 1 cuts, finding piecemeal ways to curb immigration into the U.S.
Camarota believes the government should screen legal immigrants for income potential and education, reducing the number who might rely on public benefits once they cross the border.
“You need immigrants who are unlikely to need welfare,” he said, or those with high educational attainment.
The administration recently revived a federal rule that could deny green cards to immigrants who use public benefits that could include food stamps, Medicaid, housing vouchers and others.
Chacon believes the cuts to Medicaid coverage are part of the administration’s clampdown on immigrants. She said her son is in no condition to travel.
“I know that’s what he’s doing, but, as my son is, I couldn’t go to Mexico,” Chacon said.
Millions more will be dropped from Medicaid
Medicaid, jointly funded by states and the federal government, has become a political focal point during Trump’s second term. The president has pushed to root out what he describes as fraud in the program. In July, the administration deferred over $1 billion in Medicaid payments to California and Minnesota, claiming there was suspected fraud; critics argued the move targeted Democratic-led states.
As more people are cut from Medicaid, the federal government is predicted to reduce program spending by $911 billion, according to healthcare research nonprofit KFF.
In Arizona, officials said 29,000 legal immigrants were cut from Medicaid rolls on Oct. 1. In Florida, estimates are closer to 177,000. Overall, more than 281,000 immigrants from nine states and the District of Columbia are estimated to lose Medicaid coverage, according to KFF.
As more states implement various restrictions to coverage, 7.5 million people are expected to lose coverage by 2034, according to analysis by the Congressional Budget Office.
Without coverage, people will turn to emergency rooms for care. When people delay seeing a doctor, conditions can worsen and become even more expensive to treat.
“At the end of the day, it does raise the cost for the states because once you get these people in for something that could have been prevented, they could not go to the doctor because they were uninsured; they most likely will end up at a hospital in an emergency room,” said Carmen Feliciano, the vice president of policy and advocacy at UnidosUS, a Latino civil rights organization.
UnidosUS partners with community organizations to help provide medical care, but Feliciano said they already are overwhelmed and would not be able to support the number of people who are going to lose medical coverage in the coming months.
“We are not going to have the capacity to serve all the people who need it,” Feliciano said.

title: Hearts of Pine allow another stoppage time goal in loss to AC Boise
text:
PORTLAND — It looked like the Portland Hearts of Pine were about to buck a season-long trend.
Instead, the problem that has haunted the USL League One team for most of the season did them in again.
For the 12th time this season, Portland allowed a late goal that flipped an outcome from positive to negative. This time, Thomas Ang’s goal in the 93rd minute gave Athletic Club Boise a 2-1 win at Fitzpatrick Stadium. It was the 10th goal allowed by the Hearts in the 90th minute or later in 30 USL1 matches.
“I think that’s the 20-some odd point we’ve dropped in the last 10 minutes of games,” Portland coach Bobby Murphy said. “My frustration is, they play their hearts out, they do so much good, and then we don’t respect the moments that it takes to get something from the game.”
Overall, Portland has given up 26 potential points when a tie turned to a loss, or a would-be win became a tie or loss. With the loss of one point Saturday, Portland has squandered 21 points in the final 10 minutes of matches.
Portland (7-13-10, 31 points) was officially eliminated from the playoffs on Wednesday. If half of those 26 points had gone their way, the Hearts would be a single point out of playoff contention with two matches remaining.
“We’re still trying to ask ourselves why, and why it happens to us,” said right back Mo Mohamed. “Today, it felt like we had the game for the majority of it and momentum especially toward the end, and for them to score that goal, it’s kind of like heartbreaking.”
Boise (15-8-7) moved up a spot in the standings and is now in fourth place, in line for a quarterfinal home game.
HOME STRUGGLES
Portland played before the franchise’s 38th consecutive sellout (6,318 fans) at Fitzpatrick Stadium. But the fan support has not translated into much success. Portland is 5-7-3 at home this season.
After an evenly played first half with few chances for either team, Boise opened the scoring in the 54th minute on a strike by 32-year-old Tumi Mosobane after a long throw-in to the box caromed out away from the pack.
It was the eighth time in 15 home matches that Portland has conceded the first goal. Portland is 1-6-1 in those games, 0-6 the last six times it has happened.
After Diego Gonzalez took a Diogo Barbosa pass, then turned and rifled a shot into the right-third of the goal in the 74th minute, it began to feel like Portland was going to be the team to get the late winning tally.
Aboubacar Camara had the best chance in the 84th minute when he got behind the Boise defense but popped a short-range shot over the net.
RISK, NOT REWARD
Boise’s winner was a sharp shot by Amang from about 12 yards that zipped past keeper Hunter Morse (three saves) and inside the right post.
Murphy said the issue started with a “diagonal goal kick into Diego’s head, which he’s not going to be able to do anything with.”
Then it was Boise’s Denys Kostyshyn winning a ball from Barbosa and quickly passing to the right sideline to Jonathan Ricketts, who had several steps on left back Josh Drack. With Drack chasing and Barbosa closing, Ricketts slid a pass to his left that Amang one-timed through traffic.
“At the end, we had a couple moments where were trying to get too much from situations where there was nothing to be gained, really,” Murphy said. “The game comes down to moments, and in those moments, we’ve fallen short far too often.”
Portland is at Forward Madison next Saturday and finishes its season hosting current league-leader Charlotte Independence on Oct. 24.
NOTES
National Soccer Hall of Famer Landon Donovan was in the house after a holiday weekend of Maine-oriented activities. It was not the four-time U.S. Player of the Year’s first connection to the Hearts of Pine. Donovan modeled the Hearts’ “lighthouse” jersey for a video and photo shoot at West Quoddy Lighthouse when the team announced the alternate kit.
Best chant: “Our potatoes are better.” … Mid-year signing Felipe Rodriguez Gentile, who scored his second goal in Portland’s 3-3 tie at Spokane, started at the left wing spot normally held down by injured Ollie Wright.

title: Coroner reveals cause of death for woman who went missing after leaving a Planet Fitness
text:
LEXINGTON COUNTY, S.C. (WIS/Gray News) - Authorities say a Lexington County woman who was found dead after being reported missing over the summer died of natural causes.
Lexington County Coroner Margaret Fisher shared the results of Elena Moore’s autopsy during a press conference on Friday.
Moore’s cause of death was linked to various previously diagnosed heart conditions, which included an irregular heartbeat, with the autopsy not finding any signs of traumatic injuries or physical trauma, the coroner said.
“Beautiful girl. Such a tragic story,” Fisher added.
According to Fisher, the findings came from a pathologist at the Medical University of South Carolina who specializes in cardiovascular health.
“It is the opinion of the pathologist that the decedent died as a result of complications of cardiac dysrhythmias with premature ventricular contractions. The manner of death is natural,” Fisher said.
Lexington County coroner also shared details about Moore’s history that were provided with permission from her family.
Some of those details included the irregular heartbeat as well as behavioral issues and problems with alcohol dating back to her teenage years.
The coroner said that Moore was additionally diagnosed with mental health disorders in 2025.
“This is mental illness. Her heart condition — she probably could have lived through that heart condition with her medication, but she was in a full mental health crisis,” Fisher said.
Moore was first reported missing in early June, with neighbors notably capturing her on doorbell cameras appearing confused, picking up a delivery driver’s food and looking through packages at an apartment complex.
After she was located, Moore was admitted to an unnamed inpatient mental health facility.
Fisher said Moore was diagnosed there with an “unspecified psychosis” and was said to be in a “full mental crisis.” She also said that Moore did not seem to be getting her prescribed heart medication at the facility.
Five days after being admitted, Moore was released. Her husband, Brannon Slice, was called and offered to pick her up.
Fisher, however, said the facility instead arranged a taxi for Moore.
That taxi was said to have taken Moore to a CVS Pharmacy where she used to work. Fisher claimed Moore had left her wallet but reportedly left the store with bottles of wine and water, promising to pay for the items later.
Fisher said Moore had also called police, claiming the taxi driver had been stalking her, but neither Moore nor the driver were found by responding officers.
Moore was then seen nearby, in places such as a Planet Fitness and a nearby parking lot. She was eventually seen crossing North Lake Drive, near the area where her body was found.
Moore also allegedly took clothes that didn’t belong to her from the Planet Fitness, along with an AirPod.
Fisher said Moore’s toxicology showed a .089 blood-alcohol level, but noted that excessive heat during the time could have also played a role in that finding, along with the wine she took from CVS.
The coroner said Slice was never criminally implicated in the investigation.
“So I would hope that now some of these people that were doing justice for Elena, I hope they will continue to do justice for Elena and only focus on the fact that mental illness needs to be addressed now. Mental illness. Let’s have some justice for those folks who are suffering with mental illness,” Fisher said.
The South Carolina Law Enforcement Division closed its missing persons case into Moore, but it’s unclear if the agency closed its investigation specifically into Moore’s death.

title: Tornadoes spotted across multiple counties as severe weather from Isaias remains
text:
AUGUSTA, Ga. (WRDW/WAGT/Gray News) - Tornadoes are blamed for damage in at least three Central Savannah River Area counties Saturday, sparking warnings across the CSRA as severe weather spun off from Hurricane Isaias.
A tornado warning was in effect until 7:30 p.m. for Aiken and Saluda counties.
As of 7:02 p.m., a severe thunderstorm capable of producing a tornado was located near Ridge Spring, or near Batesburg-Leesville, moving north at 25 mph.
It was the second radar-indicated tornado warning for the same area in a couple of hours. One expired at 6:30, but a new one was issued at 7:02 p.m. and not set to expire until 7:30.
The earlier warning came after the New Holland area saw a confirmed tornado on the ground.
Also getting a second tornado warning of the day was Screven County, where a warning was in effect until 6:30. That warning was allowed to expire.
This all came after confirmed damage in Allendale, Screven and Burke counties.
News 12 drone video showed damage to at least four buildings on Story Mill Road in Burke County about halfway between Hephzibah and Waynesboro. Two were missing parts of their roof, and one entire side was taken out of a third. A fourth was flattened. Drone video also showed trucks and trailers overturned.
Officials said there were no injuries in Burke County.
Power lines were down along Highway 80 West.
At 4:18 p.m., a confirmed tornado was 5 miles south of Appleton, moving north at 30 mph, according to the National Weather Service. That’s between the Burtons Ferry Bridge and downtown Allendale.
The storm also spawned an earlier tornado in Screven County. Then the storm moved across the river to Allendale County. Barnwell County was then added to the warning.
After that came the Aiken County warning.
There was confirmed damage in Screven County, with trees down in a 200-yard path near Old Savannah Highway and Highway 21.
A tornado warning expired earlier in Burke County.
That warning was based on radar activity just north of Waynesboro along Highway 25. The warning expired at 4 p.m.

title: Christa Pike released from hospital, recovering in prison, attorneys say
text:
NASHVILLE (WVLT/Gray News) - Christa Pike has been discharged from a hospital and returned to the Tennessee prison where she has been housed for more than 30 years, her attorneys said.
Pike is receiving continued medical care at the Deborah K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center, according to a statement from her attorneys with Federal Defender Services of Eastern Tennessee and the Tennessee Office of the Post-Conviction Defender.
Deborah K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center is the primary state correctional facility and intake/classification center for female offenders in Tennessee.
Pike, 50, survived two doses of pentobarbital as the state sought to give her a lethal injection eight days ago for the 1995 beating and stabbing death of classmate Colleen Slemmer. The drug didn’t kill her, and her arms were left burned and blistered, according to her lawyers. For the first few days of her hospitalization, Pike was unconscious and on a ventilator.
Her first steps on Wednesday were “limited,” and she required some assistance as she walked on Thursday, her lawyers said in a statement. She is also regaining mobility in her arms, and she was able to eat for the first time.
Gov. Bill Lee has ordered an independent review of the Department of Correction’s actions and paused the remaining scheduled execution this year while the review is underway.
TDOC Commissioner Frank Strada has offered his resignation and is expected to step down this month. An interim commissioner has not yet been announced.

title: Don’t waste one vote this November
text:
The Aug. 23 letter declaring the writer’s intent to cast a write-in vote for Graham Platner in November was alarming. The writer is apparently unaware that a write-in candidate must file a declaration of write-in candidacy in Maine 70 days prior to the election, or the vote won’t count.
This election is paramount. We must unseat Sen. Susan Collins as a step toward healing the damage done by this presidential administration and, to do so, we must unite behind Troy Jackson. A vote for an undeclared write-in candidate — or any other candidate besides Jackson — is a wasted vote.
I was also a Platner fan, but we cannot afford to risk the continuing soaring cost of foreign war, gasoline, groceries and healthcare, or continue suffering the unending assaults on our lands, air and freedoms by casting philosophical votes. The preservation of democracy is a task we must not fail to achieve this November.
Robin Johnson
Waterville

title: Eastern Maine Walk to End Alzheimer’s draws hundreds in Bangor
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Hundreds of people walked Saturday in the fight for a cure for Alzheimer’s disease, a condition impacting more than 29,000 Mainers.
Another 66,000 Mainers are caring for them, many as unpaid caregivers, according to the Alzheimer’s Association.
Walkers carried pinwheel flowers of various colors, each representing their personal connection to the disease.
The Eastern Maine Walk to End Alzheimer’s is one of seven held across Maine.
Howard Goodrow, executive director of the Alzheimer’s Association’s Maine and Vermont chapters, said the walks are personal. Goodrow lost his mother to Alzheimer’s.
“The impact that the research has is great, but events like this are the things that bring attention to the disease,” Goodrow said. “It gets people who have the disease and caregivers more comfortable talking about it. Once we talk about it, it becomes more of a reality and becomes something we look at and say, this is something we can solve.”
Funds raised at Saturday’s event will support care and research efforts of the Alzheimer’s Association.
Donations can be made at alz.org.
The final walk in Maine will be held in Portland Saturday, October 17th at Payson Park.

text:

title: Bruins rout Flyers for 2nd straight win
text:
BOSTON — Fraser Minten had a goal and two assists, Pavel Zacha scored his first goal of the season and the Boston Bruins beat the struggling Philadelphia Flyers 5-1 on Saturday.
Mason Lohrei, Marat Khusnutdinov and Casey Mittelstadt also scored for Boston (4-2), which won its second straight game.
Starting for the fifth time in the Bruins’ first six games, Jeremy Swayman faced just three shots in the opening 30 minutes and finished with 14 saves. His bid for his second shutout of the season was spoiled when Porter Martone got a power-play goal 6:32 into the final period. Swayman earned his 136th win, tying Andy Moog for eighth on Boston’s all-time list.
Dan Vladar made 27 saves for the Flyers (0-4-2), who are the Eastern Conference’s only winless team.
Top Boston defenseman Charlie McAvoy served the final game of his six-game suspension to start the season from a slashing incident during last spring’s playoffs.
Coming off a lopsided win over Utah at home on Thursday, the Bruins jumped ahead on Zacha’s goal 12:21 into the opening period when he took a backhand pass from David Pastrnak in the slot and fired a wrister that broke into the net off Vladar’s right pad.
Following a tough loss at Ottawa on Thursday, the Flyers were outshot 19-3 in the opening 30 minutes and 22-8 through two periods.
Lohrei beat Vladar over his shoulder with a wrister with 2:48 left in the second, making it 2-0.
Khusnutdinov scored off a nice feed from Minton just under two minutes into the third.
Flyers winger Michael Bunting played his second game after signing as a free agent this week.
Up next
Flyers: Host the Carolina Hurricanes on Sunday night.
Bruins: Visit the San Jose Sharks on Tuesday night, the first of a four-game road trip.

title: Who is Katie Zacharia? What to know about the next White House press secretary
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump announced Friday that Katie Zacharia, a communications adviser for his media company, will succeed Karoline Leavitt as White House press secretary.
Trump revealed his selection of Zacharia on his Truth Social platform, where he often makes political and official announcements. Zacharia is a conservative commentator for Trump Media & Technology Group, which operates the social media site.
In naming Zacharia, Trump described her as “a loyal and brilliant supporter, right from the beginning.”
In a social media post, Zacharia thanked Trump and called it the “honor of a lifetime.” She added that Trump’s leadership is “a blessing to this country.”
“The work ahead is to continue delivering strong results for our Country and communicating to the American people the major wins that this Administration is making every single day,” she wrote on X.
Zacharia briefly worked as a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security earlier this year and has been a commentator for Fox News and Newsmax. Trump said Zacharia had been involved in his presidential campaigns, notably in swing states.
A request for comment left with Zacharia was not immediately answered. A LinkedIn profile noted that she earned a law degree from Pepperdine University.
Leavitt announced her departure Aug. 12 and left the position Aug. 27.
She will serve as an on-air contributor on Fox News Channel beginning Nov. 1, the network said Monday.
Leavitt became press secretary in January 2025, and left the position, she said, to spend more time with her young children. Prior to serving in the White House, Leavitt was national press secretary for Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign.

title: Spaghetti models, rapid intensification, storm surge. Confused? Here’s what hurricane terms mean
text:
It’s a confusing time when a hurricane threatens, and some terms used by officials aren’t known by everyone, so here’s a storm glossary.
Tropical cyclones
Let’s start with the broad category of these storms, called tropical cyclones. In the northern hemisphere, a tropical cyclone is a rapidly counterclockwise-rotating storm that forms in Earth’s warmer areas and is organized with a center that winds flow out of. Tropical cyclones rotate clockwise in the southern hemisphere.
Hurricanes and typhoons
The strongest tropical cyclones in the Atlantic and eastern and central Pacific oceans are called hurricanes. In the northwest Pacific they are called typhoons and in the south Pacific and Indian oceans they are called cyclones or tropical cyclones.
Tropical depressions, tropical storms
In the Atlantic, the weakest of these systems are called tropical depressions. They have winds of less than 39 mph (63 kph).
When a tropical depression reaches 39 mph (63 kph) but is weaker than 74 mph (119 kph), they are called a tropical storm and receive a name from a pre-established list.
Category 1 and 2 hurricanes
When a tropical storm hits 74 mph (120 kph), it achieves hurricane status. There are five categories of hurricanes based on maximum sustained wind speed in a rating system called the Saffir-Simpson Scale.
The weakest is a Category 1, with winds of 74-95 mph (120-150 kph), and it will have dangerous winds that produce some damage. Tree branches will snap and some will be uprooted. Extensive power damage is likely.
A Category 2 has winds of 96-110 mph (155-175 kph) and can be disastrous, with near-total power loss expected near the center.
Major hurricanes: Category 3, 4 and 5
When hurricanes sustain winds exceeding 111 mph (180 kph), they get major hurricane status, with devastating consequences. Even well-built homes may be severely damaged by a Category 3 hurricane with winds of 111-129 mph (180-210 kph).
A Category 4 hurricane is considered catastrophic, with winds of 130-156 mph (210-250 kph) that leave entire areas uninhabitable for weeks or months.
The scale tops out at Category 5, when a hurricane’s winds exceed 157 mph (250 kph). A high percentage of the homes in the disaster region will be destroyed. Power outages could last for months.
Storm surge and tide
Storm surge is the deadly rise of water generated by a storm that’s above and beyond the normal tide. It starts in the ocean but could include rivers and canals. Storm surges once caused nearly half of a hurricane’s deaths, but surge-related fatalities have come down with warnings and education to about 11% of all direct deaths. Surges can reach as much as 20 feet or more and that does not include waves, which are on top of storm surge.
Storm tide is storm surge plus tides.
Eye and eyewall of hurricane
A hurricane’s center is called the eye. It is calm inside the eye, but it is crucial to the storm’s formation and continuation. It is circular and is usually 20 to 40 miles (30 to 60 km) in diameter, but can be bigger. The smaller the eye is, the stronger the storm. After a while, a storm can form a new second eyewall around the first in a process called eyewall replacement that temporarily weakens the storm’s intensity but enables it to grow larger overall.
The outside of the eye is the eyewall and it is the storm’s most dangerous area with the strongest winds. When an area on the ground is hit by the eyewall, it will be buffeted by intense winds, then get a break before being slammed by the other side of the eye in a second round of the storm’s strongest winds.
Landfall
When the eye of a hurricane or tropical storm goes over land, that point is called landfall. But high winds, rain and storm surge can cause all sorts of damage many hours before landfall, and last many hours thereafter. Landfall is not necessarily where the strongest winds are, and the wider swirl of a storm can spread destruction across large areas.
Dirty side of a hurricane
The right front quadrant of a hurricane or northeast part of the eyewall tends to cause the most damage as the strongest winds blow counterclockwise around the center, so this at times is called a storm’s dirty side. In the southern hemisphere, it’s the left front quadrant that is the dirty side.
Forecast and spaghetti models
There are dozens of computer-generated models that forecast changes in each storm’s track and intensity. They vary because each one uses different assumptions about how storms operate and some prove better during certain storms and worse during others. Forecasters advise to avoid concentrating on one individual model. When many or all of the models are put on one map, they generally show an overall sense of what will happen. Sometimes they show a lot of lines going in different directions, which can look like cooked spaghetti.
Hurricane cone
The National Hurricane Center’s official forecast is not one specific line, but rather a cone of uncertainty that expands with time, up to five days out. That cone shows the most probable area where the eye of the storm could move over time, but it doesn’t mean the storm will be in the center of that cone. It is designed so that 67% of the most likely tracks fall within the cone.
Watches and warnings
A hurricane or tropical storm watch means conditions are possible within an area during the time specified by the National Weather Service. A hurricane or tropical storm warning means those conditions are no longer just possible, but expected. One way to think about it: A watch is having the ingredients to bake a cake, while a warning comes when the cake is pretty much done.
Wind shear
Wind shear is a change in wind speed or direction, or both, and it can weaken a storm. Crosswinds at high levels, such as 40,000 feet (12,200 meters) above sea level, can often decapitate a storm. Wind shear also can describe when winds up at the top of the storm blow in different directions than at bottom or middle.
Rapid intensification
When a storm, usually fed by unusually warm water, suddenly gathers a lot of strength, sustaining winds that increase in speed by at least 35 mph (56 kph) in 24 hours, it is called rapid intensification. This is a dangerous situation if it happens close to land.

title: UMaine men’s hockey earns split with Quinnipiac

Lee Parks scored the go-ahead goal in the second period and UMaine handed sixth-ranked Quinnipiac its first loss of the season Saturday night, beating the Bobcats 5-3 in a nonconference men’s hockey game in Orono.

title: Coyotes are often misunderstood, and confused for other animals
text:
One of our regular readers, Joan from Portland, wrote to us with a handful of questions about coyotes, which always strike me as one of Maine’s most misunderstood mammals. That title might actually go to the fisher (often, and inappropriately, called the fisher cat) because everyone wants to ascribe nocturnal noises to them, when 99% of the time it is actually a fox. That said, the coyote and its many noises deserve some attention.
Coyotes have an interesting history in Maine, because they weren’t always here. I grew up in Hollis, a wonderfully small rural town where coyotes were often heard (and seldom seen). But they aren’t just in rural areas; coyotes can be found across the entire state, often thriving in suburban and surprisingly urban areas too.
If we go back to the 1920s, these wild dogs (canids) had never been seen in the state. The first recorded sightings are from the ’30s. They expanded their range northeast, coming into the state to fill a void left by the extirpation of wolves. That niche was opened after humans killed off the eastern wolves that once lived in Maine, eradicating them in the 19th century.
As the coyotes moved into these newly accessible areas, they encountered some wolves en route and began hybridizing, which gave us the variety of coyote hybrids, often called “coywolves,” that are seen in Maine today. To be a bit more specific, they are officially called eastern coyotes, one of the nineteen subspecies of coyotes across Northern and Central America.
It is worth reflecting on these mixed genes a bit further. The eastern coyote is a majority coyote with other canines mixed in. A study published in 2014, led by Javier Monzón of Stony Brook University, looked at eastern coyote genomes and found that genetic parentage broke down as: 65% western coyote, 17% western wolf and 18% eastern wolf. Furthermore, there were some eastern coyotes with four canid parentage, thanks to dogs contributing. Those broke down to: 61% western coyote, 14% western wolf, 14% eastern wolf and 11% domestic dog.
I emphasize this point because we see a lot of reports of wolves in Maine. While it is possible that eastern wolves could wander into Maine, there are no established populations of them here, but plenty of wolfish-looking coyotes.
Despite their wide distribution, coyotes are rarely encountered in Maine. You are more likely to find signs left behind, like footprints or scat. Their droppings are most likely to be confused for that of a large dog, but a dog’s diet is consistent, and so is their poop. A coyote will typically have scat showing their omnivorous diet, with many indigestible contents like hair (from the small mammal prey) and seeds (from fruit).
The next best way to detect their presence is through their loud vocalizations. Howling is perhaps the most iconic of their noises, typically given in long-distance and territorial communications. I also hear my local coyotes doing a lot of dog-like yipping, sometimes mixed with howls. This mixing can be done by just a couple of individuals, vocalized in a way to sound like a large group, which is known as a “Beau Geste” effect. They are so vocal, which is how they got their specific epithet: latrans, which is Latin for “barking”, so Canus latrans is the “barking dog.”
The last thing we need to address, given all the coyotes around us, is that they are generally harmless, unless you are a small rodent. In general, coyotes are much more afraid of humans than humans need to be of them. That said, keeping them wild is important, so do not leave food out for them. And while a cat is larger than most coyote prey, you should keep your cats safe and indoors all the time anyway as cats are also the No. 1 anthropogenic cause of mortality in birds.
Have you got a nature or wildlife question of your own? It doesn’t have to be about birds! title: Bowdoin football falls on last-minute touchdown
text:
Tufts quarterback Nate Johnson ran 17 yards for the winning touchdown with 10 seconds remaining as the Jumbos rallied for a 20-13 win over Bowdoin in a New England Small College Athletic Conference football game Saturday in Brunswick.
Bowdoin (0-4) took a 13-10 lead on a 41-yard field goal by Caden Perry with 10:47 left. Tufts (3-1) then missed a 44-yard field goal, but the Jumbos blocked a Bowdoin punt and the ball went out of the back of the end zone for a safety that made it 13-12 with 3:36 to play.
Tufts took over at its own 43 following the free kick, and Johnson capped a 57-yard drive with a run around left end.
Soren Hummel’s 3-yard touchdown pass to Peter Macaulay gave Bowdoin a 7-3 lead late in the first quarter. Perry kicked a 36-yard field goal in the second quarter, but Tufts tied it in the third quarter on a 2-yard TD run by Caden McCallum.
Hummel was 19 of 27 for 125 yards. Bowdoin was outgained 402-193.
WESLEYAN 21, COLBY 7: The Mules (0-4) fell behind by 14 points in the first half and couldn’t recover in a NESCAC loss to the Cardinals (4-0) in Middletown, Connecticut.
The Mules pulled within seven when Jagger Matera threw a 4-yard touchdown pass to Sean Trinder with 5:19 remaining, but Wesleyan answered less than two minutes later on a 69-yard pass from Matt Fitzsimons to Blake Newcomb.
Fitzsimons scored on 1-yard runs in the first and second quarter. He completed 22 of 28 passes, with a touchdown and three interceptions.
Colby managed just 155 yards and nine first downs.
WILLIAMS 34, BATES 0: The Ephs (3-1) held the Bobcats (0-4) to 84 yards and seven first downs and cruised to a NESCAC win in Williamstown, Massachusetts.
Drew Weiler, Brady Stahelski and Aiden Clark each had a rushing touchdown in the second quarter as Williams took a 21-0 lead. Leonardo Maiuolo kicked a 34-yard field goal in the third quarter and a 21-yarder in the fourth. Quinn Rucker added a 4-yard scoring run.
NORWICH 28, MAINE MARITIME ACADEMY 7: Jahmir Dixon caught 11 passes for 228 yards and a touchdown to lead the Cadets (2-3) past the Mariners (0-5) in Castine.
MMA quarterback Harris Stone completed 21 of 37 passes for 214 yards, with one touchdown and one interception.
Will Patenaude scored on touchdown runs of 6, 8 and 57 yards for Norwich.

title: Mayor Dion is moving in the right direction on addiction crisis
text:
When it comes to Portland’s policies on addiction problems on our streets, forget for a moment the cost burden on property taxpayers (as some past and present city councilors have apparently done).
Consider current policies that haven’t worked, as evidenced by increasing homeless populations and intoxicated public displays, resulting in challenges for others to compensate for Portland City Council’s complacency: city staff picking up contaminated needles and sanitation residue in public places; hospital emergency staff exposed to violent offenders; business and property owners cleaning up areas around their stores and buildings — while apologizing to customers for the person outside screaming obscenities.
These were not the accepted conditions on Portland’s streets years ago, when the city
council diligently worked with businesses and citizens to revitalize our desolate downtown,
which was in economic collapse. They were not our traditional mores (accepted customs,
attitudes, observances) exemplified to visitors and our children.
The sights and sounds that today’s unfortunate schoolchildren are exposed to should be intolerable to all councilors. Some councilors seem incapable of understanding the negative life consequences to children and incapable of accepting the need for policy changes to help improve these conditions.
Let’s ask those running for Portland City Council this November if they will support Mayor Dion’s rational and humanistic approach to benefit residents, visitors and the addicted by
instituting constructive changes to the city’s addiction policies (“Portland mayor calls for drug treatment sentencing option to curb downtown crime,” Sept. 10).
Robert Kahn
Portland

title: Despite Hurricane Isaias, couple celebrates wedding weekend on Florida’s coast
text:
PENSACOLA BEACH, Fla. (AP) - Even the approaching hurricane couldn’t dampen the celebratory atmosphere at a wedding in Pensacola Beach, Florida.
On Thursday evening, David and McKenzie Pipes welcomed guests to their wedding weekend at a beachfront condo. Caterers, bartenders and guests arrived ahead of the storm to celebrate the couple based in Perdido Key, Florida.
Couple celebrates a year after wedding
Though the two wed a year ago, this weekend was their celebration with friends and family.
As a bright orange sunset took over the sky, the Pipeses headed down to the beach to take pictures as their dog Hank ran around in the sand.
Ceremony rescheduled around storm
The couple did have to make some changes: They moved their wedding ceremony and reception to Sunday after Hurricane Isaias is expected to pass, and some out-of-town guests canceled.
Still, family arrived from Maryland and Arizona to celebrate the happy couple, and nothing in the excitement hinted at the storm ahead.

title: UMaine men’s hockey earns split with Quinnipiac
text:
Lee Parks scored the go-ahead goal in the second period and UMaine handed sixth-ranked Quinnipiac its first loss of the season Saturday night, beating the Bobcats 5-3 in a nonconference men’s hockey game in Orono.
The Black Bears (2-2) fell behind 3-2 on a goal by Mason Marcellus just 1:04 into the second period, but Isa Parekh tied it just over two minutes later. Parks then put Maine ahead at 6:07 after Max Scott stole the puck in the Quinnipiac zone and passed to Will Gerrior, who found Parks all alone in front.
Loic Usereau and Samuel Alfano scored for Maine in the first period, and Sully Scholle clinched the win with an empty-netter with 1:49 remaining.
Maine goalie Albin Boija finished with 20 saves.
Quinnipiac, which beat the Black Bears 2-1 on Friday night, dropped to 3-1.

title: 17-year-old is living in hospitals with nowhere else to go, lawyer says
text:
WATERTOWN, New York (WWNY/Gray News) - A 17-year-old has been living in North Country hospitals since August because the system allegedly has nowhere else for her to go.
“This is a hard situation to be in for everybody,” Rebecca Simser, the teen’s lawyer, said.
Living without a plan
A stay-away order was issued in June because of the teen’s reported behavior problems that barred her from returning to her caregiver’s home.
Since then, Simser said the 17-year-old has moved through four homes and four North Country facilities.
“I have a family offense petition involving a minor alleged perpetrator, and so we are trying to protect the victim, which is our job, but we also need to be doing what’s in the best interest of the child,” Simser said.
According to Simser, her client has been living in hospitals since the end of August, with nowhere to go and no safety plans.
“She’s not in school at this point. I don’t know if she’s getting medication. She’s definitely not getting one-on-one mental health treatment because she’s discharged and just sitting in an ER bed,” Simser said.
No qualifying treatment options
Simser said her client doesn’t qualify for voluntary or involuntary inpatient treatment.
With no other options, Simser wants the court to declare her client “destitute” — legally homeless, with no income or support.
That status would mean the Department of Social Services would take custody of the teen.
Jefferson County’s Department of Social Services would have to file a petition, but Simser said she’s been told the agency won’t.
“I’m not saying that my client is blameless in all of this, but she’s not being afforded any protections that I can tell at this point,” Simser said.
A statewide issue
State numbers show this is a growing issue statewide.
Last year, over the course of three months, 52 children in New York experienced delayed discharge from the hospital or emergency room due to lack of available care or housing options, resulting in more than 5,100 days of medically unnecessary inpatient hospitalization.
“My hope is that if the system worked the way it was supposed to work, we could protect the victim, but we could also get services and help for my client and make sure that she wasn’t suffering and displaced, and lacking while she transitioned into a more independent form of living away from the victim,” Simser said.
Simser noted that she doesn’t fault any of the facilities.
The Department of Social Services was unable to comment on this specific case.
