title: Trump says Ukraine should get a new president as he blames Zelenskyy for US diesel prices
text:
Trump says Ukraine should get a new president as he blames Zelenskyy for US diesel prices
Meanwhile, Russian strikes killed at least 20 people in Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia region on Saturday
Trump says Ukraine should get a new president as he blames Zelenskyy for US diesel prices
Meanwhile, Russian strikes killed at least 20 people in Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia region on Saturday
President Donald Trump said Saturday it was time for Ukraine to get a new president, suggesting Volodymyr Zelenskyy has not done enough to end his country's war with Russia and blaming him for high diesel prices in the U.S.
"I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal because he could have made many deals and for some reason he never does," Trump said.
Related video above — 'Total betrayal of Ukraine': Lawmakers react to Trump's diesel deal with Russia
The president, who on Friday struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to buy diesel from Russia in an attempt to address high fuel prices ahead of the U.S. midterm elections, has been urging Zelenskyy for weeks to stop strikes on Russian energy infrastructure. He has also sought to blame record U.S. diesel prices on Ukraine rather than the U.S.-led war in Iran, which has elevated world energy prices.
"He wants to make problems for the world. He wants to make problems for our farmers, our ranchers, with diesel fuel," Trump said, before departing for Tennessee, where he was set to rally Republican voters.
An Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research poll conducted last month and published Oct. 1 found that Americans disapprove of Trump's handling of Iran, and blame him for higher prices.
Trump also suggested that if he had been U.S. president in 2022, "that war would have never started. There was no reason that that war with Ukraine and Russia started. It started due to incompetence."
Zelenskyy has "lost 30% of your country, and you've had over a million people go between the two of them, over 2 million people killed. That's a war that should have never started. And I think it's time for Ukraine to get a new president," Trump said.
Independent estimates are that about 20% of Ukraine's territory is under Russian control. British defense officials recently estimated that about half a million Russian soldiers have been killed in the war; there are no reliable recent estimates about how many Ukrainians have died.
20 people killed in Russian bombing in Ukraine Saturday
Trump's extraordinary intervention came after Russian strikes killed at least 20 people in Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia region, Ukrainian officials said Saturday.
Three children were among those killed when Russian aerial bombs hit residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine's State Emergency Service said Saturday. At least 18 people were wounded.
Russia and Ukraine are locked in a long-range aerial war while their armies remain largely deadlocked on the front line, more than 4 1/2 years since Moscow's full-scale invasion. Ukraine is struggling to counter escalating Russian bombardments that have killed more than 60 people over the past four days.
Anger in Kyiv over diesel deal
"Today, Russia expressed its thanks for the lifting of sanctions on diesel exports by dropping five glide bombs on residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy wrote Saturday on X.
He said the attacks show Moscow understands "any easing of pressure to mean they can keep fighting, to mean they can keep dropping bombs on cities."
"Russia's choice is war," Zelenskyy said in a later Telegram post, after drone attacks on energy facilities and a ballistic missile attack on Kyiv. He said every additional billion dollars Russia earns from exports would help pay for weapons components, drone upgrades, missile production and the recruitment of mercenaries, and that Moscow would only be ready to stop when its ability to fight diminished.
Moscow received from diesel deal "signals that it is apparently permissible to continue attacking. And this needs to be corrected," he said, urging the U.S., Europe and other partners to limit Russia's capacity to wage war.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine was coordinating steps to counter the extra revenue Russia will receive, and that he had spoken to French President Emmanuel Macron about shoring up air defenses, warning of an increased risk of further missile strikes in the coming days.
He also said he had discussed the developments with Finnish President Alexander Stubb, and that Ukraine would receive ammunition in the coming days for the F-16s it uses to intercept Shahed drones.
Trump had been set to discuss a suspected case of plague in Russia with President Vladimir Putin in a phone call.
Instead, the American leader announced Friday that Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons "immediately thereafter." Russia will deliver an additional 3 million tons "within a short period of time" after that, he wrote.
In Kyiv, people gathered at a memorial to fallen soldiers on Independence Square greeted the deal with a mix of anger and resignation.
"Trump has once again shown his true face," said Oleksandr Petrenko, 26. "He didn't care about the situation, the shelling or the destruction of our homes. All he's interested in is oil or the fuel prices and how much Americans have to pay."
"Knowing Trump, he tries to manipulate the markets. He's got an election coming up soon," Petrenko said. "So he needs to emphasize to his voters that gasoline will be cheap. But it won't be effective."
For Oksana Yakunina, a financial adviser from the central city of Kropyvnytskyi, the announcement "didn't really come as a surprise."
"Trump has been working with Putin for a long time," she told The Associated Press.
European allies question US-Russia deal
Ukraine's European allies expressed dismay at the deal and said they stood by their commitment to sanctions.
Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson said Stockholm regretted the agreement, "as energy revenues are central to the Russian war chest," and noted that the European Union would adopt its most comprehensive sanctions package yet on Monday, with 1,600 listings targeting Russia's military-industrial complex.
The German government "remains committed to the sanctions imposed on Russia and is working with its European partners on further sanctions," spokesperson Stefan Kornelius said, adding that support for Ukraine "remains unwavering."
Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski questioned whether Russia could deliver at all. Citing his embassy's reports of fuel shortages even in Moscow, and "serious sources" saying Ukraine has damaged about half of Russia's refining capacity, he asked on X: "So where will the surpluses for export come from?"
Trump's announcement was in stark contrast to a sweeping Russia sanctions law he signed last month that aimed at clamping down on the oil and gas revenues that fuel Russia's war against Ukraine.
Trump announced the deal as his envoy Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner met with Ukrainian officials in Miami on Friday to discuss a proposal to end the war.
"I believe our team is simply being used as a smoke screen. And that is certainly not fair. It is certainly not how partners should treat each other," Zelenskyy said Friday.
Speaking about Friday's announcement, a senior Ukrainian official told AP that the Ukrainian side was not aware of the deal before the announcement.
The official, who spoke on condition of anonymity as he was not authorized to discuss the issue publicly, said Saturday the diesel deal announcement was not tied to anything under discussion between the U.S. and Ukrainian negotiating teams meeting in Florida.
He confirmed the Ukrainian delegation had left Florida and was on its way back to Ukraine.
Daly reported from Washington and Morton reported from London. Associated Press journalists Bela Szandelszky in Kyiv, Ukraine, and Collin Binkley in Washington contributed to this report.

title: Thankful Maine is without the death penalty
text:
This is in reference to the news report on the botched execution in Tennessee. I fervently hope that anyone who is on the fence about whether to oppose or support this evil, unnecessary practice of the death penalty will now see it for what it is and oppose it.
The reasons go on and on: that it is arbitrary and targets far more Black folks and other minorities; that it is actually more expensive to execute than to sentence to life without parole; that the United States is the only country in the Western world that uses it.
I grew up and lived in Iowa for many years, a state without the death penalty. I met folks from Nebraska, which has the death penalty. They continue to work to defeat it.
Through these folks, I met and became friends with a death row inmate. The state killed him. The night before, he called to say goodbye.
It was horrifying to know this was the last time I would speak with him. This was a man who had been redeemed by good folks. There was no reason to kill him, except for vengeance.
I am so grateful that Maine does not have the death penalty. I would not live here if it did.
Barbara Doughty
Portland

title: Coroner reveals cause of death for woman who went missing after leaving a Planet Fitness
text:
LEXINGTON COUNTY, S.C. (WIS/Gray News) - Authorities say a Lexington County woman who was found dead after being reported missing over the summer died of natural causes.
Lexington County Coroner Margaret Fisher shared the results of Elena Moore’s autopsy during a press conference on Friday.
Moore’s cause of death was linked to various previously diagnosed heart conditions, which included an irregular heartbeat, with the autopsy not finding any signs of traumatic injuries or physical trauma, the coroner said.
“Beautiful girl. Such a tragic story,” Fisher added.
According to Fisher, the findings came from a pathologist at the Medical University of South Carolina who specializes in cardiovascular health.
“It is the opinion of the pathologist that the decedent died as a result of complications of cardiac dysrhythmias with premature ventricular contractions. The manner of death is natural,” Fisher said.
Lexington County coroner also shared details about Moore’s history that were provided with permission from her family.
Some of those details included the irregular heartbeat as well as behavioral issues and problems with alcohol dating back to her teenage years.
The coroner said that Moore was additionally diagnosed with mental health disorders in 2025.
“This is mental illness. Her heart condition — she probably could have lived through that heart condition with her medication, but she was in a full mental health crisis,” Fisher said.
Moore was first reported missing in early June, with neighbors notably capturing her on doorbell cameras appearing confused, picking up a delivery driver’s food and looking through packages at an apartment complex.
After she was located, Moore was admitted to an unnamed inpatient mental health facility.
Fisher said Moore was diagnosed there with an “unspecified psychosis” and was said to be in a “full mental crisis.” She also said that Moore did not seem to be getting her prescribed heart medication at the facility.
Five days after being admitted, Moore was released. Her husband, Brannon Slice, was called and offered to pick her up.
Fisher, however, said the facility instead arranged a taxi for Moore.
That taxi was said to have taken Moore to a CVS Pharmacy where she used to work. Fisher claimed Moore had left her wallet but reportedly left the store with bottles of wine and water, promising to pay for the items later.
Fisher said Moore had also called police, claiming the taxi driver had been stalking her, but neither Moore nor the driver were found by responding officers.
Moore was then seen nearby, in places such as a Planet Fitness and a nearby parking lot. She was eventually seen crossing North Lake Drive, near the area where her body was found.
Moore also allegedly took clothes that didn’t belong to her from the Planet Fitness, along with an AirPod.
Fisher said Moore’s toxicology showed a .089 blood-alcohol level, but noted that excessive heat during the time could have also played a role in that finding, along with the wine she took from CVS.
The coroner said Slice was never criminally implicated in the investigation.
“So I would hope that now some of these people that were doing justice for Elena, I hope they will continue to do justice for Elena and only focus on the fact that mental illness needs to be addressed now. Mental illness. Let’s have some justice for those folks who are suffering with mental illness,” Fisher said.
The South Carolina Law Enforcement Division closed its missing persons case into Moore, but it’s unclear if the agency closed its investigation specifically into Moore’s death.

title: Bruins rout Flyers for 2nd straight win
text:
BOSTON — Fraser Minten had a goal and two assists, Pavel Zacha scored his first goal of the season and the Boston Bruins beat the struggling Philadelphia Flyers 5-1 on Saturday.
Mason Lohrei, Marat Khusnutdinov and Casey Mittelstadt also scored for Boston (4-2), which won its second straight game.
Starting for the fifth time in the Bruins’ first six games, Jeremy Swayman faced just three shots in the opening 30 minutes and finished with 14 saves. His bid for his second shutout of the season was spoiled when Porter Martone got a power-play goal 6:32 into the final period. Swayman earned his 136th win, tying Andy Moog for eighth on Boston’s all-time list.
Dan Vladar made 27 saves for the Flyers (0-4-2), who are the Eastern Conference’s only winless team.
Top Boston defenseman Charlie McAvoy served the final game of his six-game suspension to start the season from a slashing incident during last spring’s playoffs.
Coming off a lopsided win over Utah at home on Thursday, the Bruins jumped ahead on Zacha’s goal 12:21 into the opening period when he took a backhand pass from David Pastrnak in the slot and fired a wrister that broke into the net off Vladar’s right pad.
Following a tough loss at Ottawa on Thursday, the Flyers were outshot 19-3 in the opening 30 minutes and 22-8 through two periods.
Lohrei beat Vladar over his shoulder with a wrister with 2:48 left in the second, making it 2-0.
Khusnutdinov scored off a nice feed from Minton just under two minutes into the third.
Flyers winger Michael Bunting played his second game after signing as a free agent this week.
Up next
Flyers: Host the Carolina Hurricanes on Sunday night.
Bruins: Visit the San Jose Sharks on Tuesday night, the first of a four-game road trip.

title: Mike Ditka tributes pour in from President Trump, former President Obama, Chicago and the NFL
text:
(AP) - Mike Ditka was “Iron Mike” as a player who revolutionized the tight end position and later became the easily recognizable and often imitated fiery, mustached and sweater vest-wearing “Da Coach” of the Chicago Bears during a Super Bowl-winning tenure.
Ditka died Friday at 86, his family announced in a statement.
The Pro Football Hall of Famer was remembered by the sports world and beyond for his impact on the game as both a player and a coach, and later as a TV analyst.
Here are some notable reactions to Ditka’s death and tributes to his legacy:
Chicago Bears
“We are deeply saddened by the passing of legendary and treasured Chicago Bear and Pro Football Hall of Famer Mike Ditka. Mike’s impact on the Chicago Bears organization, over decades as a player, coach, and proud icon and ambassador for our organization, is immeasurable. His integral role in bringing world championships to our city and our franchise, both as a player and as our coach, established prominence and excellence at a world-class level, but also created a lifetime of cherished memories in the hearts and minds of Bears fans that will last for generations.
“We extend our love, prayers, and heartfelt condolences to the Ditka family, and join all Bears fans in deep sadness and reverence as we remember and honor Mike Ditka.” — via team site.
President Donald Trump
“He was a great guy. He was with me all the way. He was tough. Mike Ditka, that’s a sad one. ... Wow, he was great. He was a big supporter of mine and he was a winner. He was a tough cookie.”
Former President Barack Obama
“When I got to Chicago in the summer of 1985, Mike Ditka and the Chicago Bears were king. Coach Ditka set the tone for a team that was punishing, dominant, and fun — and the city loved him for it. I’m thinking of the Ditka family and Bears fans everywhere on the passing of a legend.” — via X.
NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell
“Mike Ditka epitomized football over so many years. He brought intensity, authenticity, and an unmistakable personality to everything he did. As a Hall of Fame player, Super Bowl-winning coach with his beloved and iconic Bears, and as a broadcaster, Mike served as an ambassador for the game and inspired generations of fans. Through his work with the Gridiron Greats Assistance Fund, Mike was a champion for taking care of those who helped build our game. We extend our deepest condolences to Diana and the Ditka family.”
New Orleans Saints
“We proudly honor his chapters as a head coach in New Orleans. While his time leading our franchise on the field was brief in longevity, his presence left an indelible mark on our organization. Mike approached his tenure with the Saints with the same bold authenticity and relentless drive that defined his entire career. Beyond the wins and losses, his genuine kindness, vibrant personality, and immense generosity to many within our facility created an enduring legacy that our staff and community still fondly remember.
“While the football world remembers ‘Iron Mike’ for his unparalleled competitive spirit, we admire the true character, passion, and unique energy he brought to our franchise.” — via team site.
Ben Johnson, current Bears coach
“I just want to start off by extending my condolences to the Ditka family. Sad news here this morning, obviously. As far as I’m concerned, Coach Ditka is the gold standard in terms of this place. He’s a legend around here as a player, as a coach. His impact is still being felt to this day. As the head coach of the Bears, I feel humbled to be in that same chair that he was once in. It’s a sad day, just hearing he’s passing on. He’s in our thoughts and prayers.”
Chicago Bulls
“We are deeply saddened by the passing of legendary Chicago Bears coach and player, Mike Ditka. Coach Ditka helped define Chicago sports, represented everything great about Chicago and left an unforgettable imprint on our city. He was tough, passionate, loyal and proud and will be forever remembered as a champion, both of his team and of our city.” — via X.
Chicago Cubs
“We join the Bears and the city of Chicago in remembering the legendary Mike Ditka. Thank you for the memories, Coach. — via X.
Chicago White Sox
“The White Sox send our condolences to the family, friends and fans of legendary Mike Ditka. He will be greatly missed.” — via X.
Chicago Blackhawks
“Remembering a Chicago legend. We join the Bears in honoring the life and legacy of Mike Ditka. Thank you, Coach for all you did for Chicago.” — via X.
Chicago Sky
“Forever Chicago. Rest in peace, Mike Ditka. Our thoughts are with his family and loved ones during this time.” — via X.
Jarrett Payton, son of the late Walter Payton
“It’s with a heavy heart that I’m sharing the Ditka family has announced the passing of Mike Ditka this morning. Da Coach. Hall of Famer. The heartbeat of the ’85 Bears and a Super Bowl champion. Chicago won’t be the same. Prayers to Diana and the family. RIP, Coach.” — via X.
Jim Harbaugh, current Los Angeles Chargers coach and former Bears quarterback
“May coach rest in peace. He’s an American original. From Aliquippa, PA, to ‘Iron Mike.’ If you want to know anything about him, like if you want to know who he was, I would suggest reading the poem by Rudyard Kipling, ‘If.’ He could’ve been talking about Mike Ditka. Or Teddy Roosevelt’s ‘The Man in the Arena.’ It’s Mike Ditka. And always true to himself. Always the same person, no matter who he was around, who he was with., where he was. ... I loved him. I loved playing for him.”
Brett Favre, Pro Football Hall of Fame quarterback
“My condolences to the Ditka family and to all Bear fans on the passing of Coach Mike Ditka. It was truly an honor to play against you and your teams. Now rest in peace and God Bless you Coach.” — via X.
Green Bay Packers, longtime division rival
“One of the fiercest competitors in NFL history, Mike helped define the intensity and tradition of the Packers-Bears rivalry, the oldest in professional football. He embodied the toughness and passion that have made the rivalry one of the most storied in all of sports. While he was a formidable opponent, his contributions to the game and to a rivalry that has meant so much to both franchises will always be respected and remembered by the Green Bay Packers.” — via X.
C. Allen Greene, University of Pittsburgh Athletic Director
“Mike Ditka was the embodiment of a Pitt man. He brought the toughness and pride of western Pennsylvania to the University of Pittsburgh, became one of the greatest players in the history of our program and carried the Pitt name with him to the Pro Football Hall of Fame. He achieved everything as a player and a coach, yet he never lost his connection to where he came from. On behalf of the entire Pitt Athletics family, I extend our deepest condolences to the Ditka family.”
Pat Narduzzi, current Pitt football coach
“When our players see Mike Ditka’s name, I want them to understand how he competed. He gave everything he had and expected the same from the guys beside him. That’s Pitt. He showed us that tough people find a way through tough times and taught us to fight for the names on the front and back of our jerseys. Our thoughts and prayers are with his family and everyone he impacted throughout his tremendous life. His toughness will forever be a part of this program.”
Chris Berman, ESPN NFL host
“Mike Ditka was a national treasure. His accomplishments as a player and coach for the Chicago Bears long ago put him in the Pro Football Hall of Fame for both. We were lucky at ESPN to have him as a teammate on Sunday NFL Countdown for over a decade. Not only did he put a smile on our faces every week, he did the same for millions of viewers.
“Our heartfelt condolences to Mike’s family, his Bears family, and to the countless people he touched from near and afar. It is impossible to think of the history of the NFL without seeing his face and his famous mustache. Sadly, Mike has passed on, but his legend will live forever.”
Ozzie Guillen, former White Sox player and manager
“Coach, man, we had some great times, laughs, and memories over the years. Always admired your style. Thank you for the talks, advice, and friendship. Chicago lost a legend Rest easy, Coach.” — via X.

title: Tornadoes spotted across multiple counties as severe weather from Isaias remains
text:
AUGUSTA, Ga. (WRDW/WAGT/Gray News) - Tornadoes are blamed for damage in at least three Central Savannah River Area counties Saturday, sparking warnings across the CSRA as severe weather spun off from Hurricane Isaias.
A tornado warning was in effect until 7:30 p.m. for Aiken and Saluda counties.
As of 7:02 p.m., a severe thunderstorm capable of producing a tornado was located near Ridge Spring, or near Batesburg-Leesville, moving north at 25 mph.
It was the second radar-indicated tornado warning for the same area in a couple of hours. One expired at 6:30, but a new one was issued at 7:02 p.m. and not set to expire until 7:30.
The earlier warning came after the New Holland area saw a confirmed tornado on the ground.
Also getting a second tornado warning of the day was Screven County, where a warning was in effect until 6:30. That warning was allowed to expire.
This all came after confirmed damage in Allendale, Screven and Burke counties.
News 12 drone video showed damage to at least four buildings on Story Mill Road in Burke County about halfway between Hephzibah and Waynesboro. Two were missing parts of their roof, and one entire side was taken out of a third. A fourth was flattened. Drone video also showed trucks and trailers overturned.
Officials said there were no injuries in Burke County.
Power lines were down along Highway 80 West.
At 4:18 p.m., a confirmed tornado was 5 miles south of Appleton, moving north at 30 mph, according to the National Weather Service. That’s between the Burtons Ferry Bridge and downtown Allendale.
The storm also spawned an earlier tornado in Screven County. Then the storm moved across the river to Allendale County. Barnwell County was then added to the warning.
After that came the Aiken County warning.
There was confirmed damage in Screven County, with trees down in a 200-yard path near Old Savannah Highway and Highway 21.
A tornado warning expired earlier in Burke County.
That warning was based on radar activity just north of Waynesboro along Highway 25. The warning expired at 4 p.m.

title: Auburn school comes together for a canine cause, motivated by its comfort dog Luna
text:
Every Monday, Wednesday and Friday since the start of the school year, students and faculty at Auburn’s Franklin Alternative School have run — or walked — in the surrounding High Street neighborhood to prepare for a 5K race. The event not only supported a favorite school cause but ended up bringing them together and teaching lessons in ways they never expected.
“So many of our students face barriers when it comes to being part of their community. Sometimes they are tangible — poverty, abuse, instability — and sometimes in their heads — anxiety, depression — but all of those barriers send the message to kids that they don’t belong. A 5K is such a simple thing but it’s an event that has a strong sense of community,” said Principal Melissa McLeod.
Despite the rigors of a 5K, the students didn’t need much convincing right from the start, McLeod said, because the 5K benefited the organization behind the school’s beloved comfort dog, Luna.
And as far as McLeod was concerned, it didn’t matter that there ended up being more walking then running as training for the 5K progressed, because it was all about the effort and the cause.
“A lot who wanted to run are now walking,” McLeod joked last week, before eight school staff and 22 students lined up Oct. 4 for Moxie’s Memorial 5K in Oxford.
Franklin School is an alternative learning environment that students at risk of not graduating can choose to attend. It serves about 100 students from Lewiston and Auburn. In the eight years McLeod has served as principal, the school has always had a wait list, she said.
The school secured a $125,000 grant two years ago from The John T. Gorman Foundation, a philanthropic organization in Maine, to pilot trauma-informed programming that can bolster academic achievement and social outcomes.
McLeod said the school implemented an aerobic movement program three times a week as part of the wellness side of the grant. She explained that academic research shows that movement not only helps regulate a person’s nervous system, but can help improve academic performance.
The addition of training for a 5K felt like a perfect way to implement that exercise, she said. And the staff idea to do the Moxie’s Memorial 5K was a great motivator: The event raises funds for the nonprofit that brought Franklin Alternative’s comfort dog Luna into the school’s life.
Every student and staff member who could participate, did, and they were out of the building every Monday, Wednesday and Friday to train. The staff had a lot of fun with it, McLeod said, and some even started lifting weights.
“One thing I emphasized to staff is that if we are going to get the kids to do this, we have to show enthusiasm, and there ended up being a lot more than we thought,” she said.
Luna has become a staple to Franklin Alternative School. She has a distinctive personality and free reign through the school’s hallway. McLeod said Luna helps the students immensely. If students, or even staff, are having a difficult day, they can spend some time cuddling with Luna to lift their spirits. At the end of the day, Luna goes home to McLeod and her family.
Luna has also made an impact on the greater Auburn school community. McLeod jokes that if she goes anywhere with Luna, it will take twice as long because everyone wants to pet her.
Luna came to Franklin School from Mission Working Dogs, which hosts the Moxie’s Memorial 5K in Oxford. The organization breeds, raises and trains service dogs for disabled veterans and civilians who are suffering from post-traumatic stress disorder, or mobility issues, while also providing comfort dogs to hospitals and schools.
Christy Gardner, an Auburn Edward Little High School graduate, was injured in 2006 while serving as a sergeant in the U.S. Army Police Military in Asia. After returning to Maine, Gardner adopted her service dog, Moxie, in 2010 and in 2020 founded Mission Working Dogs.
Auburn Police Department’s comfort dog, Benny-Bud, also came from Mission Working Dogs.
Gardner said after the 5K event Oct. 4 that it was “awesome” to have the Franklin students and Luna participate in the race.
“They brought great attitudes and smiles to the event. We love our partnership with their school and the difference therapy dog Luna brings to the environment there,” Gardner said.
McLeod said she knows it sounds cliché, but participating with students and staff in an event like the one this past weekend reinforces the feeling of family that the school has.
Often, students at Franklin Alternative School arrive needing more than just academics, they need a support system. The combination of physical movement training for the recent 5K and the new statewide cellphone ban have strengthened that bond, McLeod said.
“We have these kids who are always walking around the city, but now they’re forced to walk with adults and other kids. They are all talking to each other, and they’re still at school so they can’t have their phones. It’s forcing the kids to be more social with adults and it’s been great, just walking around chatting,” she said.
Several teachers, including Stevie Dunton, a special education teacher, got involved in the 5K. He said he is not a runner, but he wanted to show his students that they could do whatever they put their minds to.
Melissa Anderson, a social worker, said Luna is an integral part of the support system at Franklin. Anderson herself is a new member of the “Franklin family” and being a part of the training for the 5K and seeing the success of the students was meaningful to her.
“The conversations that grew out of morning walks and the confidence built through this opportunity were truly wonderful to observe and be a part of,” said Anderson.
Moving forward, staff at Franklin Alternative School will continue to remind their students that they have a sense of belonging in the community, whether they are training together or bonding in the classroom with Luna, especially in the light of conversations around youth and the gun violence Lewiston is experiencing.
“Kids who are told that they don’t have value and don’t belong in their communities have no incentive to protect their streets or contribute in positive ways. They also have no incentive to hold each other accountable. We will continue to encourage our kids at Franklin to be a part of their world and will open any doors we can to get them passage into their community,” McLeod said.

title: Don’t waste one vote this November
text:
The Aug. 23 letter declaring the writer’s intent to cast a write-in vote for Graham Platner in November was alarming. The writer is apparently unaware that a write-in candidate must file a declaration of write-in candidacy in Maine 70 days prior to the election, or the vote won’t count.
This election is paramount. We must unseat Sen. Susan Collins as a step toward healing the damage done by this presidential administration and, to do so, we must unite behind Troy Jackson. A vote for an undeclared write-in candidate — or any other candidate besides Jackson — is a wasted vote.
I was also a Platner fan, but we cannot afford to risk the continuing soaring cost of foreign war, gasoline, groceries and healthcare, or continue suffering the unending assaults on our lands, air and freedoms by casting philosophical votes. The preservation of democracy is a task we must not fail to achieve this November.
Robin Johnson
Waterville

title: Lincoln Academy gets its turn, wins first Class B golf championship
text:
VASSALBORO — For years, with players like Bailey Plourde and Kellen Adickes coming through the program, the Lincoln Academy golf team had seen individual success at the Class B state championships.
Team success, however, kept eluding the Eagles. It was always another team’s time, another team’s turn at the top.
Until Saturday, that is. With medalist Colin Mitchell leading the way with a 2-over 74, Lincoln won its first state championship, shooting 317 to hold off Freeport (326), Yarmouth (334), Cape Elizabeth and Fryeburg Academy (both 341) in the Class B tournament at Natanis Golf Course.
“It was a huge goal of ours. We won KVACs, which was nice, but we knew that this was a bigger goal on our minds,” Mitchell said. “We knew it was definitely doable. … We knew if we played well, we would have a fighting chance.”
Freeport’s Ryan Savona finished second to Mitchell with a 76. He was followed by Henry Stone of Gray-New Gloucester and Caden Chretien of Nokomis at 77, and Declan Hickey of Yarmouth at 78.
Carla Ferraris of Fryeburg Academy and Kathryn Peterson of Lake Region tied for girls medalist honors at 90.
Lincoln Academy finished ninth the last two seasons and had only one top-five finish the previous four years while failing to qualify twice. But after winning the KVAC B qualifier by 15 strokes, the Eagles had the answers this year.
“It’s been on my mind for a couple of years,” coach Todd Brackett said. “This team has a lot of potential. They’re young, and we’ve seen it coming up.
“They’ve had some great (individual) performances, but just never put it all together. Obviously, it came together today.”
In addition to Mitchell, the Eagles got a 79 from Brody Day, an 80 from Drew Nichols and an 84 from Max Blake — all juniors. The medalist honors were particularly sweet for Mitchell, who shot a 91 in the tournament last year and began making frequent trips to Natanis in the spring to ensure he’d be ready in October.
“This is one of the first courses to open in the spring. It’s kind of far from my house, but it’s worth the trip,” he said. “(Then) I’d play every day in the summer, like four to five hours a day, if not more.”
The work paid off Saturday. Mitchell got his round going with birdies on the fourth and sixth holes, and after bogeys on the eighth, ninth and 11th, he played his final seven holes at even par to maintain his lead.
“I felt like I was still swinging it good, so I just had to trust that,” he said. “It’s easy to drift out of focus a little bit. … I definitely checked back in mentally.”
Savona’s 76, combined with Liam Nihill’s 81, Will Obrin’s 84 and Charlie MacDonald’s 85, kept Freeport close. Savona opened with a birdie, then got two more on the 11th and 17th while playing the back nine at 1 under.
“It got kind of scrappy for a little bit, but I felt like I held it together well,” he said. “I made a couple of double (bogeys) out there, and my mentality was (that) it wasn’t even a bad double, I hit a couple of bad shots. I still feel solid about my game.”
Yarmouth also got an 82 from Lucas D’Alessandro, an 86 from Rory Truesdell and an 88 from Charles Hughes. Cape Elizabeth was led by an 82 from Charlie Lampman. Fryeburg’s Sergio Trejo shot an 81.
Lake Region’s Shane Plummer also finished in the top 10 with an 80 that tied him with Lincoln Academy’s Nichols for seventh.

title: Hearts of Pine allow another stoppage time goal in loss to AC Boise
text:
PORTLAND — It looked like the Portland Hearts of Pine were about to buck a season-long trend.
Instead, the problem that has haunted the USL League One team for most of the season did them in again.
For the 12th time this season, Portland allowed a late goal that flipped an outcome from positive to negative. This time, Thomas Ang’s goal in the 93rd minute gave Athletic Club Boise a 2-1 win at Fitzpatrick Stadium. It was the 10th goal allowed by the Hearts in the 90th minute or later in 30 USL1 matches.
“I think that’s the 20-some odd point we’ve dropped in the last 10 minutes of games,” Portland coach Bobby Murphy said. “My frustration is, they play their hearts out, they do so much good, and then we don’t respect the moments that it takes to get something from the game.”
Overall, Portland has given up 26 potential points when a tie turned to a loss, or a would-be win became a tie or loss. With the loss of one point Saturday, Portland has squandered 21 points in the final 10 minutes of matches.
Portland (7-13-10, 31 points) was officially eliminated from the playoffs on Wednesday. If half of those 26 points had gone their way, the Hearts would be a single point out of playoff contention with two matches remaining.
“We’re still trying to ask ourselves why, and why it happens to us,” said right back Mo Mohamed. “Today, it felt like we had the game for the majority of it and momentum especially toward the end, and for them to score that goal, it’s kind of like heartbreaking.”
Boise (15-8-7) moved up a spot in the standings and is now in fourth place, in line for a quarterfinal home game.
HOME STRUGGLES
Portland played before the franchise’s 38th consecutive sellout (6,318 fans) at Fitzpatrick Stadium. But the fan support has not translated into much success. Portland is 5-7-3 at home this season.
After an evenly played first half with few chances for either team, Boise opened the scoring in the 54th minute on a strike by 32-year-old Tumi Mosobane after a long throw-in to the box caromed out away from the pack.
It was the eighth time in 15 home matches that Portland has conceded the first goal. Portland is 1-6-1 in those games, 0-6 the last six times it has happened.
After Diego Gonzalez took a Diogo Barbosa pass, then turned and rifled a shot into the right-third of the goal in the 74th minute, it began to feel like Portland was going to be the team to get the late winning tally.
Aboubacar Camara had the best chance in the 84th minute when he got behind the Boise defense but popped a short-range shot over the net.
RISK, NOT REWARD
Boise’s winner was a sharp shot by Amang from about 12 yards that zipped past keeper Hunter Morse (three saves) and inside the right post.
Murphy said the issue started with a “diagonal goal kick into Diego’s head, which he’s not going to be able to do anything with.”
Then it was Boise’s Denys Kostyshyn winning a ball from Barbosa and quickly passing to the right sideline to Jonathan Ricketts, who had several steps on left back Josh Drack. With Drack chasing and Barbosa closing, Ricketts slid a pass to his left that Amang one-timed through traffic.
“At the end, we had a couple moments where were trying to get too much from situations where there was nothing to be gained, really,” Murphy said. “The game comes down to moments, and in those moments, we’ve fallen short far too often.”
Portland is at Forward Madison next Saturday and finishes its season hosting current league-leader Charlotte Independence on Oct. 24.
NOTES
National Soccer Hall of Famer Landon Donovan was in the house after a holiday weekend of Maine-oriented activities. It was not the four-time U.S. Player of the Year’s first connection to the Hearts of Pine. Donovan modeled the Hearts’ “lighthouse” jersey for a video and photo shoot at West Quoddy Lighthouse when the team announced the alternate kit.
Best chant: “Our potatoes are better.” … Mid-year signing Felipe Rodriguez Gentile, who scored his second goal in Portland’s 3-3 tie at Spokane, started at the left wing spot normally held down by injured Ollie Wright.

title: Philadelphia police officer killed, another injured after responding to reports of man with a gun
text:
(AP) - Authorities are charging Eric Lewis, 35, with homicide for the alleged killing of a police officer early Saturday morning, according to Philadelphia District Attorney Larry Krasner.
Shane Seiber, 40, was shot and killed in west Philadelphia after responding to a report of a man with a gun, police said. An officer who was with him was also shot.
Seiber, a 10-year veteran of the Philadelphia Police Department, and the other officer were transported to Penn Presbyterian Medical Center and underwent surgery, according to Police Commissioner Kevin Bethel. The surviving officer, who was shot 12 times, is in stable condition, Bethel said.
Along with charges for Seiber’s death, Lewis is facing a host of others, including attempted homicide, for allegedly shooting the officer and shooting at nine other officers who responded to the scene, Krasner said. None of those nine were injured.
Lewis is being held without bail and will be arraigned soon, Krasner said. Lewis was previously convicted of criminal offenses including assault, theft and carrying a firearm publicly, according to court records.
Gov. Josh Shapiro said he ordered flags to fly at half-staff for Seiber, who is survived by his wife and two children — a 7-year-old boy and a 3-year-old girl.
“This is a brutal, senseless, horrific killing,” Krasner said.

title: Maine cannot afford to lose Susan Collins’ bipartisan voice in Washington
text:
KC Johnson is a professor of history at Brooklyn College and lives in Scarborough.
By now, most of us have seen the ad dozens of times. Four (identified) female narrators castigate Sen. Susan Collins for never standing up to President Trump.
The narrators focus on three issues: the Iran war, Medicaid cuts and the Supreme Court’s reversal of Roe v. Wade. They cite four votes by Collins: against a measure to invoke the War Powers Resolution on the Iran war, in favor of a measure to allow Senate debate on Trump’s major funding bill last year and to confirm Brett Kavanaugh and Neil Gorsuch, two of the five justices who voted to overturn Roe.
The ad doesn’t mention that Collins (along with 2nd District Democrat Jared Golden,
whose votes followed a similar path) subsequently voted in favor of invoking the
War Powers Resolution on Iran. Or that she voted against passing the Trump 2025
spending bill.
Most misleadingly, the ad does not note that Collins has voted to confirm all three pro-choice justices on the Court (Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan and Ketanji Brown Jackson). Nor does it reveal that she broke from Trump to oppose the 2020 confirmation of Amy Coney Barrett, who provided the fifth vote necessary to reverse Roe. In fact, if the Court consisted solely of justices who earned Collins’ support, it seems likely that Roe would still be the law of the land.
The thrust of the ad, funded by a group called WinSenate, seems to be that independence or open-mindedness is a bad thing in a senator. Two of the narrators place independence in air quotes as they describe Collins. And the three issues chosen — Iran, the 2025 spending bill and Trump’s Supreme Court nominees — are ones where Collins has taken independent positions from the president.
Perhaps such a claim is unfair to WinSenate. Their ads identify a website — winsenate.org — where Maine voters can go to learn more about the group’s positions, which is funded by a super PAC affiliated with Senate Democrats.
I visited the website to try to get more information on why the organization seems so hostile to an independent approach in the Senate, and in particular what justification the group could have to attribute the reversal of Roe to Collins, given her opposition to Barrett’s confirmation.
The website consists solely of a photograph of the American flag. It provides no statement of principles about the group’s mission, no rationalization for its hostility to a senator who doesn’t always vote a party line and no explanations to bolster its claims.
The two WinSenate ads about Collins analyzed by the fact-checking website PolitiFact
are rated “false” and “mostly false.”
As someone who voted for Joe Brennan in the 1996 Senate race, Chellie Pingree in
2002, Tom Allen in 2008 and even Shenna Bellows (who lost by a greater than 2-1 margin to Collins) in 2014, I understand the impulse to vote against Collins. But 2026 is not 1996, nor even 2014.
With Collins chairing the Appropriations Committee, her demonstrated clout on behalf of the state highlights her importance to the state.
Perhaps more importantly, at a time when American politics is more polarized than it’s been in decades, it’s critical to maintain one of the Senate’s few bipartisan voices — especially since the Democrats’ replacement nominee, Troy Jackson, seems likely to be little more than an automatic vote for whatever position Bernie Sanders or Elizabeth Warren take, rather than an independent vote for Maine.
A 2026 vote for Collins provides a way to resist the two parties’ race to ideological extremes — and, perhaps, also a way to reject misleading ads that, as here, quite literally wrap themselves in the American flag and hope that voters don’t look too closely into their underlying claims.

title: Simon strengthens into a Category 4 hurricane as it approaches Mexico’s coast
text:
MIAMI (AP) — Simon has strengthened into a powerful Category 4 hurricane as it barrels toward Mexico’s coast.
The National Hurricane Center in Miami said early Saturday Simon’s maximum sustained winds increased to 150 mph (240 kph). A storm of that strength or greater is considered a major hurricane. Simon could bring as much as 10 to 20 inches (25-50 cm) of rain over parts of southwestern Mexico, with some areas receiving up to 30 inches, the center said.
The bulletin also urged residents to take immediate action to prepare, saying the hurricane will make landfall early Sunday, but tropical storm-strength winds could arrive much sooner.
Simon is expected to bring heavy rainfall to parts of southwestern Mexico, possibly concentrated along Jalisco’s coast and in parts of Michoacan, Colima and Nayarit.
“This rainfall will produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides, especially in areas of steep terrain,” the NHC said.
Jalisco suspended classes on Friday and Monday in 22 coastal municipalities and began evacuating dozens of people from at-risk areas. It also asked the tourism sector in Puerto Vallarta, a popular destination for U.S. tourists, to ensure that both workers and visitors are fully accommodated in shelters or safe zones by Friday afternoon.

title: Coyotes are often misunderstood, and confused for other animals
text:
One of our regular readers, Joan from Portland, wrote to us with a handful of questions about coyotes, which always strike me as one of Maine’s most misunderstood mammals. That title might actually go to the fisher (often, and inappropriately, called the fisher cat) because everyone wants to ascribe nocturnal noises to them, when 99% of the time it is actually a fox. That said, the coyote and its many noises deserve some attention.
Coyotes have an interesting history in Maine, because they weren’t always here. I grew up in Hollis, a wonderfully small rural town where coyotes were often heard (and seldom seen). But they aren’t just in rural areas; coyotes can be found across the entire state, often thriving in suburban and surprisingly urban areas too.
If we go back to the 1920s, these wild dogs (canids) had never been seen in the state. The first recorded sightings are from the ’30s. They expanded their range northeast, coming into the state to fill a void left by the extirpation of wolves. That niche was opened after humans killed off the eastern wolves that once lived in Maine, eradicating them in the 19th century.
As the coyotes moved into these newly accessible areas, they encountered some wolves en route and began hybridizing, which gave us the variety of coyote hybrids, often called “coywolves,” that are seen in Maine today. To be a bit more specific, they are officially called eastern coyotes, one of the nineteen subspecies of coyotes across Northern and Central America.
It is worth reflecting on these mixed genes a bit further. The eastern coyote is a majority coyote with other canines mixed in. A study published in 2014, led by Javier Monzón of Stony Brook University, looked at eastern coyote genomes and found that genetic parentage broke down as: 65% western coyote, 17% western wolf and 18% eastern wolf. Furthermore, there were some eastern coyotes with four canid parentage, thanks to dogs contributing. Those broke down to: 61% western coyote, 14% western wolf, 14% eastern wolf and 11% domestic dog.
I emphasize this point because we see a lot of reports of wolves in Maine. While it is possible that eastern wolves could wander into Maine, there are no established populations of them here, but plenty of wolfish-looking coyotes.
Despite their wide distribution, coyotes are rarely encountered in Maine. You are more likely to find signs left behind, like footprints or scat. Their droppings are most likely to be confused for that of a large dog, but a dog’s diet is consistent, and so is their poop. A coyote will typically have scat showing their omnivorous diet, with many indigestible contents like hair (from the small mammal prey) and seeds (from fruit).
The next best way to detect their presence is through their loud vocalizations. Howling is perhaps the most iconic of their noises, typically given in long-distance and territorial communications. I also hear my local coyotes doing a lot of dog-like yipping, sometimes mixed with howls. This mixing can be done by just a couple of individuals, vocalized in a way to sound like a large group, which is known as a “Beau Geste” effect. They are so vocal, which is how they got their specific epithet: latrans, which is Latin for “barking”, so Canus latrans is the “barking dog.”
The last thing we need to address, given all the coyotes around us, is that they are generally harmless, unless you are a small rodent. In general, coyotes are much more afraid of humans than humans need to be of them. That said, keeping them wild is important, so do not leave food out for them. And while a cat is larger than most coyote prey, you should keep your cats safe and indoors all the time anyway as cats are also the No. 1 anthropogenic cause of mortality in birds.
Have you got a nature or wildlife question of your own? It doesn’t have to be about birds! Email questions to [email protected] and visit www.maineaudubon.org to learn more about birding, native plants, and programs and events focusing on Maine wildlife and habitat. Maine Audubon Staff Naturalist Doug Hitchcox and other naturalists lead free bird walks on Thursday mornings starting at 7 am, at Maine Audubon’s Gilsland Farm Audubon Sanctuary in Falmouth.

title: UMaine men’s hockey earns split with Quinnipiac
text:
Lee Parks scored the go-ahead goal in the second period and UMaine handed sixth-ranked Quinnipiac its first loss of the season Saturday night, beating the Bobcats 5-3 in a nonconference men’s hockey game in Orono.
The Black Bears (2-2) fell behind 3-2 on a goal by Mason Marcellus just 1:04 into the second period, but Isa Parekh tied it just over two minutes later. Parks then put Maine ahead at 6:07 after Max Scott stole the puck in the Quinnipiac zone and passed to Will Gerrior, who found Parks all alone in front.
Loic Usereau and Samuel Alfano scored for Maine in the first period, and Sully Scholle clinched the win with an empty-netter with 1:49 remaining.
Maine goalie Albin Boija finished with 20 saves.
Quinnipiac, which beat the Black Bears 2-1 on Friday night, dropped to 3-1.

title: Democrats appear to be our only hope on healthcare
text:
I think I speak for many as I age, requiring more encounters with our healthcare system.
I used to speak of our need for a single-payer healthcare system in the U.S. I reminded people I knew about the fact that we are the only industrialized nation in the world that doesn’t provide healthcare for its citizens. I worked to encourage my political representatives to make the changes needed to bring about that end. Was it all for nothing? Now that I truly need healthcare, where am I?
Maine hospitals are cutting departments or closing down for various reasons — Medicaid cuts, nurse shortages, etc. Nursing homes, birthing centers and even local medical practices, especially in our more rural areas, are suffering as well. We read about this crisis almost every day in our newspapers. And we hear many explanations. OK, now what?
I have friends who have looked for solutions — from seeking alternative medicine locally to traveling to specialized treatment centers in other states and even to using eye surgeries, dental care and joint replacement in other countries. I’m not likely to do any of those things. I’m simply hoping for my government to provide the healthcare we all need.
One thing I do know — the government we have now won’t come to my aid. I believe the only hope for the changes we need will come under a government led by Democrats.
Betsy Braunhut
Deer Isle

title: Deputy body camera video offers glimpse inside home weeks before children found dead
text:
LADSON, S.C. (WCSC/Gray News) — South Carolina authorities released body camera footage this week showing a mother and her daughters weeks before the two girls were found dead inside the home.
The footage offers the clearest look yet at daily life inside the Ladson-area home, where Emory Deacon, 2, and Harlow Deacon, 15 months old, died.
The Charleston County Sheriff’s Office said the two young children were found starved to death at the home during a welfare check by deputies on Sept. 29.
Authorities said the girls died three to five days before they were found, with their mother, Justine May, facing charges that include two counts of homicide by child abuse.
According to the Charleston County Sheriff’s Office, deputies had responded to numerous calls at the Pinewood Drive residence before ultimately finding the children dead.
The body camera footage released shows Charleston County deputies visiting the home on Aug. 30 and a mobile crisis unit visit on Sept. 12.
The Aug. 30 footage is about 22 minutes and begins with May answering the door while holding Harlow, who can be seen wearing only a diaper.
Deputies entered the home as a dog could be heard in the background. The home appears well-maintained, with music playing from a speaker in the kitchen.
During May’s conversation with authorities, Harlow was placed on the floor and soon began crawling while Emory was sitting on the couch.
Most of the discussion between deputies and May centered on her former fiancé, Zachary Deacon.
Deacon, who is also the girls’ father, said he had requested multiple welfare checks at the home, telling authorities about what he described as May’s unusual behavior.
Deacon and May ended their eight-year relationship in early August. They had been engaged for five years.
A caseworker could be seen taking notes throughout the conversation with May during the home visit, while the children could be seen interacting with others in the home.
In the Sept. 12 footage, May is seen for most of the video, which took place at the home’s front door. Dogs could once again be heard barking, along with occasional sounds of children playing.
May answered the door, asking authorities, “How may I help you?” before telling them that no one could enter the home.
May asked whether her ex-fiancé requested the welfare check. Authorities said it was May’s parents who made the call.
May shared that she was frustrated but not suicidal when she was asked about her mental state, including whether she was hearing or seeing things.
“My family has been taunting the **** out of me,” May can be heard saying.
May told authorities Deacon was spreading “crazy lies,” including that she was having a mental breakdown. She also said she had cut off contact with her family because they were “harassing” her.
May also mentioned an email from her mother, describing it as “horrible.”
“I’m clearly not crazy,” May said at one point. “And no, I’ve never had any mental health issues.”
At the very end of the visit, both of the children could be seen on video with May holding Harlow and Emory standing in the doorway.
May was said to have shared screenshots online of text messages and emails that she described as coming from concerned family members following the authorities’ checks at the home.
One email expressed concerns about May’s parenting.
The Charleston County Sheriff’s Office said authorities found the children dead after they were called back to the home following a 911 call asking deputies to conduct a welfare check.
According to the sheriff’s office, the caller said that the two girls had not been seen in a while, and that their mother was acting differently and was seen walking around the neighborhood by herself.
When deputies arrived at the home on Sept. 29, they said May exited the house and was crying and speaking incoherently. Upon entering, that’s when they saw the two children dead that afternoon.

title: Obituary: Lisa Bonarrigo Bruni
text:
PORTLAND – Lisa Bonarrigo Bruni, born Feb. 4, 1961, died on Oct. 8, 2026, at her home in Portland, surrounded by the life and family she had built there.
Lisa grew up in Pembroke, Massachusetts, and Thomaston, before making Portland her home in the early 1980s. An artist from an early age, she studied ceramic arts at Alfred University in upstate New York and spent a year living and studying in Japan, experiences that deepened what would become a lifelong devotion to clay, craft and making things by hand.
That devotion eventually became Portland Pottery on Washington Avenue. Lisa began simply, teaching ceramics from her second-floor apartment in Portland. From those early classes grew a studio, school, gallery and supply business that became part of Portland’s creative community and one of the Northeast’s largest ceramic supply operations. Together with her husband, Chris Bruni, Lisa expanded Portland Pottery over nearly three decades, creating a place where generations of students, teachers, working artists and beginners could learn, work and find community.
Lisa’s imagination rarely stopped with one idea. Over the years, she also created or helped create Portland Pottery Café, Clay Farm and Lena’s Italian Comfort, bringing together many of the things she loved: art, food, teaching, hospitality and people gathered around a table. She also built and managed a thriving real estate portfolio, approaching property with the same instinct she brought to her other ventures: seeing possibility, creating value and making something useful out of what was there.
She met Chris Bruni at Bruni’s Market on Munjoy Hill, the neighborhood store owned by his family. From then on, the two were inseparable. They married in 1989 and built a life together in Portland, raising their family and building businesses side by side.
Family life was never confined to home. Lisa and Chris traveled extensively with their children, creating a childhood shaped by movement, curiosity and seeing the world together. The water was always part of Lisa’s life. She loved the ocean, spent years sailing the coast of Maine, and spent part of each summer at the family cottage in Harpswell. She chose to live close to the water, and in her final days looked out from her home to see the ocean beyond her porch.
Lisa loved to grow things. Her gardens were filled with fruit, vegetables and flowers, and she found real pleasure in tending them and watching what came up each season. She also loved to cook, and she cooked often. Food, like art, was part of the way she cared for people and brought them together.
Lisa is survived by her husband, Chris Bruni; their children, Andrew, Abigail and Jordynn; and their granddaughter, Aurora. She is also survived by her mother, Barbara Whitney; her siblings; Laura, JJ, Joby, Angela, Andrew, Julia, and the large extended families on both the Bonarrigo and Bruni sides, including generations of nieces, nephews and cousins, as well as the many friends, students and members of the Portland community whose lives crossed hers.
Lisa was an artist, teacher, entrepreneur, restaurateur, real estate investor, gardener, cook, mother, sister, wife and friend. She could be generous, demanding, funny, opinionated and fiercely involved in the lives of the people she loved. She believed in making things, feeding people, teaching people, taking chances and expecting people to use what they had been given.
Near the end of her life, Lisa said she was “going on vacation.” It was very much in character. She imagined herself still being herself, just somewhere else, traveling to places she had not yet seen and reconnecting with the people she missed. That is how her family likes to think of her now: off on her next trip.
Visiting hours will be held on Sunday, October 11, from 2-4 p.m., at the new Conroy-Tully Walker Funeral Homes, 300 Allen Avenue, Portland. To view Lisa’s memorial page, please visit http://www.ConroyTullyWalker.com.
In lieu of flowers, they ask you to make donations to Good Shepherd Food Bank of Maine or Adoptive & Foster Families of Maine (AFFM).

title: Mike Ditka tributes pour in from President Trump, former President Obama, Chicago and the NFL
text:
(AP) - Mike Ditka was “Iron Mike” as a player who revolutionized the tight end position and later became the easily recognizable and often imitated fiery, mustached and sweater vest-wearing “Da Coach” of the Chicago Bears during a Super Bowl-winning tenure.
Ditka died Friday at 86, his family announced in a statement.
The Pro Football Hall of Famer was remembered by the sports world and beyond for his impact on the game as both a player and a coach, and later as a TV analyst.
Here are some notable reactions to Ditka’s death and tributes to his legacy:
Chicago Bears
“We are deeply saddened by the passing of legendary and treasured Chicago Bear and Pro Football Hall of Famer Mike Ditka. Mike’s impact on the Chicago Bears organization, over decades as a player, coach, and proud icon and ambassador for our organization, is immeasurable. His integral role in bringing world championships to our city and our franchise, both as a player and as our coach, established prominence and excellence at a world-class level, but also created a lifetime of cherished memories in the hearts and minds of Bears fans that will last for generations.
“We extend our love, prayers, and heartfelt condolences to the Ditka family, and join all Bears fans in deep sadness and reverence as we remember and honor Mike Ditka.” — via team site.
President Donald Trump
“He was a great guy. He was with me all the way. He was tough. Mike Ditka, that’s a sad one. ... Wow, he was great. He was a big supporter of mine and he was a winner. He was a tough cookie.”
Former President Barack Obama
“When I got to Chicago in the summer of 1985, Mike Ditka and the Chicago Bears were king. Coach Ditka set the tone for a team that was punishing, dominant, and fun — and the city loved him for it. I’m thinking of the Ditka family and Bears fans everywhere on the passing of a legend.” — via X.
NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell
“Mike Ditka epitomized football over so many years. He brought intensity, authenticity, and an unmistakable personality to everything he did. As a Hall of Fame player, Super Bowl-winning coach with his beloved and iconic Bears, and as a broadcaster, Mike served as an ambassador for the game and inspired generations of fans. Through his work with the Gridiron Greats Assistance Fund, Mike was a champion for taking care of those who helped build our game. We extend our deepest condolences to Diana and the Ditka family.”
New Orleans Saints
“We proudly honor his chapters as a head coach in New Orleans. While his time leading our franchise on the field was brief in longevity, his presence left an indelible mark on our organization. Mike approached his tenure with the Saints with the same bold authenticity and relentless drive that defined his entire career. Beyond the wins and losses, his genuine kindness, vibrant personality, and immense generosity to many within our facility created an enduring legacy that our staff and community still fondly remember.
“While the football world remembers ‘Iron Mike’ for his unparalleled competitive spirit, we admire the true character, passion, and unique energy he brought to our franchise.” — via team site.
Ben Johnson, current Bears coach
“I just want to start off by extending my condolences to the Ditka family. Sad news here this morning, obviously. As far as I’m concerned, Coach Ditka is the gold standard in terms of this place. He’s a legend around here as a player, as a coach. His impact is still being felt to this day. As the head coach of the Bears, I feel humbled to be in that same chair that he was once in. It’s a sad day, just hearing he’s passing on. He’s in our thoughts and prayers.”
Chicago Bulls
“We are deeply saddened by the passing of legendary Chicago Bears coach and player, Mike Ditka. Coach Ditka helped define Chicago sports, represented everything great about Chicago and left an unforgettable imprint on our city. He was tough, passionate, loyal and proud and will be forever remembered as a champion, both of his team and of our city.” — via X.
Chicago Cubs
“We join the Bears and the city of Chicago in remembering the legendary Mike Ditka. Thank you for the memories, Coach. — via X.
Chicago White Sox
“The White Sox send our condolences to the family, friends and fans of legendary Mike Ditka. He will be greatly missed.” — via X.
Chicago Blackhawks
“Remembering a Chicago legend. We join the Bears in honoring the life and legacy of Mike Ditka. Thank you, Coach for all you did for Chicago.” — via X.
Chicago Sky
“Forever Chicago. Rest in peace, Mike Ditka. Our thoughts are with his family and loved ones during this time.” — via X.
Jarrett Payton, son of the late Walter Payton
“It’s with a heavy heart that I’m sharing the Ditka family has announced the passing of Mike Ditka this morning. Da Coach. Hall of Famer. The heartbeat of the ’85 Bears and a Super Bowl champion. Chicago won’t be the same. Prayers to Diana and the family. RIP, Coach.” — via X.
Jim Harbaugh, current Los Angeles Chargers coach and former Bears quarterback
“May coach rest in peace. He’s an American original. From Aliquippa, PA, to ‘Iron Mike.’ If you want to know anything about him, like if you want to know who he was, I would suggest reading the poem by Rudyard Kipling, ‘If.’ He could’ve been talking about Mike Ditka. Or Teddy Roosevelt’s ‘The Man in the Arena.’ It’s Mike Ditka. And always true to himself. Always the same person, no matter who he was around, who he was with., where he was. ... I loved him. I loved playing for him.”
Brett Favre, Pro Football Hall of Fame quarterback
“My condolences to the Ditka family and to all Bear fans on the passing of Coach Mike Ditka. It was truly an honor to play against you and your teams. Now rest in peace and God Bless you Coach.” — via X.
Green Bay Packers, longtime division rival
“One of the fiercest competitors in NFL history, Mike helped define the intensity and tradition of the Packers-Bears rivalry, the oldest in professional football. He embodied the toughness and passion that have made the rivalry one of the most storied in all of sports. While he was a formidable opponent, his contributions to the game and to a rivalry that has meant so much to both franchises will always be respected and remembered by the Green Bay Packers.” — via X.
C. Allen Greene, University of Pittsburgh Athletic Director
“Mike Ditka was the embodiment of a Pitt man. He brought the toughness and pride of western Pennsylvania to the University of Pittsburgh, became one of the greatest players in the history of our program and carried the Pitt name with him to the Pro Football Hall of Fame. He achieved everything as a player and a coach, yet he never lost his connection to where he came from. On behalf of the entire Pitt Athletics family, I extend our deepest condolences to the Ditka family.”
Pat Narduzzi, current Pitt football coach
“When our players see Mike Ditka’s name, I want them to understand how he competed. He gave everything he had and expected the same from the guys beside him. That’s Pitt. He showed us that tough people find a way through tough times and taught us to fight for the names on the front and back of our jerseys. Our thoughts and prayers are with his family and everyone he impacted throughout his tremendous life. His toughness will forever be a part of this program.”
Chris Berman, ESPN NFL host
“Mike Ditka was a national treasure. His accomplishments as a player and coach for the Chicago Bears long ago put him in the Pro Football Hall of Fame for both. We were lucky at ESPN to have him as a teammate on Sunday NFL Countdown for over a decade. Not only did he put a smile on our faces every week, he did the same for millions of viewers.
“Our heartfelt condolences to Mike’s family, his Bears family, and to the countless people he touched from near and afar. It is impossible to think of the history of the NFL without seeing his face and his famous mustache. Sadly, Mike has passed on, but his legend will live forever.”
Ozzie Guillen, former White Sox player and manager
“Coach, man, we had some great times, laughs, and memories over the years. Always admired your style. Thank you for the talks, advice, and friendship. Chicago lost a legend Rest easy, Coach.” — via X.
Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved.
