title: This Maine point is a front-row seat to a massive bird migration happening now
text:
Outdoors
The BDN outdoors section brings readers into the woods, waters and wild places of Maine. It features stories on hunting, fishing, wildlife, conservation and recreation, told by people who live these experiences. This section emphasizes hands-on knowledge, field reports, issues, trends and the traditions that define life outside in Maine. Read more Outdoors stories here. 
Imagine if there was one place you could sit and watch all of Canada fly by. Forgive the slight exaggeration, but this actually happens at Schoodic Point.
Millions of waterbirds nest across Canada. Virtually all of them need to head south before Canada freezes into a 3.85-million-square mile block of winter ice. Many of those birds are migrating through Maine waters right now. It’s a spectacle almost nobody notices, unless they are tipped off by a highly popular newspaper columnist.
All these birds are flying south, but not randomly. They follow predictable pathways. One of the major flyways takes them past Schoodic Point. Why? To answer that question, you need to think like a duck.
You float. You’re comfortable on water. Your food is in water. If you fly over water, you can put down anywhere and not worry about land-based predators.
However, you probably nested in freshwater wetlands across Canada. You’re not an ocean bird, except in winter. You’re not built to fly across a vast open sea. Therefore, you choose to fly a coastal route, over water but close to land. And if any part of that land sticks into the ocean, you’re going to fly right by it. “Schoodic” comes from a Mi’kmaq word meaning “place at the end,” which literally describes Schoodic Point.
Not all those migrating waterbirds hug the coastline. Some take the scenic route, following rivers and lakes southward. Northern Maine sees a fair number of migrants passing through this time of year. Still, if there is one single place to view the spectacle best, it’s Schoodic Point. That’s how SeaWatch got started ten years ago.
SeaWatch operates under the auspices of Schoodic Institute. Every year, naturalists make daily observations through the fall from the edge of the parking lot at Schoodic Point. They tally every waterbird species they spot heading south. Double-crested cormorants usually chalk up the biggest numbers. Common eiders run a close second. Surf scoters and black scoters typically outnumber white-winged scoters more than 3-1. Red-breasted mergansers and long-tailed ducks pass the point in smaller numbers.
Common loons get counted. Most of Maine’s loons merely head east to the ocean when the lakes freeze up, but Canadian loons are apt to find winter more bearable farther south than their home territories.
Thousands of northern gannets make the list every year. Gannets nest in two enormous colonies in Québec and Newfoundland. Unlike most species passing the point, these huge birds are perfectly comfortable flying across open ocean, beyond the sight of land. However, the fish they eat often run closer to shore, so some gannets pass by close enough to get counted.
SeaWatch runs every morning from now until mid-November. Anyone can join the watch party. The primary naturalist is on hand Saturday through Wednesday, from sunrise to 10 a.m. Assistant naturalists cover Thursday and Friday.
New this year, “Seawatch Saturdays” are educational sessions centered around migrating birds of the Atlantic Coastal Flyway. You’re invited, Saturdays from 1-3 p.m. until November 14.
I spend at least one morning at SeaWatch every year. Here is some advice for your own visit.
Good binoculars are essential, and a spotting scope comes in handy. Most migrating birds will be far away. On a southerly breeze, birds pass closer to the point. On winds from the north, they may be miles away, barely perceptible on the horizon. Most of the SeaWatch birding happens early, from sunrise to midmorning. After that, the birds settle down, and the spectacle abates. Avoid mornings of thick fog or high wind.
I tried my luck last Sunday. The northeast breeze pushed everything away. Only about 2,000 seabirds were observed that morning. I’ll try again, knowing that some days can be awesome.
On October 17, 2018, an astounding migration flight took place. The counters tallied 29,147 birds in one day. The flood of birds was so intense, it was like watching disappointed Miami Dolphins fans streaming out of their football stadium at halftime.
SeaWatch began in 2016, inspired by a similar program operated by New Jersey Audubon at Avalon, NJ. NJA has been counting waterbirds since 1995.
Why count? Many migrating ducks are game species — a resource that requires proper management. It’s impossible to count them across the Canadian wilderness. It’s easy to count them as they fly by Schoodic Point. Comparing counts from year to year offers the best clue to whether climate change and Canadian wildfires are destroying remote habitats and threatening the entire ecosystem.
Plus, it’s fun.

title: After 60 years, America puts a reactor back in space, and it’s headed for Mars
text:
After 60 years, America puts a reactor back in space — and this time it’s headed for Mars
NASA and the Department of Energy signed an agreement Thursday to expand their collaboration on nuclear power and propulsion technologies intended to support longer and more ambitious missions to the moon, Mars and beyond.
Related video above — 'Beautiful but hostile': NASA administrator talks moon base
NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman and Energy Secretary Chris Wright signed the memorandum of understanding during the Golden Age Summit at the Donald J. Trump Institute of Peace in Washington. Michael Kratsios, director of the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy, attended the signing.
The agreement, titled "Accelerating American Leadership in Space Nuclear Power and Propulsion," takes effect Nov. 1. It establishes a framework for cooperation across nuclear technology research, fuel production, testing, launch integration and space operations, with safety serving as a central focus.
"We are entering the 'Nuclear NASA-era,' which represents a major transformation for space exploration," Isaacman said. "Nuclear power will allow us to go farther, operate longer, and field more capable spacecraft and instruments than ever before."
Isaacman said the partnership would help lay the foundation for future fission-powered spacecraft and create new opportunities for exploration and scientific discovery.
"Thanks to President Trump, America’s nuclear renaissance is reaching a new frontier," Wright said. "The Energy Department is proud to partner with NASA as we help American space missions reach uncharted territory."
The agencies said the agreement strengthens their existing work on fission and radioisotope power systems. Such technologies could provide power for habitats, communications equipment, scientific instruments, rovers and other infrastructure in locations where sunlight is limited or unavailable.
A December 2025 executive order from President Donald Trump directed NASA to develop a launch-ready lunar surface reactor by 2030. NASA said it is working with the Energy Department toward that goal.
NASA plans to launch its Space Reactor-1 Freedom in 2028, moving nuclear propulsion from laboratory research to an operational deep-space application. The agency said that mission would help prepare for Lunar Reactor-1, a surface fission system designed to power a future moon base during extended periods of darkness.
NASA said the two reactor programs are intended to help establish a domestic space-nuclear industry, support permanent lunar outposts and develop technologies needed for future missions to Mars and other destinations.
The agency is also expanding its use of radioisotope power systems, which convert heat from radioactive decay into electricity.
NASA’s Dragonfly mission, scheduled to launch in 2028, will use a Multi-Mission Radioisotope Thermoelectric Generator and 24 lightweight radioisotope heater units. The systems will power and warm the car-sized rotorcraft as it travels to multiple locations on Titan, Saturn’s largest moon, to investigate whether the world could support life.
NASA and the Energy Department also plan to provide 24 radioisotope heater units for the European Space Agency’s Rosalind Franklin Mars rover. The units would protect the rover’s instruments from extreme cold as it searches for evidence of past or present life on Mars.

title: 9 dead, including suspected gunman, in mass shooting in Erie, Pennsylvania
Needle exchanges save lives
text:
My dad died in 2003, just before his 58th birthday. Since before I was born he had been an alcoholic and a heroin user. He died of liver cancer brought on by hepatitis C. He likely contracted that hepatitis from a shared needle.
I don’t know if there were needle exchange services where he was then. Probably not; it was the 1970s, when even having “drug paraphernalia” was criminalized in the United States. Criminalization did not stop people from using. Those who ran clean needle services were usually activists, risking imprisonment in their attempts to halt the spread of diseases.
Dad was a Navy veteran. He’d complained of abdominal pain and loss of appetite for years. By the time he was diagnosed by a Veterans Affairs doctor in 2002, his cancer was terminal. He said his earlier attempts to have his pain addressed were probably dismissed as “drug-seeking behavior.”
It can be uncomfortable to be around people who use street drugs. Just because someone uses does not mean that they deserve to catch a deadly illness. I don’t pretend to know why Dad started using. But I’m reasonably confident that people use drugs for reasons that are very real to them; they stop for their own reasons too.
Addiction is complicated. I know people who were given powerful pain medicines during hospitalization and quickly became addicted to them.
Helping people avoid reusing needles is good. One needle not getting shared can mean one person not getting hepatitis or HIV that day. That’s why it’s called “harm reduction.” That person might be someone’s dad, mom, brother, sister, daughter, spouse or friend. Everyone is someone’s something.
Siiri Cressey
Lewiston

title: Maine farm is home to USA Today's best corn maze and pumpkin patch
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine farm is home to the best corn maze and pumpkin patch in country, according to USA Today
Treworgy Family Orchards earned the No. 1 spot in both categories as part of the 2026 10Best Readers' Choice Awards.
Maine farm is home to the best corn maze and pumpkin patch in country, according to USA Today
Treworgy Family Orchards earned the No. 1 spot in both categories as part of the 2026 10Best Readers' Choice Awards.
USA Today readers and editors have determined that a Maine farm has both the best corn maze and best pumpkin patch in the nation.
Treworgy Family Orchards in Levant earned the No. 1 spot in both polls conducted as part of USA Today's 2026 10Best Readers' Choice Awards.
This marks the fifth straight year that Treworgy Family Orchards was named the best corn maze in the country by USA Today. Treworgy has been named USA Today's best pumpkin patch in three out of the last four years.
To determine the USA Today 10Best Readers' Choice Awards, a panel of experts provides nominees for each award category and the final set of 10 nominees is selected by USA Today editors. Once the nominees are announced, the public is invited to vote for their favorites over a period of four weeks.
Treworgy Family Orchards is home to the longest continually running corn maze in Maine. The maze covers more than 4 acres and consists of 60,000 corn plants grown to a height of 10 feet. Guests who find the center of the maze are able to sign their names on the farm's Hall of Fame Board. This year, Treworgy's corn maze design pays tribute to the 250th anniversary of the United States with the Statue of Liberty, the Liberty Bell, a bald eagle and a 250 symbol. Treworgy's corn maze first earned the No. 1 spot on the 10Best list in 2018 and ranked No. 2 for three straight years (2019-21) before earning the top spot in each of the past five years (2022-26).
The pumpkin patch at Treworgy Family Orchards covers 8 miles of rows, and the farm grows more than 60 varieties of pumpkins, squash and gourds in every shape, size and color. Treworgy's pumpkin patch was at the top of the 10Best list in 2023 and 2024, and ranked No. 2 on the list last year before reclaiming the top spot.
Treworgy Family Orchards is typically closed on Mondays but the farm will be open this Monday, Oct. 12, for the long holiday weekend. In addition to the corn maze and pumpkin picking, guests can also enjoy apple picking and tractor rides.

title: Man seen riding out Hurricane Isaias in boat as storm surged in Gulf
text:
DAUPHIN ISLAND, Ala. (WALA/Gray News) - A man was reportedly on a boat off the east end of an Alabama island as Hurricane Isaias drew closer to landfall.
Police said they had been in contact with the boater on Dauphin Island earlier on Thursday. Officials said the boater is a local man who wanted to be on his boat.
Police said the man is aware of the dangers of being aboard the boat during the storm and was willing to take the risk.
The hurricane was expected to make landfall around 9:30 p.m. near Pensacola, about 95 miles away.
Maximum sustained winds were recorded up to 120 miles per hour by Thursday evening, dropping down to about 110 mph an hour before expected landfall.
A storm surge of up to 4 to 6 feet was expected for Dauphin Island, and 4 to 8 inches of rain were expected across the southern part of Alabama.

title: Country singer Ella Langley cancels concert Friday. Here’s why
text:
TULSA, Okla. (CNN) — Country singer Ella Langley canceled her concert in Tulsa, Oklahoma, on Friday, citing what she called a “serious security threat.”
Langley announced the cancellation in a social media post.
The show had been scheduled at Tulsa’s BOK Center, and the cancellation came only hours before she was set to take the stage.
Langley wrote that the decision was made in coordination with local authorities, venue officials and her security team.
The 27-year-old said the move was not made lightly, but she refuses to “put anyone in harm’s way.”
Police said they conducted a security sweep and found no credible threat.
An official statement from Langley’s team said details on ticket refunds will be coming as soon as possible.
